title: CRA's prescribed interest rate stays at 3% for early 2027: what it means for you
description: The federal prescribed rate will stay at 3% from January 1 to March 31, 2027. Here's what that means for family loans, company loans and CRA interest.
text: The federal government has confirmed that the prescribed interest rate used for tax purposes will stay at 3% for the quarter starting January 1, 2027. That matters if you lend money to family members, borrow from your own corporation, or owe the CRA money. What happened The Department of Finance Canada publishes the rate the CRA uses for loans and interest calculations. Its page now says the rate for the quarter beginning January 1, 2027 is 3%, the same as for the current quarter (October 1 to December 31, 2026). The prescribed rate is reset every three months. It is based on the average yield on three-month Government of Canada Treasury bills in the first month of the previous quarter, rounded up to the next whole percentage point. The Treasury bill yields Finance Canada lists for October 2026 were just under 2.5%, which rounds up to 3%. This comes after the Bank of Canada raised its key rate to 2.5% on October 28, 2026 (see our article on the Bank's latest signals ). Short-term yields have not risen enough to push the prescribed rate up yet. What it means for you Family loans for income splitting Normally, if you give or lend money to your spouse or common-law partner and they invest it, the investment income is taxed back to you. These are called the attribution rules . The Income Tax Act makes an exception for a proper loan, as long as: the loan charges interest at least equal to the prescribed rate in effect when the loan was made (or a commercial rate, if lower), and the interest for each year is actually paid no later than 30 days after that year ends. Because the rate is locked in when the loan is made, a loan set up while the rate is 3% keeps that rate for as long as it is outstanding. With the rate unchanged until at least March 31, 2027, there is no year-end rush, but the rate can rise later if Treasury bill yields climb. If you already have a family loan, the interest for 2026 must be paid by January 30, 2027 . Missing that date, even once, means the attribution rules apply for that year and every later year of the loan. Interest the CRA charges and pays For October 1 to December 31, 2026, the CRA charges 7% on overdue personal and corporate taxes, CPP contributions and EI premiums, compounded daily. It pays 5% on refunds owed to individuals and 3% on refunds owed to corporations. The CRA's method adds four percentage points to the prescribed rate for overdue amounts, so an unchanged base rate points to the same charges in early 2027, but the CRA has not yet posted its full table for that quarter. Our tax instalments guide explains how instalment interest works. What it means for small businesses If your corporation lends money to an employee or a shareholder at little or no interest, the person may have a taxable benefit : extra income they must pay tax on. The CRA works it out quarter by quarter, using the prescribed rate for each quarter (3% for both late 2026 and early 2027), minus any interest the borrower actually paid during the year or within 30 days after it ends. For employees, the benefit goes on the T4 slip (code 36 in box 14), and income tax and CPP are withheld on it, but not EI. For shareholders, the benefit goes on a T4A slip (code 117). Under a CRA administrative policy, small, short employee loans are not taxed: $10,000 or less in total in a calendar year, for 60 days or less, and not received because the person is a shareholder. Shareholder loans also have other rules that can make the whole loan taxable if it isn't repaid in time. Our guide to paying yourself from a corporation covers them. What to do now If you have a family or spousal loan, diarize January 30, 2027 to pay the 2026 interest, and keep proof such as a bank transfer record. If you are thinking about a new prescribed-rate loan, put it in writing and set it up properly; the rate in effect on the day it is made is the one that counts. Business owners: list any loans to employees or shareholders so the 2026 benefit can be calculated and shown on T4 or T4A slips. If you owe the CRA, paying sooner limits daily compounding interest. Prescribed-rate loans and shareholder loans have strict rules, so check your own situation before acting.

title: Ottawa extends relief from counter-tariffs on U.S. goods to June 2028, with some cuts
description: Finance Canada extended tariff relief on many U.S. imports to June 30, 2028, widened it for some uses and is ending it for trailers, aluminum and paperboard.
text: On November 9, 2026, the Department of Finance Canada announced that relief from Canada's counter-tariffs on many goods imported from the United States will continue for another year, until June 30, 2028 . At the same time, the relief is being widened for some uses and removed for a few products that are also made in Canada. What happened Since 2025, Canada has charged extra duties, often called surtaxes or counter-tariffs, on a range of U.S. goods in response to U.S. tariffs. On September 8, 2026, Canada added further counter-tariffs of 15% to 50% on more U.S. products. To soften the blow for Canadian businesses that rely on U.S. inputs, the government offers remission , which means the surtax is waived or refunded. The broadest form is called horizontal remission : it applies to every importer, as long as the goods are used for certain purposes. It started on April 16, 2025, and has been extended and changed several times since. The November 9 changes are: One more year. Horizontal remission now runs to June 30, 2028. New eligible uses. Non-steel goods used in mining, quarrying or oil and gas extraction now qualify. All goods used by public education bodies now qualify too, including those mandated by Indigenous organizations. Relief ending for some products made in Canada. Certain trailers lose the relief on December 1, 2026. Certain aluminum wire and extrusions, and certain paperboard products, lose it on February 1, 2027. The government says the lead time is meant to let importers find other suppliers or apply for case-by-case relief. Targeted relief. Some goods in short supply in Canada, and some companies facing exceptional circumstances (such as contracts signed before the tariffs), are getting specific relief. Longer time to claim. Importers now have four years after the date of importation to make a remission claim, instead of two. Clearer product lists. Detailed product schedules will be posted on the Finance Canada website. Which goods qualify Under the current rules, horizontal relief covers U.S. goods imported for these end uses: goods used by certain public health, public safety, national security or public education organizations; non-steel goods used for manufacturing or processing, farming, packaging farm products, packaging food or drinks as part of manufacturing, or mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction. Products listed in Schedule 7 of the government's remission list stop being eligible on the expiry date shown there. That is how the trailer, aluminum and paperboard changes take effect. What it means for small businesses If you import from the U.S. and the goods go into something you make, grow or package, this relief can make a real difference to your costs. A few points to keep in mind: You don't apply to Finance Canada for horizontal relief. Instead, you must keep records showing the goods were actually used for an eligible purpose. Keep them ready in case the CBSA or Finance Canada asks. Resale isn't a listed use. Goods bought simply to resell, such as stock for a store, are not among the eligible uses listed above. Check your product list. If you buy trailers, aluminum wire or extrusions, or paperboard from U.S. suppliers, check whether your items are on the list losing relief, and plan for higher landed costs from December 1, 2026 or February 1, 2027. Budget for it. Higher import costs can squeeze margins. The Bank of Canada has noted that businesses plan to pass on more costs over the next year, as we covered in our November 11 article . What it means for you For most households, there is nothing to do. The changes mainly affect businesses that import. Over time, removing relief on some products could nudge prices up for goods made with them, but how much, if at all, will depend on suppliers. What to do now Review your 2025 and 2026 U.S. imports and how each item was used. If you paid surtax on goods that qualified, you now have up to four years from the import date to claim it back. Keep invoices, customs records and proof of how the goods were used (for example, production or job records) in one place. Talk to your customs broker about the product schedules and any special codes needed on your customs declarations. If a product you need is hard to get in Canada, you can ask Finance Canada for case-by-case remission. Its tariff relief page links to the request process. Record surtax paid and refunds received correctly in your books, so your cost of goods and GST records line up. Our GST/HST and PST guide covers the sales tax side. Tariff rules have changed often since 2025 and may change again, so check the Finance Canada pages below before making major purchasing decisions.

title: Bank of Canada says more rate hikes may be needed: what it means for borrowers
description: The Bank of Canada's October meeting summary says further increases could be needed. Here is what that means for mortgages, credit lines and savers.
text: On November 10, 2026, the Bank of Canada published a summary of the discussions behind its October rate increase. The main message: its leaders believe further increases could be needed , but they will decide one meeting at a time. Separately, on November 5 the Bank and the federal government renewed the Bank's 2% inflation target for another five years. What happened On October 28, 2026, the Bank raised its key interest rate from 2.25% to 2.5% , its first increase since 2023. We covered that decision in our earlier article . About two weeks after each decision, the Bank releases a "summary of deliberations", a plain account of what its six-member Governing Council weighed before deciding. This is the new information. According to the summary: The council considered holding rates steady. Members who leaned that way pointed out that inflation was concentrated in energy and energy-heavy services, that core inflation measures were near 2%, and that new US tariffs would slow the economy. The case for a hike won out. Oil prices were about US$35 a barrel higher than the Bank assumed in July, and markets expect them to stay high for longer. The council judged that the risk of high energy costs spreading into broad, lasting inflation had grown. Inflation is expected to stay above target for a while. Consumer prices have been rising at around 3% a year since April. The Bank expects inflation to reach about 3.5% by the end of 2026, stay above 3% for much of 2027 and return to 2% by mid-2028. Businesses expect to pass on more costs. So far, most higher costs (mainly fuel, but also some imported materials) have not reached store shelves. The Bank's surveys suggest businesses plan to pass on a larger share over the next year. The economy has held up. Growth was 3.3% (annual pace) in the second quarter and about 2% in the third. Unemployment has been around 6.5%. The Bank expects growth of about 1% for 2026, then about 2% in each of 2027 and 2028, although trade tension with the US is a risk. The Bank's position, in its own words, is that it will not let higher energy prices turn into "broad-based, persistent inflation". The 2% target stays The Bank and the Government of Canada renew their inflation agreement every five years. The new agreement, announced on November 5, 2026, keeps the target at 2% , in the middle of a 1% to 3% range, and runs from January 2027 to December 2031. In practice, this means the Bank will keep using interest rates to pull inflation back toward 2%, which is why it is willing to raise rates now. What it means for you Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit. These usually follow the Bank's rate through your lender's prime rate. Another increase would raise your interest cost again. If your budget is already tight, plan now for a possible further 0.25 percentage point rise. Fixed-rate mortgages. Nothing changes until renewal. If you renew in the next year, start comparing options early and ask your lender or broker how a higher rate would change your payment. Savers. Rates on savings accounts and GICs tend to rise when the Bank raises rates, so it may be worth checking what your bank is paying. Household budgets. With inflation expected to stay above 3% for much of 2027, prices for fuel and travel in particular may keep rising faster than usual. What it means for small businesses Floating-rate business loans and lines of credit could cost more if the Bank raises again. It is a good time to review your cash flow forecast for early 2027, pay down expensive debt where you can, and think about whether higher fuel and supply costs need to show up in your own prices. If you are planning a larger purchase of equipment, talk to your lender about locking in a rate. What to do now Check the rate and renewal date on your mortgage and any lines of credit. Work out what a further 0.25 percentage point increase would do to your monthly payment. Shop around for better interest on your savings. Keep an eye on the next rate decision on December 9, 2026 . We will explain what it means once it is announced. The Bank stresses that its outlook is uncertain, citing the war in the Middle East, Canada-US trade relations and global financial conditions. No further increase is certain, and nobody can say for sure where rates will go.

title: Budget 2026 proposes one May 15 tax deadline for everyone, starting with 2027 returns
description: Ottawa wants all individuals, including the self-employed, to file and pay by May 15, starting with 2027 returns. Nothing changes for your 2026 return.
text: The federal budget tabled on November 5, 2026 proposes a single May 15 deadline for both filing your personal tax return and paying any balance owing, including for self-employed people. It would start with the 2027 tax year, so the first returns affected would be filed in spring 2028. It is a proposal for now, and nothing changes for the 2026 return you will file next spring. We covered the budget's headline measures in our budget overview . Since then, the filing-deadline change has drawn a lot of questions, so here is a closer look, along with two related changes to the filing rules. What happened Right now, Canada has two personal tax deadlines that often confuse people: Most individuals must file their return and pay any balance owing by April 30 . Self-employed people, and their spouses or common-law partners, have until June 15 to file, but any tax they owe is still due April 30. Many miss that detail and end up paying interest. Budget 2026 proposes to replace both dates with May 15 as the single filing and payment due date for all individuals, including the self-employed and their spouses or partners. The budget's tax-measures document says this applies to the 2027 and later tax years. The government's reasoning is that an extra two weeks gives people, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), more time to receive and process tax slips such as T4s, T5s and T3s. That should mean fewer reassessments, when the CRA changes your return after the fact because a slip was missing. Finance Canada estimates Canadians would avoid about $230 million in interest and penalties over five years. What it means for you Your 2026 return (filed in 2027): no change. The usual rules apply: file and pay by April 30, or file by June 15 if you or your spouse are self-employed, with payment still due April 30. Your 2027 return (filed in 2028): if the measure becomes law, you would have until May 15 to file and pay. If you usually get a refund: a later deadline is only a deadline. You can still file as soon as the CRA opens online filing each year. If you are self-employed: you would lose about a month of filing time (May 15 instead of June 15) but gain about two weeks to pay. One date for both makes it harder to get caught by the payment deadline. Two related changes in the same budget The budget also proposes other changes that make filing simpler. Like the deadline, these are proposed and need Parliament to pass them. Higher threshold for reporting foreign property. Form T1135 reports investments and property held outside Canada, such as a bank account or fixed deposit in India. The filing threshold would rise from $100,000 to $200,000 of total cost, and the simpler reporting option would apply below $500,000 (up from $250,000). This would apply to tax years ending after 2026. Our guide to foreign income and the T1135 explains the current rules. Fewer people paying instalments, from 2028. Instalments are quarterly tax prepayments for people who don't have enough tax withheld at source. The threshold to have to pay them would rise from $3,000 to $7,500 of net tax owing (outside Quebec), indexed to inflation, for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2028. People whose main income is from a business could choose one payment by December 31 instead of four. Our new guide to tax instalments explains today's rules. What it means for small businesses The proposed May 15 date applies to personal (T1) returns, so it covers sole proprietors and partners who report business income on their own return. The budget documents we read describe no change to corporate tax deadlines or to the deadlines for issuing T4, T4A or T5 slips, so plan to issue slips on the usual schedule. What to do now Plan your 2026 return around the current dates. Self-employed? Set aside money to pay by April 30, even though you can file later. If you owe instalments for 2026, the last one is due December 15. See our December 15 instalment reminder . If you hold property outside Canada, keep filing the T1135 under the current $100,000 rule until the change becomes law. Watch for the budget legislation. We will report when these measures pass.

title: RDSP grants and bonds: contribute by December 31 to get 2026's government money
description: Families with an RDSP can get up to $3,500 in grants and $1,000 in bonds for 2026, but only for contributions made by December 31.
text: If you or someone in your family has a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP), December 31, 2026 is the last day to put money in and have it count for this year's government grant. The federal government can add up to $3,500 in grants and $1,000 in bonds for 2026, and many families leave some of that on the table. What is an RDSP? An RDSP is a long-term savings plan for a person who is approved for the disability tax credit (DTC). The person the plan is for is called the beneficiary . The plan holder (often a parent for a child) opens it at a bank or credit union, and anyone can contribute with the holder's written permission. Contributions are not tax-deductible, but the money grows inside the plan without yearly tax. The real attraction is the free government money that comes with it: Canada Disability Savings Grant: the government matches your contributions. Canada Disability Savings Bond: extra money for lower-income families, paid even if you contribute nothing. To open a plan, the beneficiary must be a resident of Canada with a Social Insurance Number, be approved for the DTC, and apply before December 31 of the year they turn 59. If you are not sure whether you qualify for the DTC, our guide to often-missed tax credits explains how it works. How much the government adds for 2026 The grant depends on family income. For 2026, Employment and Social Development Canada uses income from the 2024 tax return: Family income of $117,045 or less: the government adds $3 for each of the first $500 you contribute, then $2 for each of the next $1,000. Contributing $1,500 in the year gets the maximum grant of $3,500. Family income above $117,045: the government matches $1 for $1 on up to $1,000, so contributing $1,000 gets a $1,000 grant. The bond needs no contribution at all: Family income of $38,237 or less: the full $1,000 bond. Between $38,237 and $58,523: a smaller bond that shrinks as income rises. $58,523 or more: no bond. There are lifetime limits of $70,000 in grants, $20,000 in bonds and $200,000 in total contributions. Grants and bonds stop after December 31 of the year the beneficiary turns 49. Why December 31 matters The grant is based on what you put in during the calendar year. Unlike an RRSP, there is no extra 60-day window in the new year. A contribution made on January 2, 2027 counts toward 2027, not 2026. This matters most in two situations: The beneficiary turns 49 in 2026. Only contributions made by December 31, 2026 can earn a grant. After that, no more grants or bonds are paid, although the plan can stay open. You haven't contributed yet this year. If you skip a year, you can usually catch up later, but the rules have limits (see below), and the money starts growing later. Catching up on missed years If the beneficiary was eligible for the DTC in earlier years but you didn't contribute, unused grant and bond entitlements from the past 10 years can be carried forward. While you are catching up, the grant can be as high as $10,500 in one year, and a new plan can receive up to $11,000 in bonds (up to $1,000 for each eligible year in the last 10, plus the current year). Catch-up grants still need contributions; catch-up bonds don't. The 10-year window keeps moving, so entitlement from the oldest year drops off each year you wait. What it means for families File tax returns every year. Grants and bonds are based on family income from filed returns. For a child under 18, that's the parents' or guardians' returns. The CRA says the beneficiary should start filing their own returns in the year they turn 17 so the amounts stay correct when the income test switches to their own income. Think long term. If you withdraw money, you generally have to pay back $3 of grants and bonds received in the previous 10 years for every $1 you take out (up to the total received in those 10 years). Closing the plan triggers full repayment of that 10-year amount. An RDSP works best as money left alone for the future. What to do now Check that the beneficiary's DTC approval is in place. Without it, no new contributions, grants or bonds are allowed. Look at your RDSP statement or ask your financial institution how much has gone in for 2026 so far. If your family income is $117,045 or less, aim for $1,500 by December 31; above that, $1,000 gets the full matching grant. Don't leave it to the last week of December: banks need time to process deposits before year end. Make sure everyone whose income counts has filed their 2024 and 2025 returns. If you haven't opened an RDSP yet but the beneficiary qualifies, opening one now also starts the bond and catch-up process. Ask us if you'd like help checking DTC eligibility or filing missed returns.

title: CCB, CPP and OAS payment dates for November and December 2026
description: The last 2026 benefit deposits: CCB and B.C. family benefit on Nov. 20 and Dec. 11, CPP and OAS on Nov. 26 and Dec. 22, and what to do if one is late.
text: Two more Canada child benefit payments, two more CPP and Old Age Security deposits and two Canada Disability Benefit payments are left in 2026, and the December dates come earlier than usual because of the holidays. Here is the schedule for the rest of the year, taken from the federal government's official payment calendars, plus what to do if a payment doesn't show up. What happened The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Service Canada publish their payment dates in advance. With the year winding down, the remaining dates for 2026 are now the ones that matter. December payments are generally earlier in the month than you might expect, so plan holiday spending around the real deposit date, not the usual one. Payment dates for the rest of 2026 Benefit November 2026 December 2026 Canada Disability Benefit November 19 December 17 Canada child benefit (CCB), including the B.C. family benefit November 20 December 11 Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and Old Age Security (OAS) November 26 December 22 Veterans disability pension November 27 December 23 The official calendars do not list any Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit payment (the benefit that replaced the GST/HST credit in July 2026) or advanced Canada workers benefit payment in November or December. The last scheduled payments for both were in October 2026, and the government has not yet posted its 2027 dates. If you were expecting one of these in the next few weeks, nothing is missing. What it means for families in B.C. If you get the CCB for a child under 18, the B.C. family benefit is added to the same monthly deposit. You don't apply for it separately: once your child is registered for the CCB and you (and your spouse or partner) have filed your tax returns, the CRA works out the amount automatically. For July 2026 to June 2027, the B.C. family benefit is up to $1,750 a year for a first child, $1,100 for a second child and $900 for each additional child, according to the B.C. government. That is about $145.83 a month for a first child. The amount is based on your 2025 adjusted family net income. Families with income below $30,176 receive the maximum; the amount is reduced above that. If you share custody, each parent gets half the amount for that child. Our guide to the Canada child benefit and B.C. family benefits explains how these amounts are calculated and who qualifies. What it means for seniors CPP and OAS are paid on the same day each month. The December deposit lands on December 22, 2026 , a few days before Christmas. If you are retired or helping a parent manage their money, our retirement income guide covers how CPP, OAS and RRIF withdrawals are taxed. If a payment doesn't arrive Payments can take a few days to reach your account, and cheques take longer than direct deposit. Before you call: Wait. For the CCB, the CRA asks you to wait 5 working days after the payment date. For other programs, the federal calendar suggests waiting 5 to 10 business days. Check your online account. For the CCB and B.C. family benefit, your CRA account shows the status of your payments. For CPP and OAS, check with Service Canada. Check your information is current. A new address, a change in marital status or a child moving out can pause or change payments. If you move out of B.C., tell the CRA promptly so you don't receive B.C. family benefit payments you would later have to pay back. What to do now Sign up for direct deposit if you still get cheques. Cheques can take longer to arrive than direct deposit, especially with holiday mail. Make sure both you and your spouse or partner have filed your 2025 tax returns. Benefits like the CCB and B.C. family benefit stop or shrink when a return is missing. Mark the early December dates in your calendar: December 11 for the CCB and December 22 for CPP and OAS. Keep an eye on 2027. Budget 2026 proposed a one-time extra grocery benefit payment in early 2027; our Budget 2026 article explains it. We will share the 2027 payment calendar once the government publishes it.

title: Canada's unemployment rate rises to 6.7% in October: what it means for you
description: Canada's jobless rate rose to 6.7% in October as hiring stalled, while B.C. added 12,000 jobs. What it means for workers, borrowers and small businesses.
text: Statistics Canada reported on November 6, 2026 that Canada's unemployment rate rose to 6.7% in October, up from 6.5% in September. The number of jobs barely moved, but British Columbia bucked the trend and added about 12,000 jobs. What happened Each month, Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey measures how many people are working and how many are looking for work. Here are the October highlights: Jobs: employment slipped by 4,700, which is essentially no change. That follows losses of 68,000 jobs in September and 42,000 in August. Unemployment rate: up 0.2 percentage points to 6.7%, the second increase in a row. It is still a little lower than a year ago and below the April 2026 peak of 6.9%. Employment rate (the share of adults who have a job): down to 60.5%, its third monthly decline in a row. Wages: average hourly pay was $37.89, up 2.2% from a year earlier. Young people: unemployment for ages 15 to 24 jumped to 13.7%. Longer job searches: 23.7% of unemployed people had been looking for 27 weeks or more, up from 21.5% a year earlier. The private sector lost 53,000 jobs, while public-sector jobs rose by 50,000. Wholesale and retail trade shed 29,000 positions, and construction and education added jobs. What it means in B.C. B.C. was one of the brighter spots. Employment rose by 12,000 (0.4%) after a drop of 20,000 in September, and the province's unemployment rate was 6.3%, little changed from the month before and below the national rate. Statistics Canada's monthly release doesn't break out figures for Metro Vancouver. What it means for you The picture is a softening job market rather than a sharp downturn: layoffs were still low (0.7% of workers), but people who lose a job are taking longer to find a new one. If you lose your job, apply for Employment Insurance (EI) right away. EI regular benefits generally pay 55% of your average insurable weekly earnings, up to a maximum of $729 a week in 2026. EI benefits are taxable, so keep the slip you receive for your tax return. If you get severance pay, the CRA treats it as a retiring allowance . Your employer deducts income tax on a lump sum (no CPP or EI). Ask before you sign whether part of it can go straight into your RRSP: depending on your years of service and your unused RRSP room, a direct transfer can reduce the tax taken off now. If you have a variable-rate mortgage or line of credit, remember the Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% on October 28, 2026. A weaker job market is one of the things the Bank weighs, so this report adds to the uncertainty about its next move. See our article on the October rate increase . What it means for small businesses A slower job market can make hiring a little easier, but it can also mean customers spend more carefully, especially in retail, where jobs fell most in October. If you plan to hire for the busy holiday season, our guide to hiring your first employee in B.C. covers payroll accounts, deductions and WorkSafeBC. If you need to let someone go, issue their Record of Employment promptly so they can apply for EI. What to do now Build or top up an emergency fund if your job or income feels less secure. If you were laid off this year, set money aside for tax on EI or severance, since the tax withheld may not cover your full bill. Borrowers: check what your payment would be if rates rise again before your renewal. Watch for the next two data points: the Bank of Canada's rate decision on December 9, 2026, and the November jobs report on December 4, 2026.

title: Federal Budget 2026: grocery benefit top-up, refundable caregiver credit and more
description: Budget 2026 keeps tax rates the same but proposes a one-time grocery benefit boost, a refundable caregiver credit and an 'RRSP for life'.
text: The federal government tabled Budget 2026 on November 5, 2026. It does not change personal or corporate income tax rates, but it proposes a one-time boost to the grocery benefit, a refundable caregiver credit, a bigger workers benefit, a new GST/HST exemption for massage therapy and a plan to drop the age-71 RRSP deadline. Here is what matters for families and small businesses in Metro Vancouver. What happened The government projects a deficit of $62.3 billion for 2026-27, falling to $52.9 billion by 2030-31. Remember that a budget is a plan: most of the tax changes below are proposed and only become law once Parliament passes the legislation. Some start right away; others start in 2027. What it means for you Extra grocery benefit payment in early 2027. The Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit gets a one-time supplement equal to a 50% top-up of the 2026-27 benefit. Finance Canada says this means up to $339 for a single person without children and up to $679 for a couple with two children. You don't apply: it is based on your tax return, so make sure you have filed. Caregiver credit becomes refundable. The Canada Caregiver Credit, for people who support a family member with a physical or mental impairment, would become refundable starting with the 2027 tax year. "Refundable" means you get the full value even if you owe little or no tax. Finance Canada puts the benefit at up to $1,260 a year. Bigger benefit for lower-income workers. The Canada Workers Benefit would be renamed the Build Canada Workers Benefit from 2027. The maximum would rise from $1,709 to $1,859 for single people without children and from $2,943 to $3,143 for families, and you would start qualifying once you earn $500 (down from $3,000). The trade-off: advance payments shrink to 25% of the 2026 amount in 2027 and end in 2028, so more of the benefit would arrive when you file. An "RRSP for life". Today an RRSP has to be wound up by the end of the year you turn 71, usually by converting it to a RRIF. The government wants to combine the two so there is no forced conversion at 71, though minimum withdrawals would still apply. This is only a consultation (submissions are due January 8, 2027), so nothing changes yet. If you or a parent turn 71 this year, the current deadline still applies; see our article on the turning-71 RRSP deadline and our retirement income guide . More time to object. If you disagree with a CRA assessment, the deadline to file an objection would become one year after the notice of assessment, or two years from your filing due date if that is later. This would apply once the law passes. Volunteer firefighters and search and rescue. The two separate 14% credits would merge into one from 2027, and hours from both kinds of service would count toward the 200-hour minimum. What it means for small businesses Massage therapy exempt from GST/HST. Services by qualifying massage therapists (licensed or certified where the province requires it) become exempt for supplies made after November 5, 2026. If you are a registered massage therapist, talk to your accountant soon about how this affects your invoices, your GST/HST registration and the input tax credits you claim on business costs. Our GST and PST guide explains how this works. Tax debts and your credit report. The CRA would be allowed to report income tax or GST/HST debts over $50,000 to credit bureaus, but only once all objection and appeal rights are used up or expired, and only after 30 days' written notice and a chance to set up a payment plan. Canada Growth Incentive. Individuals who invest in qualifying new shares of Canadian businesses issued on or after November 5, 2026 could shelter up to $15 million of capital gains, with holding-period rules and many excluded sectors (including professional practices, real estate and food and accommodation). A related rollover for reinvested small-business gains is extended from January 1, 2027. Artists. Employed artists could deduct expenses up to the full amount of their artistic employment income (instead of 20%) from 2027. What to do now File any missing tax returns so you receive the early-2027 grocery benefit supplement and other benefits automatically. If you care for a family member, keep records now: the refundable credit would apply to your 2027 return. Massage therapists should review their GST/HST registration and invoicing from November 6, 2026 onward. Don't change your year-end plans on the strength of proposals alone. We will report when these measures become law.

title: Holiday gifts and parties for staff: how to keep them tax-free in 2026
description: Planning gifts or a holiday party for your team? Here are the CRA's $500 gift rule, $150 party limit and gift card conditions, explained.
text: Many small businesses thank their staff in December with a gift, a gift card or a party. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) lets you do this tax-free for employees, but only if you stay within a few clear limits. Here is what to check before you buy or book. Why this matters now The rules haven't changed, but this is the season when they matter most. The CRA's policies on gifts, awards and social events are set out on its payroll pages, last updated in 2025 and 2026. A taxable benefit is something of value an employer gives an employee that has to be added to the employee's income on their T4 slip. If you stay inside the CRA's limits, a gift or party is not a taxable benefit and you have nothing extra to report. Separately, the federal government is tabling Budget 2026 on November 5, 2026. We will cover any changes it announces in a separate article. Gifts: the $500 rule Non-cash gifts and awards are tax-free if their total value, including taxes, is $500 or less per employee for the year . There is no limit on the number of items. Anything above $500 is taxable. For example, if you give an employee gifts worth $650 in a year, $150 is a taxable benefit. Small items such as coffee, T-shirts, mugs, plaques and trophies don't count toward the $500. Cash and near-cash gifts are always taxable , whatever the amount. Near-cash means things that work like cash, such as securities, precious metals and gift cards that don't meet the CRA's conditions. A reward for job performance, such as hitting a sales target, is always taxable. The $500 rule covers gifts for special occasions (such as a holiday or birthday) and awards for overall contribution to the workplace. Gift cards: three conditions A gift card counts as a non-cash gift (and can fit inside the $500 limit) only if all of these are true: it can only be used at one store, or at a group of stores named on the card, its terms say the balance can't be turned into cash, and you keep a log showing the employee's name, the date, the reason, the type of card, the amount and the store or stores. A general prepaid card that works almost anywhere may not qualify. If a card fails these tests, it is treated as near-cash and is fully taxable. Holiday parties: the $150 rule An in-person holiday party or other social event is not a taxable benefit if: it is open to all employees (a whole branch or division counts), it costs $150 or less per person, including taxes , where spouses and common-law partners who attend count as persons, and it is within the limit of six employer-paid social events a year. Taxi rides home and overnight hotel rooms for people attending are left out of the $150 count. If the cost goes over $150 per person, the whole amount becomes taxable, not just the part above $150. The CRA gives a simple example: a party costing $16,500 for 100 people works out to $165 per person, so each employee has a $165 benefit (or $330 if their spouse also came). For virtual events, the CRA's limit is $50 per employee for meals, drinks and delivery, or $100 if entertainment is included. What it means for small businesses Owners and family are different. Gifts to relatives, shareholders and other people who aren't at arm's length are outside the CRA's gift policy, so their full value is taxable. Your deduction. Normally only 50% of food, drink and entertainment costs can be deducted. The Income Tax Act makes an exception for up to six special events in a calendar year where the food or entertainment is generally available to all employees at a place of business. If a gift is taxable, you must add it to the employee's pay for that period, withhold income tax and CPP, and report it on the T4. For cash gifts, you also deduct EI. Our guide to hiring your first employee in B.C. explains payroll deductions and T4 slips in more detail. What to do now Add up what each employee has already received this year before buying more gifts. Choose physical gifts or store-specific gift cards instead of cash or general prepaid cards. Start a gift card log now, with all six details the CRA asks for. Budget your party at $150 per person or less, including taxes and partners, and invite everyone. Keep receipts and a guest count so you can show the cost per person if asked. A little planning means your team gets the full value of your thank-you, without a surprise on their T4.

title: Turning 71 in 2026? Your RRSP must be wound up by December 31
description: If you turn 71 this year, December 31, 2026 is your last day to contribute to your RRSP and to choose a RRIF, an annuity or cash.
text: If you turn 71 at any point in 2026, you have until December 31, 2026 to make your last RRSP contribution and to decide what happens to the savings in your registered retirement savings plan (RRSP). With about eight weeks left, now is a good time to call your bank or advisor so the paperwork isn't rushed into the holidays. What happened Nothing new has changed here. This is a fixed deadline set by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) rules: December 31 of the year you turn 71 is the last day you can contribute to your own RRSP. By the same date, you must pick one of three options for the money already in the plan. People born in 1955 reach 71 this year, so this deadline applies to them. The federal budget is scheduled for November 5, 2026 . If it announces anything that changes these rules, we'll cover it in a follow-up article. Your three options The CRA lists three choices for your RRSPs in the year you turn 71: Transfer to a RRIF. A registered retirement income fund (RRIF) is the usual choice. Your investments can stay invested, and the transfer itself is not taxed. You pay tax only on the money you take out each year, and you report it on your return for that year. Buy an annuity. An annuity is a contract, usually with an insurance company, that pays you a set income, often for life. No tax is withheld when your RRSP money is used to buy one. Take it as cash. The whole amount becomes taxable income in the year you withdraw it. Your financial institution withholds some tax (between 10% and 30% outside Quebec, depending on the amount), but the CRA notes this may not cover all the tax you owe. For most people with sizable savings, this is the costliest choice. You can also mix these, for example moving most of your savings to a RRIF and using part to buy an annuity. Ask your financial institution to do the move as a direct transfer so no tax is taken off. How RRIF withdrawals work Once your money is in a RRIF, you must take out at least a minimum amount each year. Here is how it works, based on the CRA's rules: There is no minimum in the year you open the RRIF . If you convert in 2026, your first required withdrawal is in 2027. The minimum is the RRIF's value at the start of the year multiplied by a factor set by your age on January 1. The factor is 5.28% at age 71, 5.40% at 72 and 5.53% at 73, rising each year after that. You can take more than the minimum, but not less. You can choose to base the minimum on your spouse's or common-law partner's age instead. If your partner is younger, this lowers the minimum. You must make this choice before you receive your first RRIF payment, and you can't change it later. Illustration only: if you are 71 on January 1, 2027 and your RRIF is worth $200,000 on that date, your minimum for 2027 is $200,000 × 5.28% = $10,560. What it means for you Make any last contribution by December 31. The usual 60-day window in the new year does not help you after the year you turn 71, because you can't contribute to your own RRSP after that year ends. Have a younger spouse? You can still contribute to a spousal RRSP until the end of the year your spouse or common-law partner turns 71, if you have RRSP room. You get the deduction; the money belongs to their plan. Still repaying the Home Buyers' Plan? You can't make repayments after the year you turn 71. You can repay the rest this year; otherwise, the unpaid balance is spread over your remaining repayment years and added to your income each year. Tax credits and splitting. RRIF income received at 65 or older can qualify for the pension income amount, and it can be split with your spouse on your tax return. Our new guide to retirement income explains how this works with OAS and CPP, including the OAS clawback. What to do now Check your birth year. If you were born in 1955, this deadline is yours. Also check any spousal RRSP or group RRSP at work. Call each institution where you hold an RRSP and ask how they handle the conversion and by what date they need your instructions. Decide whether to base RRIF payments on your own age or a younger partner's age before the first payment. Ask how often payments can be made and whether to have tax withheld. Tax is withheld on amounts above the minimum, but you may want more taken off so you don't owe a lump sum at tax time. Make any final RRSP or spousal RRSP contribution, or Home Buyers' Plan repayment, before December 31, 2026. A RRIF and an annuity each have trade-offs, and the right mix depends on your other income, your health and your family. If you're unsure, it's worth getting advice before your institution's cut-off date.

title: Paying tax by instalments? Your last 2026 payment is due December 15
description: The final 2026 income tax instalment is due Tuesday, December 15. Here's who has to pay, how to check your amount and how to avoid CRA interest.
text: If you are self-employed, earn rental income or have a pension or investment income with little tax taken off, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) may expect you to pay your 2026 tax in instalments. The fourth and final instalment for 2026 is due on Tuesday, December 15, 2026 , and the CRA currently charges 7% interest, compounded daily, on amounts that are paid late or short. What is a tax instalment? An instalment is a partial payment of the current year's income tax, made during the year instead of in one lump sum at tax time. Employees rarely need it, because tax comes off every paycheque. For most individuals, 2026 instalments are due on March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15. If your main income comes from farming or fishing, you have a single due date of December 31 instead, and the CRA sends that reminder in November. Who has to pay For 2026, you have to pay by instalments if both of these are true: your net tax owing for 2026 (roughly, the tax left to pay when you file, after tax already withheld) is more than $3,000 ($1,800 if you live in Quebec on December 31), and your net tax owing was also more than that amount in either 2025 or 2024. The CRA sends instalment reminders to people it expects will need to pay. The February reminder covers the March and June payments, and the August reminder covers September and December. A reminder is not a bill. If you are confident your 2026 net tax owing will be $3,000 or less, the CRA says you don't have to pay 2026 instalments, even if you received a reminder. The catch is that if your estimate turns out to be wrong, you may owe interest. Three ways to work out your amount The CRA offers three options: No-calculation option: pay the amounts printed on your CRA reminders. These are based on your most recent assessed return. The CRA says this suits people whose income, deductions and credits stay about the same each year. Prior-year option: base your payments on your 2025 return, using the CRA's 2026 instalment calculation chart. This can work well if 2026 looks like 2025 but 2024 was quite different. Current-year option: estimate your actual 2026 tax, CPP contributions and any voluntary EI premiums, and pay based on that. This helps if your income dropped this year, but if your estimate is too low you can be charged interest. If you choose the prior-year or current-year option and pay the full amounts by each due date, the CRA will not charge instalment interest or a penalty, unless your estimated amounts were too low. What happens if you pay late or too little Instalment interest is charged at the CRA's prescribed rate and compounded daily. For October 1 to December 31, 2026, that rate is 7%. You are only charged if the interest for the year is more than $25. A separate penalty applies only if your instalment interest for 2026 is more than $1,000. In that case, the penalty is half of the amount by which your interest exceeds the greater of $1,000 or 25% of the interest you would have owed if you had made no instalments at all. There is some good news if you missed or underpaid an earlier 2026 instalment. The CRA says paying your next instalment early, or paying more than required, earns credit interest that can offset the interest on the late or short payment for the same year. This credit can't be refunded or carried to another year. What to do now Check your August reminder in your CRA account to see the amount the CRA suggests for December. Compare it with your 2026 reality. If your self-employment, rental or investment income changed a lot this year, a quick estimate of your 2026 tax may show you can pay less, or that you should pay more. Pay early enough. The CRA counts the date your payment is received, not the date you sent it. It suggests allowing 3 business days for online payments to show up, and 10 business days for cheques or money orders, before checking that a payment was processed. Use the right account. When paying in person or by mail, use your instalment remittance voucher (form INNS3) so the money goes to your instalment account, not to an older tax debt. Keep proof of payment until it shows in your CRA account or on the instalment summary the CRA sends in February. Think ahead to 2027. If you receive OAS or CPP, you can ask Service Canada to withhold tax from those payments (forms ISP3520OAS and ISP3520CPP), which can reduce or remove the need for instalments. What it means for small-business owners If you run a business as a sole proprietor, your business profit is part of your personal return, so these personal instalment rules apply to you. Your instalments also cover CPP contributions on self-employment income. Corporations follow separate instalment rules. For more on reducing your tax bill as a self-employed person or landlord, see our guides to self-employed expenses and deductions and rental income tax . Our year-end tax checklist covers other steps to take before December 31.

title: Moved from Canada to India this year? Your Canadian tax to-do list
description: Leaving Canada for India in 2026? Here's what to file with the CRA: your final return, departure tax forms, and what happens to your accounts and benefits.
text: If you moved from Canada to India for good in 2026, Canada still expects one more tax return from you: a "final" return for the part of the year you lived here. Are you an "emigrant" for tax purposes? Moving away is not enough on its own. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) treats you as an emigrant when you leave to live in another country and cut your residential ties here. Examples include giving up your Canadian home for a permanent home in India, your spouse or children leaving with you, and closing down your personal and social ties in Canada. Your date of departure usually falls on the latest of these dates: the day you left Canada, the day your spouse or common-law partner and dependants left, or the day you became a resident of India. If you kept strong ties (for example, your family stayed in Canada), you may still be a resident of Canada and the rules in this article may not apply. If you are unsure, the CRA's Form NR73, Determination of Residency Status (leaving Canada) , lets you ask the CRA for its view. What to do now: your final Canadian return For a 2026 move, your final return is the 2026 return. Non-residents file by April 30 of the following year (June 15 if you or your spouse carried on a business), and any balance owing is due by April 30. For a 2026 move, that means April 30, 2027. Use the right package. File using the tax package for the province you lived in on your departure date, for example British Columbia. Enter your departure date on page 1, in the "Residence Information" area. Report world income for the resident part of the year. That means everything you earned anywhere, including in India, from January 1 to your departure date, converted to Canadian dollars. After departure, report only certain Canadian income, such as Canadian employment income. Other Canadian income, such as dividends or pensions, is usually taxed through withholding instead (see below). Credits may be limited for a part-year resident, and moving expenses to India are generally not deductible. The "departure tax" When you emigrate, Canada treats you as if you sold most of your property at its fair market value on the day you left, and bought it back right away. Any increase in value becomes a capital gain on your final return, even though you sold nothing. Common examples are shares and mutual funds held outside registered plans. Some property is not caught by this rule, including: Canadian real estate, such as a condo you keep and rent out, RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, RESPs, RDSPs and pension plans, and for newer Canadians: property you already owned when you arrived (or inherited after), if you lived in Canada for 60 months or less in the 10 years before leaving. The forms to know: Form T1243 calculates the gains or losses from the deemed sale. Form T1161 , List of Properties by an Emigrant of Canada , is required if everything you owned when you left was worth more than $25,000 . Cash, bank deposits, registered plans and personal items worth less than $10,000 each are left off the list. It is due by your filing due date, even if you don't otherwise need to file. Filing late can cost $25 a day, up to $2,500. Form T1244 lets you put off paying the departure tax, without interest, until you actually sell. It must be filed by April 30 of the year after you leave. If the federal tax being deferred is more than $16,500, the CRA will ask for security, so contact it before that date. Your accounts and benefits after you leave Tell your Canadian bank and other payers you are now a non-resident living in India. Withholding tax. Canadian pensions, CPP benefits, RRSP and RRIF withdrawals, dividends and rent paid to non-residents usually have 25% tax withheld, unless the Canada–India tax treaty lowers the rate. Interest from an arm's-length payer is generally exempt. Renting out your Canadian home? You can choose to file a separate return under section 216 to pay tax on your net rental income, which may get you a refund of some withholding. TFSA: you can keep it and it stays tax-free in Canada, but you cannot contribute while a non-resident and you won't get new room. FHSA: you can keep it, but you cannot make a tax-free withdrawal to buy a home while you are a non-resident. Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan balances: special repayment rules apply when you leave, so check these before you file. Benefits stop. Non-residents are generally not eligible for the Canada child benefit or the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which replaced the GST/HST credit in July 2026. Tell the CRA your departure date. If payments keep arriving, contact the CRA right away. A checklist before April 30, 2027 Keep proof of your departure date (ticket, home sale or lease end, Indian address). Update your address and residency status with the CRA and your Canadian financial institutions. Get fair market values for your investments as of your departure date. File your 2026 final return, with Forms T1161, T1243 and T1244 if they apply. Remember that India has its own residency and filing rules for your income there.

title: New to Canada in 2026? Your first-year tax and benefits checklist
description: Moved to Canada this year? How to apply for benefits now, file your first return by April 30, 2027, and handle property and income from abroad.
text: Welcome to Canada! If you became a resident in 2026, your first Canadian tax return is due by April 30, 2027. You don't have to wait until then to start: you can apply for family benefits as soon as you arrive. Here is what to do and what to watch for in your first year. When you become a resident for tax purposes For tax purposes, what matters is your ties to Canada, not your immigration status. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) looks mainly at whether you have a home, a spouse or common-law partner, and dependants here. For most newcomers, tax residency starts on the first day they live in Canada. The CRA calls that first year your "newcomer year". If your situation is unclear, for example you still keep a home abroad, Form NR74, Determination of Residency Status (entering Canada) , lets you ask the CRA for its view. What to do now Get a Social Insurance Number (SIN) from Service Canada. It goes on your tax return. If you can't get one, the CRA can give you a temporary tax number. Apply for benefits right away. You don't need to file a return first: No children: Form RC151, to apply for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which replaced the GST/HST credit in July 2026. Children under 18: Form RC66, Canada Child Benefit Application , with Form RC66SCH, Status in Canada and Income Information . The CCB application also covers the groceries benefit. Spouse still abroad: Form CTB9 reports their income for the CCB. Report your income from before you arrived. The CRA asks for your world income for up to two years before you became a resident, plus your spouse's. Canada doesn't tax this income, but it uses it to work out your benefits. Write down what your assets were worth when you arrived (see below). Benefits can be meaningful. The CRA lists the CCB at up to $7,997 a year for each child under 6 and up to $6,748 for each child aged 6 to 17. The groceries benefit is up to $679 a year for a single person. Temporary residents may have to wait until their 19th month in Canada to receive the CCB. Your first tax return Your 2026 return is due April 30, 2027 . If you or your spouse are self-employed, you have until June 15, 2027 to file, but any tax owing is still due April 30. File even if you earned little or nothing, because the CRA uses your return to calculate your benefits. Enter your date of arrival on page 1, in the "Residence information" area. Income after you arrive: report your world income, meaning money from inside and outside Canada (for example, rent or interest still coming from India), converted to Canadian dollars. Income before you arrive: report only certain Canadian income, such as pay for work done in Canada. Credits are pro-rated. Most credits, including the basic personal amount, are reduced by the share of the year you lived here. The CRA's example: someone resident for 240 days gets about 240/365 of the full amount. Avoid double tax. If income from abroad is taxed in both countries, you may be able to claim a foreign tax credit on Form T2209. Canada has tax treaties with many countries to prevent double taxation. Property you brought with you When you become a resident, Canada treats most property you already own, such as shares, mutual funds or valuable collections, as if you bought it at its fair market value on your arrival date. That value becomes your cost for Canadian tax. If you sell later, you are taxed only on growth after you arrived. Keep a statement or valuation showing what each asset was worth on that date. Without it, proving your cost can be hard. Foreign property reporting (Form T1135) Canadian residents who own foreign assets costing more than $100,000 in total at any time in a year must file Form T1135. That includes foreign bank accounts, shares of foreign companies and rental property abroad. Personal-use property, such as a holiday home you mainly use yourself, is not included. The good news: the CRA confirms you don't file Form T1135 for the year you first become a resident. From your second year onward, though, it is due with your return, and the penalties for missing it can be significant. Savings accounts: RRSP and TFSA TFSA: you start earning room on the day you become a resident, if you are 18 or older. The 2026 limit is $7,000. You don't get room for years before you arrived. RRSP: if 2026 is your first Canadian return, you generally can't deduct RRSP contributions for 2026. Your Canadian earned income in 2026 creates room for later years, and the CRA shows it on your notice of assessment. Keep records and watch for scams Keep your notice of assessment and supporting documents for at least six years. You will often need them for mortgages, loans and sponsorship or citizenship applications. The CRA warns that scammers target newcomers. The real CRA will never demand payment by gift card, cryptocurrency or e-transfer, and will never threaten arrest or deportation.

title: Year-end tax checklist: what to do before December 31, 2026
description: Some tax moves only count for 2026 if they happen by December 31. Here's a plain checklist for donations, FHSAs, TFSAs, investment losses and RRSPs.
text: With two months left in the year, now is a good time to check a few tax moves that only count for 2026 if you make them by December 31, 2026 . Here is a short, plain checklist for individuals and families in Metro Vancouver. Why December 31 matters Several savings and tax-credit rules work on the calendar year, so a step taken on January 2 can land on next year's return instead. The federal government has also scheduled its 2026 budget for November 5, 2026 . Budgets can announce new tax measures, so check back after budget day; we'll explain anything that affects this checklist. What it means for you Charitable donations Gifts to a registered charity made by December 31 can be claimed on your 2026 return. A few points worth knowing: You can claim donations from the previous five years that you haven't claimed yet. Spouses and common-law partners can combine their donations on one return. You need an official receipt from a registered charity or other qualified donee. Keep receipts for six years. Our guide to often-missed tax credits covers this and other credits people forget. First home savings account (FHSA) An FHSA lets first-time buyers save for a home with a tax deduction for contributions. Unlike an RRSP, the FHSA has no 60-day window after year end: contributions must be made between January 1 and December 31 to count for that year. Your contribution room starts in the year you open your first FHSA, at $8,000 a year, up to a lifetime total of $40,000 . Unused room can carry forward, but only up to $8,000. So opening an account before December 31 starts your room this year, even if you don't put money in yet. You don't have to deduct a contribution in the year you make it. You can save the deduction for a later year when your income is higher. Tax-free savings account (TFSA) If you plan to take money out of a TFSA soon, timing matters. Amounts you withdraw are added back to your contribution room only on January 1 of the next year . Withdrawing in December rather than January means you get that room back a full year sooner. Don't put withdrawn money back in the same year unless you are sure you have room. Over-contributions are taxed at 1% a month while the excess stays in the account. Selling investments at a loss Some investors sell shares or funds that have dropped in value before year end, to use the loss against capital gains. Watch the superficial loss rule: if you, your spouse or partner, or a corporation either of you controls buys the same investment within 30 days before or after the sale, and still holds it 30 days after, the loss can't be claimed (it is usually added to the cost of the shares bought back instead). A net capital loss can be carried back three years using Form T1A, or forward with no time limit. Our new capital gains guide explains how gains and losses are taxed. RRSP The RRSP dollar limit is $33,810 for 2026 and $35,390 for 2027 , according to the CRA. Your own limit depends on your income and past contributions, so it may be lower. Unlike the FHSA, contributions made in the first 60 days of 2027 can still be deducted on your 2026 return, so the RRSP isn't a December 31 deadline for most people. What to do now Make planned donations by December 31 and keep the receipts. If you're a first-time buyer, consider opening an FHSA before year end. Time any TFSA withdrawals for December if you'll want to re-contribute early next year. Before selling investments at a loss, check what you, your spouse and your company bought in the 30 days around the sale. Watch for the federal budget on November 5, 2026, in case new measures change your plans. Everyone's situation is different, so check the numbers for your own case before acting.

title: 2027 CPP and EI numbers: lower base CPP rate, higher earnings ceilings
description: CPP's base rate drops to 4.75% each for workers and employers on January 1, 2027, while the CPP and EI earnings ceilings rise. Here's what changes.
text: The numbers that drive 2027 payroll are now mostly in place. The Canada Revenue Agency posted the 2027 Canada Pension Plan (CPP) earnings ceilings on October 28, 2026, and they arrive alongside a cut to the base CPP contribution rate, already passed into law, that takes effect on January 1, 2027. Employment Insurance (EI) figures for 2027 were confirmed in September. What happened Three separate announcements now fit together: CPP earnings ceilings are going up. The year's maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE), the top of the first CPP earnings band, rises to $76,700 in 2027, from $74,600 in 2026. The second ceiling (YAMPE), which caps the "CPP2" band, rises to $87,400 , from $85,000. The base CPP rate is going down. Bill C-30, which put the Spring Economic Update 2026 into law, received Royal Assent on June 19, 2026. It lowers the base CPP contribution rate from 9.9% to 9.5% combined, starting in 2027. That is 4.75% each for employees and employers, instead of 4.95%. EI premiums are set. The Canada Employment Insurance Commission confirmed on September 14, 2026 that the 2027 employee rate (outside Quebec) is $1.64 per $100 of insurable earnings, with maximum insurable earnings of $70,800 , up from $68,900. How the new CPP rate works CPP contributions are made of pieces, which is why the headlines can be confusing: Base CPP is the original plan. This is the part being cut, by 0.2 percentage points for each side. The first enhancement adds 1% on the same band of earnings. Together with the base, employees and employers each pay 5.95% today. The enhancement portion is not part of the cut, so the combined rate on this band falls to 5.75% each in 2027. CPP2 is a separate 4% contribution, each for employees and employers, on earnings between the first and second ceilings. In 2027 that band runs from $76,700 to $87,400. Before the change, the federal Chief Actuary looked at whether the plan could afford it. The actuarial report published by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions found the 9.5% rate is "sufficient to finance the base CPP over the long term." It also noted that contributions will fall below the plan's expenditures starting in 2027, so the plan will lean more on investment income over time. What it means for you For employees, the cut means slightly more take-home pay. Finance Canada estimates a worker earning $70,000 will save about $133 a year in 2027. Higher earners will see some of that offset, because the higher ceilings mean CPP is deducted on a bit more of their pay, and CPP2 applies to a slightly wider band. Your future CPP pension is not reduced by this change. Benefits are based on your earnings history, not the base rate you paid. If you earn above the new ceilings, you will also build a little more pensionable earnings in 2027. On the EI side, the higher maximum insurable earnings means the most a worker can pay in 2027 is $1,161.12, up $38.05 from 2026. What it means for small businesses Employers match employee CPP contributions, so they get the same saving on base CPP for every employee. For EI, employers pay 1.4 times the employee premium: the 2027 maximum is $1,625.57 per employee, up $53.27. Self-employed people pay both the employee and employer halves of CPP, so they get the base-rate saving twice, but also pay both halves on the higher ceilings. Owner-managers who take a salary from their own corporation are in a similar position, since the company pays the employer share. Two practical points for 2027 payroll: Payroll software needs the new rates and ceilings for the first pay date in January 2027. Most providers update automatically, but it is worth checking your first January pay stubs. If you pay yourself through a corporation, the change slightly shifts the math between salary and dividends. It is a good topic for a year-end planning conversation, along with the 2027 RRSP limit, which the CRA lists as $35,390. What to do now Employees: nothing to file. Expect a small change in your CPP deductions on your first pay in January 2027. Employers: confirm with your payroll provider that the 2027 CPP, CPP2 and EI figures will be loaded before your first January payroll. The CRA had not yet posted its full 2027 CPP maximum contribution table when we checked its pages today. Self-employed and owner-managers: factor the new CPP numbers into your 2027 instalment estimates and your salary-or-dividend decision.

title: CRA's new pre-filled tax return: set up your account by October 31
description: About one million Canadians will be invited to file a pre-filled 2026 return in March 2027. To qualify, your CRA account must be set up by October 31, 2026.
text: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is launching a free service that fills in your tax return for you using information it already has. Starting in March 2027, about one million Canadians will be invited to use it for their 2026 return. To be considered, you need to have your CRA account set up by October 31, 2026 . What is a pre-filled return? The CRA already receives most of the slips that simple returns need, such as your T4 from your employer or your pension slips. With the new service, the CRA puts that information into a return for you. You sign in, check everything, add anything that's missing, and then accept and submit it. It isn't automatic filing. Nothing is filed until you review and submit the return yourself, and you stay responsible for making sure it's correct. Who may be invited The first round is aimed at people with lower incomes and simple tax situations who don't owe tax. According to the CRA, you must meet all of these conditions: You have a CRA account, and your correspondence preference is set to electronic mail. You filed your 2025 tax return. You were a Canadian resident for tax purposes for all of 2026, you're filing for yourself, and you were 15 or older in 2026. Your income comes only from certain slips, such as T4, T4A, T4A(OAS), T4A(P), T4E, T5 and T5007, and is below a limit that depends on your province, age and disability tax credit status. You won't qualify if, in 2026, you sold your principal residence, went bankrupt, repaid COVID-19 benefits or amounts under the Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan, had exempt income under the Indian Act, or owned specified foreign property costing more than $100,000. Meeting the conditions doesn't guarantee an invitation. The CRA plans to invite about one million people in 2027 and expand to about 5.5 million by 2029. What to do by October 31 Sign in to your CRA account , or register if you don't have one. Check your personal information , including your address and email. Set your correspondence preference to electronic mail in your account settings. File your 2025 return if you haven't already. Free options include the CRA's SimpleFile service and community volunteer tax clinics. If you're invited, you'll get an email in March 2027 telling you the invitation is waiting in your CRA account. Why filing matters even if you owe nothing Many benefits are only paid if you file a return every year, including the Canada Child Benefit, the GST/HST credit and several BC credits. A pre-filled return makes it easier for people with simple situations to keep those payments coming. Is it right for you? If your only income is from a job or a pension and you have no deductions to claim, a pre-filled return could save you time. But it only includes what the CRA already knows. Credits and deductions that depend on your receipts, such as medical expenses, donations, tuition carry-forwards, moving costs or rent, may be missing unless you add them. If your situation is more than simple, or you're not sure what you can claim, it's worth having your return reviewed.

title: Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%: what it means for you
description: The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate on October 28, 2026, its first increase since 2023, citing higher energy prices and stubborn inflation.
text: On October 28, 2026, the Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, from 2.25% to 2.5% . It's the Bank's first rate increase since July 2023, and it signals that the long run of rate cuts is over for now. Why the Bank raised rates Inflation has been higher and has lasted longer than the Bank expected in the summer. Consumer prices have been rising at around 3% a year since April, and the Bank now expects inflation to reach about 3.5% by the end of 2026. High energy prices are the main driver. When gasoline is left out, inflation was a much lower 2.2% in September. The Bank's concern is that expensive fuel will spread into other prices, as businesses pass on higher transport and production costs. Raising rates now is meant to stop that from turning into a longer bout of inflation. The economy has also been stronger than expected. It grew at a 3.3% annual pace in the second quarter, and early estimates suggest about 2% in the third. The Bank expects growth of about 1% for 2026 as a whole, with new US tariffs likely to slow things down in the last few months of the year. Unemployment has been around 6.5% for several months. What it means for you Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit. Lenders usually move their prime rates in step with the Bank's rate, so borrowing tied to prime generally gets more expensive. Check your lender's notice to see how your payment changes. Fixed-rate mortgages. Your payment won't change until renewal. Fixed rates follow bond yields rather than the Bank's rate directly, and bond yields barely moved on the news. Renewing soon? Compare fixed and variable options carefully, since the Bank has said further increases are possible. Savers. Rates on high-interest savings accounts and GICs may edge up. What it means for small businesses Business loans and lines of credit at floating rates will cost a little more. If you carry a balance on a business line of credit, now is a good time to look at your cash flow, pay down expensive debt where you can, and think about how you would handle another increase. What's next The Bank said it may need to raise rates further, but will move carefully given the uncertainty around energy prices and trade. Economists at TD expect one more increase in early 2027, which would take the rate to 2.75%. Forecasts like this can change quickly. The next decision is on December 9, 2026 . The Bank's next full economic forecast, the Monetary Policy Report, follows on January 27, 2027.

title: CRA updates for small businesses: online debt payments, Apple Pay and more
description: Business owners can now manage payroll, GST/HST and corporate tax debts online, and pay the CRA with Apple Pay or Google Pay. Here's what's new this fall.
text: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) has rolled out several changes this fall that make dealing with it easier for business owners. Here are the ones most likely to matter to small businesses, contractors and corporations. Manage business tax debts online Owners, directors and officers can now deal with payroll, GST/HST and corporate (T2) tax balances directly in My Business Account . The new Manage Balance service lets you make a payment, set up a payment arrangement or ask the CRA to call you back, without waiting on the phone. A similar service for personal tax debts launched in October 2025. One limit to know: accountants and other representatives can't use this service through Represent a Client, so the business owner or a director needs to sign in. New ways to pay the CRA Since October 9, 2026, you can pay the CRA with Apple Pay, Google Pay or Konek , as well as by debit card or Interac through participating financial institutions. Whichever way you pay, keep the confirmation with your records. Keep your director and officer details current The CRA is reminding corporations to update their records whenever a director or officer joins, leaves or changes their details. Out-of-date information can delay access to My Business Account and stop new representative authorizations from going through. Rideshare and taxi drivers must register for GST/HST If you drive for Uber, Lyft or a taxi company, you're generally a self-employed sole proprietor. The CRA's reminder is that rideshare and taxi operators must register for a Business Number and a GST/HST account no matter how much they earn . The usual $30,000 small-supplier threshold doesn't apply to them. Other changes worth knowing T2 web access code online. Corporations can now get the access code needed to file a T2 return electronically online, without waiting. Faster SR&ED answers. Businesses doing research and development can apply for pre-claim approval, with a decision within eight weeks. Free one-on-one help. The CRA's Liaison Officer Service offers free, confidential visits and sessions for small business owners, self-employed people and landlords. 2027 deadlines. The CRA has published a factsheet of 2027 deadlines for businesses and the self-employed. Extra sign-in security. Individuals and tax preparers can add an optional verification step when filing returns online this coming tax season. What to do now Make sure you can sign in to My Business Account, and that the right people have access. Check that your directors, officers and addresses are up to date with the CRA. If you owe the CRA and can't pay in full, set up a payment arrangement early. Interest keeps adding up on unpaid balances. Drive for a rideshare platform? Make sure you're registered for GST/HST and charging and remitting it correctly.

title: Canada child benefit and B.C. family benefit explained
description: Who qualifies for the Canada child benefit and B.C. family benefit, how to apply, July 2026 to June 2027 amounts, payment dates and how to keep payments coming.
text: Guides · Benefits Canada child benefit and B.C. family benefit explained The Canada child benefit and the B.C. family benefit put tax-free money in parents' bank accounts every month. Here's who qualifies, how to apply, how much you could get from July 2026 to June 2027, and the simple steps that keep the payments coming. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 3, 2026 · Figures for July 2026 to June 2027 In short The CCB pays up to $8,157 a year for a child under 6 and $6,883 for a child aged 6 to 17 (July 2026 to June 2027). The B.C. family benefit adds up to $1,750 for a first child and is paid with the CCB, with no separate application.
