Payments are based on your family's net income from the year before, so you and your spouse must both file every year, even with no income. In B.C., you can apply for the CCB when you register your baby's birth; otherwise use your CRA account or Form RC66. With shared custody (40% to 60% of the time), each parent gets half. Report changes in address, marital status and custody quickly to avoid paying money back. On this page What these benefits are Who qualifies How to apply How much CCB you can get The B.C. family benefit Payment dates Keeping your payments on track Common mistakes and checklist What these benefits are The Canada child benefit (CCB) is a monthly payment from the federal government to help families with the cost of raising children under 18. It is tax-free , which means you don't report it as income and it doesn't raise your tax bill. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) runs it. The B.C. family benefit is a separate payment from the Province of British Columbia for B.C. families with children under 18. It is also tax-free. The province pays for it, but the CRA works out the amount and adds it to your CCB, so you get one combined deposit each month. Three terms come up again and again: Benefit year: payments run from July to the following June. This guide uses figures for July 2026 to June 2027 . Base year: the tax year the CRA uses to set your payments. For July 2026 to June 2027, it is your 2025 income, from the returns you filed in spring 2026. Adjusted family net income (AFNI): your net income from your tax return plus your spouse's or common-law partner's, with a few small adjustments, such as taking out income from a registered disability savings plan (RDSP). The lower your AFNI, the more you get. Amounts go up with inflation each July, so the same family usually gets a little more each year. Who qualifies For each child, you can get the CCB if all of these are true: the child is under 18 and lives with you; you are primarily responsible for the child, meaning you look after their daily needs, make sure their medical needs are met and arrange child care when needed; you are a resident of Canada for tax purposes (you normally live here and have strong ties, such as a home or family here); and you or your spouse or common-law partner is a Canadian citizen, a permanent resident, a protected person, a person registered (or entitled to be registered) under the Indian Act , or a temporary resident who has lived in Canada for the previous 18 months and holds a valid permit in the 19th month. Newcomers A protected person is someone who has received a positive decision from the Immigration and Refugee Board. A refugee claimant who is still waiting for a decision does not qualify yet. Temporary residents, such as work-permit holders, must wait until the 19th month in Canada. If your permit is renewed, send the new permit to the CRA through your CRA account so payments continue. Our newcomers tax guide covers your first return. Two parents in one home Only one CCB payment goes to each household, and the amount is the same whichever parent receives it. When a mother and father live together, the CRA assumes the mother is primarily responsible, so she should usually apply. If the father is the main caregiver, he can apply with a signed letter from the mother. Same-sex couples choose one parent to apply for all the children. Shared custody If your child lives with you 40% to 60% of the time, you and the other parent have shared custody . You each apply, and you each get half of what you would get with full custody, based on your own household's income. If the child lives with you less than 40% of the time, you can't apply. More than 60% counts as full custody. You can't get the CCB for a foster child in any month when the agency receives children's special allowances for that child. How to apply Apply as soon as your child is born, a child comes to live with you, or your custody arrangement starts or changes. There are three ways: When you register your baby's birth. In B.C., you can apply for the CCB at the same time as you register the birth online. You must give consent to share your information with the CRA, or the application isn't sent. You don't need to send proof of birth this way. Through your CRA account. Sign in, go to Benefits and credits and add the child under Child information . Upload any documents the CRA asks for. By mail with Form RC66 , the Canada Child Benefits Application, if you can't use the other two options. You don't apply separately for the B.C. family benefit. Once a child is registered for the CCB, they are automatically registered for the B.C. family benefit too. The same goes for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (the payment that replaced the GST/HST credit): children you get the CCB for are counted automatically. Extra paperwork in some cases Newcomers and returning residents also send Schedule RC66SCH (status in Canada and income) with Form RC66. If your spouse or partner was a non-resident for part of a year, Form CTB9 reports their income for that year. If you are asking for payments for a period that started more than 11 months ago , expect to send proof of status, residence in Canada, the child's birth and that you are the main caregiver. Documents not in English or French need a proper translation. Tip: Ticking the benefits box when you register your newborn's birth is the fastest route. It also means you don't have to mail proof of birth. How much CCB you can get Here are the most you can get per child for July 2026 to June 2027. Families with AFNI under $38,237 get these full amounts. Child's age Maximum per year Maximum per month Under 6 $8,157 $679.75 6 to 17 $6,883 $573.58 How the amount goes down as income rises The CCB shrinks gradually, in two stages. This is called a phase-out : Stage one: on family income between $38,237 and $82,847, the yearly benefit drops by 7% of the income over $38,237 for one child, 13.5% for two children, 19% for three, and 23% for four or more. Stage two: above $82,847, the drop slows down: 3.2% of the extra income for one child, 5.7% for two, 8% for three and 9.5% for four or more (on top of the stage-one reduction). Because the second stage is gentle, many middle-income families still get something. You don't have to do the maths yourself: the CRA calculates it and sends a notice each summer. The CRA's online child and family benefits calculator gives an estimate. Illustration only: a B.C. family with one child aged 3 and AFNI of $60,000. That is about $21,760 over the first threshold. 7% of that is about $1,520, so the family's CCB is about $8,157 - $1,520 = about $6,630 a year , or roughly $550 a month. Child disability benefit The child disability benefit is an extra amount added to the CCB for a child who qualifies for the disability tax credit (DTC) , a credit for people with a severe and prolonged impairment. For July 2026 to June 2027 it is up to $3,480 a year ($290 a month) per child. It starts to go down when AFNI is over $82,847. To get it, a medical practitioner fills out Form T2201 and the CRA must approve it. Once approved, the CRA automatically looks back over the current and two previous benefit years. Read more in our guide to often-missed tax credits . The B.C. family benefit For July 2026 to June 2027, the B.C. family benefit is based on your 2025 AFNI. Child Maximum per year Minimum per year (income $30,176 to $96,562) First child $1,750 $775 Second child $1,100 $750 Each additional child $900 $725 In plain words: Under $30,176: you get the maximum. $30,176 to $96,562: the benefit goes down by 4% of income over $30,176, but never below the minimum amounts in the table. Over $96,562: the remaining amount goes down by 4% of income over $96,562 until it reaches zero. Single parents with low income can get a supplement of up to $500 a year per family. It shrinks once AFNI is over $30,176. Parents with shared custody get half the amount for that child. Illustration only: for the family above (one child, AFNI $60,000), 4% of the $29,824 over $30,176 is about $1,190. That would wipe out most of the $1,750, but the minimum protects them, so they get $775 a year (about $64.58 a month), added to their CCB deposit. Coming in July 2027: a disability supplement B.C. has announced a children and youth disability supplement of up to $6,000 a year per child approved for the DTC, to be paid with the B.C. family benefit starting in July 2027 and based on 2026 returns. The province describes it as proposed in its 2026 budget legislation, so details could still change. Families already approved for the DTC should not need to apply. Moving out of B.C.? Tell the CRA right away. The B.C. family benefit is only for B.C. residents, and payments made after you move have to be paid back. Also, the province says it won't contact you by text about this benefit, so treat any such text as a likely scam. Payment dates The CCB and B.C. family benefit arrive together, usually around the 20th of each month. The remaining CCB dates for 2026 are: November 20, 2026 December 11, 2026 The CRA had not yet posted its 2027 dates when we checked on November 3, 2026. We'll update this guide once they're published. If your total for the year is under $240 , you get one lump sum with your July payment instead of monthly payments. If a payment doesn't arrive, check your CRA account and make sure your details are up to date. Wait 5 business days after the expected date before calling. Direct deposit is the most reliable way to get paid. If you change banks, keep the old account open until the first payment lands in the new one. Keeping your payments on track File your taxes every year, both of you You and your spouse or common-law partner must each file a tax return every year, even if you had no income or your income isn't taxable. The CRA can't work out your family income without both returns. File by April 30 so your new amount starts on time in July. If you file late, payments can stop for a while. You get the missed amounts once your return is assessed, but the gap can hurt a family budget. Warning: A stay-at-home parent, a student spouse or a partner with only foreign income still needs to file. If a spouse lived outside Canada for part of the year, their world income counts too. Tell the CRA about changes Marital status: report a marriage, new common-law relationship or separation by the end of the month after the change. For a separation, wait until you have been apart for more than 90 days in a row. Address: update it right away, even if you use direct deposit, or your payments may stop. Custody: if a child moves in or out, or a shared custody arrangement starts, ends or changes, each parent should tell the CRA promptly. Leaving Canada: tell the CRA if you or your spouse stop being a resident. If a child dies: tell the CRA as soon as you can. For a death on or after January 1, 2026, the family may keep getting payments for up to 6 more months. Your CRA account is the fastest way to make most changes. Common mistakes and checklist Common mistakes Not filing a return because "I had no income", which stops payments for the whole family. Waiting for the first tax return in Canada before applying. Newcomers can apply once they qualify. Forgetting to send a renewed work or study permit to the CRA. Both separated parents claiming full custody, or neither applying for shared custody. The CRA may later recalculate and ask for money back. Reporting a reconciliation or new partner late. Any amount you were overpaid has to be repaid. Never applying for the disability tax credit for a child who might qualify, missing both the child disability benefit and the coming B.C. supplement. Not telling the CRA after moving out of B.C. Checklist Applied for the CCB at birth registration, online or with Form RC66 (plus RC66SCH if new to Canada). Both spouses or partners filed returns by April 30, 2027 for the 2026 tax year. Address, marital status and bank details are current in your CRA account. Custody changes reported by each parent. Asked about the disability tax credit (Form T2201) if your child has a serious, long-lasting condition. Checked your benefit notice each summer to confirm the amounts. We prepare returns for both spouses, apply for the Canada child benefit for newcomers and new parents, and help with the disability tax credit and CRA benefit reviews. title: Capital gains in Canada: selling your home, a rental property or investments
description: How capital gains are taxed in Canada in 2026: the 50% inclusion rate, the principal residence exemption, rentals, flipping rules and capital losses.
text: Guides · Personal tax Capital gains in Canada: selling your home, a rental property or investments Selling a home, a rental condo or some shares can bring a large profit. Here's how the CRA taxes that profit, when your home is tax-free, and the reporting steps that families and small landlords in Metro Vancouver often miss. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short Only half of a capital gain is taxed; the proposed increase to two-thirds was cancelled in March 2025. The gain is the sale price minus your adjusted cost base and selling costs. The principal residence exemption can make your home's gain tax-free, but you must report the sale on Schedule 3 and Form T2091(IND). Homes owned less than 365 days can be fully taxed as business income, and B.C. adds its own flipping tax for homes owned under 730 days. Rental property gains are taxable, and past capital cost allowance can be added back to income. Net capital losses can go back three years or forward with no time limit, against capital gains. On this page What a capital gain is, in plain words How much of the gain is taxed in 2026 Selling your home: the principal residence exemption Selling a rental property, suite or second home Selling soon after buying: federal and B.C. flipping rules Selling shares, funds and other investments Using capital losses Checklist before you sell What a capital gain is, in plain words When you sell something you own as an investment, such as shares, a mutual fund, a rental condo or a piece of land, the CRA calls it capital property . If you sell it for more than it cost you, the profit is a capital gain . If you sell it for less, it's a capital loss . Three terms do most of the work: Proceeds of disposition: what you get for the property. Usually this is simply the sale price. Adjusted cost base (ACB): what the property cost you, plus the costs of buying it (such as commissions and legal fees), plus improvements that add lasting value. Normal repairs and upkeep don't count. Outlays and expenses: the costs of selling, such as real estate commissions, legal fees, advertising and surveyor's fees. The basic formula is: Capital gain = proceeds − (ACB + outlays and expenses) Illustration only: you bought shares for $10,000, including the trading fee. Years later you sell them for $16,000 and pay $100 in fees to sell. Your capital gain is $16,000 − ($10,000 + $100) = $5,900. You report the sale on Schedule 3 of your tax return. The taxable part ends up on line 12700 . How much of the gain is taxed in 2026 You don't pay tax on the whole gain. Only part of it, called the taxable capital gain , is added to your income. The share that's taxed is called the inclusion rate . With the planned increase cancelled (see below), the inclusion rate stays at one-half (50%) . In the example above, half of the $5,900 gain, or $2,950, is added to your income and taxed along with your other income for the year. The two-thirds increase is not happening. In 2024 the federal government proposed raising the inclusion rate to two-thirds, and in January 2025 it pushed the start date to January 1, 2026. On March 21, 2025, the Prime Minister announced that the increase was cancelled, and the CRA's own pages now note that the increase was cancelled. If you read older articles warning about a two-thirds rate, they are out of date. A separate break, the lifetime capital gains exemption , can shelter gains on qualifying small business shares and farm or fishing property. The government has said it is keeping the increase of this limit to $1.25 million for qualifying sales on or after June 25, 2024. It doesn't apply to your home, a rental property or publicly traded shares. Selling your home: the principal residence exemption For most families, the home is their biggest asset. The principal residence exemption can make the gain on selling it fully tax-free. A principal residence can be a house, condo, apartment, cottage, mobile home or even a houseboat. Which home qualifies For each year, the home can count as your principal residence if: you own it, alone or with someone else, you, your spouse or common-law partner (or former one), or any of your children lived in it at some time in that year, and you designate it, which means you formally name it as your principal residence for those years when you sell. Since 1982, a family can designate only one home per year . "Family" here generally means you, your spouse or partner and your unmarried children under 18. The land that comes with the home is generally limited to half a hectare (about 1.24 acres). You must report the sale, even if no tax is owed Since the 2016 tax year, the CRA allows the exemption only if you report the sale and the designation on your return for the year you sell. You do this on Schedule 3 and Form T2091(IND) . If the home was your principal residence for every year you owned it, or every year but one, you only fill in page 1 of the form. Warning: if you forget, ask the CRA to fix that year's return as soon as you can. The CRA may accept a late designation, but the penalty can be $100 for each full month it's late, up to $8,000 . When only part of the gain is exempt If the home wasn't your principal residence for every year you owned it, only part of the gain is tax-free. The exempt part is worked out like this: Gain × (1 + years designated) ÷ years owned The "plus one" protects you in the year you sell one home and buy another, since you can only designate one of them for that year. It only counts if you were a resident of Canada in the year you bought the home. This matters for newcomers who bought a home before moving here (see our newcomers' tax guide ). Illustration only: you owned a condo for 10 years and designate it for 7 of them. The exempt share is (1 + 7) ÷ 10, or 80%. On a $100,000 gain, $80,000 is tax-free and $20,000 is a capital gain, half of which is taxed. A loss on selling your home can't be claimed. Selling a rental property, suite or second home A rental condo, an investment property or a second home you don't designate is taxed like other capital property: you pay tax on half of the gain. Split land and building. When you sell a rental, you split the sale price between land and building and report each part separately. Watch for recapture. If you claimed capital cost allowance (the tax version of depreciation) on the building, some or all of it can be added back to your income in the year of sale. This is fully taxable, not half. Our rental income guide explains how this works. Part of your home rented? If you rented a suite and claimed capital cost allowance or made structural changes, part of your gain may be taxable. You split the price and ACB in a reasonable way, such as by floor area or number of rooms. Moved out and rented the home? A change in use is treated as if you sold the home at its market value and bought it back. Special elections can delay this; see the rental guide. Two properties, one designation. If your family owns a home and a cottage, you choose which one to designate for each year. Which one to choose depends on the numbers, so work it out before you file. Selling soon after buying: federal and B.C. flipping rules Two separate sets of rules target homes that are sold quickly. Both can apply to the same sale. Federal residential property flipping rule For sales on or after January 1, 2023, if you owned a home or rental property in Canada for less than 365 days in a row , any profit is treated as business income . That means it's fully taxable, not half, and the principal residence exemption isn't available. A loss on a flipped property is treated as zero. The rule doesn't apply if you sold because of, or expecting, certain life events, including: a death, or a new member joining your household (such as a birth or caring for an aging parent), a separation, if you lived apart for at least 90 days before the sale, a threat to your safety, or a serious illness or disability, a job loss, or a move for work or school that brings you at least 40 km closer, insolvency, or the home being destroyed or expropriated. B.C. home flipping tax Since January 1, 2025, B.C. has its own tax on profits from homes owned for less than 730 days . It's separate from income tax. The rate is 20% of the taxable profit if you sell within 365 days of buying. Over the following 365 days, the rate shrinks gradually, reaching zero at 730 days. If you lived in the home as your primary residence and owned it for at least 365 days in a row, you may be able to deduct up to $20,000 . If the tax applies, you must file a separate B.C. return within 90 days of the sale. Selling shares, funds and other investments Gains on shares, ETFs and mutual funds held outside a registered plan follow the same formula. Your broker may send a T5008 slip or an account statement showing the sale, but you're still responsible for getting the ACB right. Average your cost. If you bought the same shares or fund units at different times and prices, they are identical properties . Your ACB is the average cost per unit, recalculated each time you buy more, not the price of the batch you think you sold. Superficial loss rule. If you sell at a loss and you, your spouse or partner, or a corporation either of you controls buys the same investment within 30 days before or after the sale, and still owns it 30 days after, you can't claim the loss. Instead, the loss is usually added to the ACB of the shares bought back, so you get the benefit later. Foreign currency. Convert the sale price to Canadian dollars at the exchange rate on the sale date, and the cost at the rate when you bought. Paid over time? If the buyer pays you over several years, you may be able to claim a reserve , which spreads the gain over up to five years. Using capital losses Half of a capital loss is an allowable capital loss . You first use it against your taxable capital gains in the same year. If losses are bigger than gains, the leftover is a net capital loss . You can carry a net capital loss back three years to get back tax you paid on gains, using Form T1A. Don't file an amended return for this. You can carry it forward with no time limit . It can usually only reduce taxable capital gains , not your job or rental income. Losses on personal-use property, such as your home, car or furniture, can't be claimed. Tip: keep a record of unused net capital losses from past years. They can reduce or wipe out tax on a future gain, such as when you sell a rental property. Checklist before you sell Gather your purchase documents, including legal fees and commissions, to prove your ACB. Keep receipts for improvements, such as a new roof or renovation, which add to your ACB. Repairs don't. Keep the sale statement from your lawyer or notary showing the price, commission and legal fees. Note the date you bought and the date you'll sell. Under 365 days or 730 days can trigger the flipping rules. Decide which years to designate as your principal residence, especially if your family owns more than one home. Report the sale of your home on Schedule 3 and Form T2091(IND), even if no tax is owed. Check your ACB for shares and funds using average cost, and watch the 30-day window if you sell at a loss. Look up any net capital losses from past years. If you're moving abroad, read our leaving Canada guide first, because leaving Canada can affect the tax on property you still own. title: Dealing with CRA letters, reviews and audits
description: Got a letter from the CRA? How to spot scams, what each type of review or audit means, how to respond on time, and how to disagree.
text: Guides · CRA updates Dealing with CRA letters, reviews and audits A letter from the Canada Revenue Agency can be stressful, but most are routine requests for a receipt or a slip. This guide explains how to tell a real CRA letter from a scam, what the different reviews and audits mean, how to reply on time, and what to do if you disagree with the result. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 11, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short The CRA never demands payment by gift card, e-Transfer or cryptocurrency: check any contact in My Account first. Being selected for a review is not an audit and does not mean you did something wrong. Reply by the date in the letter, quote the reference number, and upload documents with Submit documents. Individuals can usually object up to the later of 90 days after the notice or one year after the filing due date. Taxpayer relief requests for the 2016 tax year must be made by December 31, 2026. You can authorize an accountant to deal with the CRA for you, but you stay responsible for your taxes. On this page First, make sure it's really the CRA The most common CRA letters and what they mean Audits: when the CRA looks more closely How to respond to a review or audit letter What happens after a review or audit If you disagree: objections and service complaints Penalties, interest and second chances Getting help: letting your accountant talk to the CRA Checklist: when a CRA letter arrives First, make sure it's really the CRA Scammers love to pretend they work for the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the federal agency that runs the tax system. So before you do anything else, check that the letter, call or message is real. The CRA says it will never : demand quick payment by Interac e-Transfer, gift card, prepaid credit card or cryptocurrency (digital currency such as Bitcoin) send refunds or payments by e-Transfer or text message threaten to arrest you, send you to jail or have you deported use aggressive or threatening language ask for personal or financial details in an email or voicemail set up a meeting in a public place to collect money The CRA does not use text or chat apps like WhatsApp to talk to you. It only texts you a sign-in code if you chose that option. Its emails never include a link asking for personal or banking details. How to check. Sign in to your CRA online account (often called My Account) by typing canada.ca into your browser yourself, not by clicking a link. Your online account shows the mail, notices and messages the CRA has sent you. If someone calls, get their name and office, hang up, and call the CRA back using the number on the official canada.ca contact page. Warning: Never give out your Social Insurance Number, bank details or passwords until you're sure you're dealing with the CRA. If you think you've been targeted, report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at antifraudcentre.ca, and tell your bank and police if you lost money. The most common CRA letters and what they mean Most CRA letters are routine. Getting one does not mean you did something wrong. Canada's tax system is based on self-assessment : you work out your own tax, and the CRA checks a share of returns to keep the system fair. Notice of assessment (NOA): the summary the CRA sends after it processes your return. It shows your refund or balance owing, plus useful numbers such as your RRSP contribution limit. Notice of reassessment (NOR): an updated summary sent only if the CRA changes a return it already assessed. It explains what changed. Review letter: a request to send receipts or other proof for something you claimed. The CRA says being picked for a review is not an audit. Here are the main review programs for personal tax returns: Review When it happens What it's about Pre-assessment review Before your NOA is issued Proof for credits or deductions you claimed Processing review After your NOA Same idea as above, but after the return is assessed Matching program After your NOA Comparing your return with slips and data from employers, banks and others Request verification Before a reassessment Checking that a change you asked for is allowed and supported Special assessment Before or after your NOA A deeper look at returns tied to patterns of non-compliance (not following the rules) A common example: you forgot to report a T5 slip for bank interest. The bank already sent that slip to the CRA, so the matching program spots the gap and the CRA may reassess your return to add the income. Audits: when the CRA looks more closely An audit is a closer examination of your books and records to make sure you paid the right tax and got only the credits and refunds you're entitled to. The CRA picks files mainly through risk assessment, which means looking for returns more likely to contain errors, or comparing your file with similar ones. An auditor will contact you by mail, phone or both to set a date, time and place. The audit may happen at your home or business, at your accountant's office, or at a CRA office. Auditors can look at your business and personal records and may borrow documents. If they do, they must give you a detailed receipt. Auditors don't accept records by email; they use the CRA's secure online services instead. For businesses , the CRA also runs trust account examinations . These check payroll deductions you withheld from employees and GST/HST you collected from customers, because that money is held "in trust" for the government. Late or missed remittances (payments to the CRA), or late or missing T4 slips or GST/HST returns, are among the reasons the CRA may pick an account. The CRA says the whole process usually takes about 60 days, and you typically get up to 15 days to get your records ready. See our guides on payroll and GST/HST . How to respond to a review or audit letter Read the whole letter. Note what the CRA is asking for and the reply date. The deadline is set in each letter, so there is no single standard time limit. Find the reference number. It's in the upper right corner of review letters. Include it with everything you send. Gather exactly what's asked for: receipts, slips, bank statements or a written explanation. If you can't find a receipt, explain why in writing and send whatever other proof you have. Send it online if you can. In My Account, use Submit documents , enter the tax year and reference number, and upload your scans (up to 10 files and 150 MB per session, in formats such as PDF or JPG). You keep your originals. Save the confirmation number. You can also mail your reply to the address in the letter. Need more time? Call the phone number at the bottom of the letter before the deadline and ask. Tip: Don't ignore a CRA letter. In a payroll or GST/HST examination, for example, if records don't arrive by the deadline the CRA may adjust your account using only the information it already has. A short phone call to ask for more time is far better than silence. Keep good records from the start. The CRA's audit guide says to keep your books and records for at least six years, and electronic records must stay in a readable electronic format. Our guide on self-employed expenses explains what to keep. What happens after a review or audit After a review, the CRA either accepts your claim or changes it and sends a notice of reassessment. If your claim was reduced and you later find new information, you can send it and the CRA will look again. An audit ends in one of a few ways: No change: you get a letter saying the audit is closed. Changes proposed: you get a proposal letter explaining what the auditor wants to change and why. You have 30 days to agree or disagree. If you disagree, send the auditor more documents. If you still can't agree, you can contact the auditor's team leader, whose details are on the letters. Final letter and reassessment: showing a balance owing, a refund, or no change. If you'll owe more, interest is usually added. The auditor can give you an estimate before the reassessment arrives, so you can pay early and limit interest. If you disagree: objections and service complaints If you think a notice of assessment or reassessment is wrong, start with the easy route. If something was simply missed or entered wrongly, you can ask the CRA to change your return. If the facts are complete and you still disagree, you can file a notice of objection . This is a formal request for the CRA's Appeals branch to take a fresh look. Objection deadlines (income tax): Individuals and graduated rate estates (a type of estate of a person who has died): the later of one year after the filing due date for that return, or 90 days after the date on the notice. Corporations: 90 days after the date on the notice. Disputes about TFSA or RRSP contributions: 90 days after the date on the notice. File online in My Account or My Business Account using Register my formal dispute , or use Form T400A or a signed letter by mail. Explain what you disagree with and why, and include your supporting documents. If you missed the deadline for a good reason, you can ask for an extension of time, up to one year after the deadline. In most cases you don't have to pay disputed income tax while your objection is being reviewed. But interest keeps building on the amount, so paying some or all of it can save money if you lose. Payroll deductions you were supposed to withhold and send in are an exception: those must be paid on time. Some things can't be objected to, such as an auditor's proposal letter or a statement of account. Respond to those directly instead. Unhappy with the service? The Taxpayer Bill of Rights lists 16 rights, including the right to be treated "professionally, courteously, and fairly" and the right to a formal review and appeal. If you had a problem with delays, rude treatment or wrong information, first talk to the employee or their supervisor. If that doesn't fix it, submit service feedback online or on Form RC193. The CRA aims to reply within 30 business days. After that, you can ask the Office of the Taxpayers' Ombudsperson to look into it. Service feedback is for how you were treated; use an objection to dispute the tax itself. Penalties, interest and second chances Taxpayer relief lets the CRA cancel or waive (forgive) penalties and interest when you couldn't meet your tax obligations because of events beyond your control. Examples include a serious illness or accident, a death in the immediate family, a flood or fire, or mistakes and delays caused by the CRA itself. Relief may also be possible if you truly can't pay. You can apply online through My Account or My Business Account, or use Form RC4288. Include a clear timeline of what happened and proof, such as a doctor's note. Expect a wait: the CRA lists an average processing time of about 16 months. There is a 10-year limit. A request made in 2026 can cover tax years that ended in 2016 or later, and interest that built up in 2016 or later. Deadline: If you want relief for the 2016 tax year, you must make your request by December 31, 2026 . On January 1, 2027, 2016 falls outside the 10-year window. Voluntary Disclosures Program (VDP). If you know you made a mistake or left something off a past return, and the CRA hasn't started an audit or investigation on it yet, you may be able to come forward through the VDP and get some relief. Your application must be complete, the information must be at least one year (or one reporting period) past its due date, and you must include an estimate of the tax owing or ask for a payment plan. Getting help: letting your accountant talk to the CRA You have the right to choose someone to represent you with the CRA, but you are still legally responsible for your taxes. To let an accountant deal with the CRA for you, you need to authorize them: Fastest: in My Account, go to Profile and add an authorized representative. Businesses do the same in My Business Account. Representative request: your accountant sends a request through the CRA's Represent a Client service, and you confirm it in your online account. By mail: Form AUT-01, which must reach the CRA within six months of the date you sign it. This gives phone and mail access only, not online access. To upload documents for you, your representative needs a "Level 2" authorization. Note that for special assessment reviews, the CRA may write to you directly even if you have a representative, so pass any letter on right away. If you're new to Canada, our newcomers' guide explains how to set up a CRA account. Checklist: when a CRA letter arrives Check it's real: look in My Account or call the CRA using the number on canada.ca, never one from a text or email. Find the reply date and the reference number. Make a list of exactly what's being asked for. Gather receipts, slips and statements; write a short explanation for anything missing. Upload with Submit documents and save the confirmation number. Call before the deadline if you need more time. Read your notice of reassessment carefully when it arrives. If you disagree, note the objection deadline the day the notice arrives. Ask about taxpayer relief if illness, disaster or CRA errors caused penalties or interest. Keep your records for at least six years, and keep your address up to date with the CRA. Got a letter from the CRA? We can read it with you, gather the right documents, reply on your behalf as your authorized representative, and help with objections or relief requests. title: Income from India or abroad while living in Canada
description: How Canada taxes rent, interest, gains and pensions from India or abroad, claiming credit for Indian tax, and when you must file Form T1135.
text: Guides · Personal tax Income from India or abroad while living in Canada Still have a flat, fixed deposits or investments back in India? Once you live in Canada, the income they earn belongs on your Canadian tax return. This guide explains what to report, how to convert rupees, how to get credit for tax paid in India, and when you must tell the CRA what you own abroad. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 8, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short Canadian residents report income from everywhere, including rent, interest, dividends and gains from India, even if the money stays there. Convert amounts to Canadian dollars using Bank of Canada rates, and rebuild India's April-to-March figures into a January-to-December year. A foreign tax credit on Form T2209 usually stops you paying tax twice, but it is capped at the Canadian tax on that income. File Form T1135 if the cost of your foreign property was more than $100,000 at any time in the year, except in your first year as a resident. Late T1135 filing costs $25 a day, up to $2,500 a year, and bigger penalties can apply. Missed past years? The CRA's Voluntary Disclosures Program may cancel penalties if you come forward first. On this page Canada taxes residents on income from everywhere Common kinds of income from India Converting rupees and matching India's April-to-March year Getting credit for tax paid in India Form T1135: reporting what you own outside Canada Penalties, and what to do if you missed past years Checklist Canada taxes residents on income from everywhere If you live in Canada for tax purposes, you are a Canadian tax resident . Once you are a resident, the CRA (Canada Revenue Agency) expects you to report your world income . That means income from every source, inside and outside Canada, on your Canadian tax return. This surprises many families who still have money or property in India. Income does not become "Canadian" only when you bring it here. Rent paid into an Indian bank account, interest that stays in a fixed deposit, and a gain on a flat sold in Pune all count, even if the money never leaves India. Two other points to know from the start: India may tax the same income. Canada and India have a tax treaty (an agreement between the two countries) that decides which country can tax which kind of income, and how much. Canada then gives you a credit for Indian tax so you are not taxed twice on the same income. You may also have to report what you own abroad, not just what it earns, on a form called T1135 . We cover it below. If you arrived recently, our first-year guide for newcomers explains when your residency starts. If you are moving back to India, see our guide to leaving Canada . Common kinds of income from India Here is how the most common types of Indian income are treated. The treaty column shows what the Canada–India tax treaty says about India's right to tax it. Income On your Canadian return Can India tax it too? Rent from a flat or house in India Report the rent and claim allowable expenses on Form T776, the rental statement Yes. Income from real estate can be taxed where the property is Interest on fixed deposits (FDs), savings, NRO or NRE accounts Report on line 12100 every year Yes, but the treaty caps India's tax at 15% of the gross interest Dividends from Indian shares or mutual funds Report on line 12100. Foreign dividends don't get the Canadian dividend tax credit Yes, but for individuals the treaty caps India's tax at 25% of the gross dividend Gain on selling property, shares or mutual fund units Report as a capital gain. Under current law, half of the gain is taxed Yes. The treaty lets both countries tax most gains Pension paid from India Report it, then deduct the treaty-exempt part on line 25600 The treaty says a pension arising in India is taxable only in India A few things that catch people out Interest on an FD is reported as it is earned, not only when the deposit matures. For a deposit that compounds over several years, the CRA wants you to report the interest earned in each full investment year, even though you haven't received it. Interest from all your Indian accounts counts, whether or not India taxed it. Rental property in India follows the same basic rules as a Canadian rental. See our rental income guide for which expenses you can claim. Selling property in India? Our capital gains guide explains how the gain is worked out. The federal government cancelled the proposed increase to the share of gains that is taxed, so it stays at one-half. Pensions need care. Whether a payment counts as a "pension" under the treaty is not always obvious, especially for lump-sum withdrawals. Ask for help before you leave one off your return. Converting rupees and matching India's April-to-March year Use Canadian dollars Everything on your return must be in Canadian dollars. The Income Tax Act says a foreign amount is generally converted using the Bank of Canada exchange rate for the day the amount arose. In practice: One-time amounts, such as the sale price of a flat, use the Bank of Canada rate on the day of that transaction. The cost of the flat uses the rate on the day you bought it. Amounts paid throughout the year, such as a monthly pension, can use the Bank of Canada annual average rate . The CRA says an average may also be acceptable for other income in some situations. Indian tax you paid should be converted at the same rate you used for the income it relates to. The Bank of Canada publishes an annual average for the Indian rupee. For 2025 it was 0.01605 Canadian dollars per rupee. Illustration only: if you received rent of ₹6,00,000 (600,000 rupees) spread over 2025, you could convert it as 600,000 × 0.01605 = $9,630 . India's year is different from Canada's India's tax year runs from April 1 to March 31 . Canada's tax year for individuals is the calendar year , January 1 to December 31. Indian bank certificates and TDS statements (TDS means tax deducted at source, the tax a bank or tenant withholds before paying you) usually follow the Indian year. For your Canadian return, you need to rebuild your figures for January to December. That means taking the last nine months of one Indian year and the first three months of the next. The CRA also expects Indian tax to be split across calendar years the same way, so the credit lines up with the income. Tip: Ask your Indian bank for monthly or quarterly interest statements, not just the yearly certificate. They make the calendar-year split much easier. Getting credit for tax paid in India When India taxes income that you also report in Canada, you can usually claim a foreign tax credit . A tax credit reduces the tax you owe, dollar for dollar. You work out the federal credit on Form T2209 , Federal Foreign Tax Credits , and enter it on line 40500. B.C. residents work out the provincial credit on Form T2036 . The basic limit For each country, the credit is generally the lower of: the foreign tax you actually paid on that income, and the Canadian tax you would otherwise pay on that same income. So the credit can cancel the Canadian tax on your Indian income, but it can never reduce the tax on your Canadian income. Illustration only: your Indian FDs earned interest worth $10,000 and the bank withheld $1,000 of TDS. If Canadian tax on that $10,000 would be $2,500, your credit is $1,000 and you pay the remaining $1,500 in Canada. If Canadian tax would only be $800, your credit is limited to $800. Other rules to know 15% cap on investment income. For interest and dividends (but not rent or gains from real estate), an individual's credit is limited to 15% of the gross income. Foreign tax above that may be deducted from income instead. Only tax you really owed counts. If India withheld more than the treaty allows, the extra is not a foreign tax for Canadian purposes. You would need to ask India for a refund of it. Refunds reduce the credit. If you get Indian tax back, for example after filing an Indian return, only the tax you finally paid counts. No carry-forward. Unused credit on this kind of income (called non-business income) can't be saved for another year. Keep proof. Keep TDS certificates, Indian returns and payment receipts. If you file on paper, the CRA asks you to attach receipts and your calculations. Documents in a language other than English or French need an acceptable translation. Watch out: Don't subtract Indian tax from the income you report. Report the full amount before tax, then claim the credit separately. Form T1135: reporting what you own outside Canada Form T1135 , the Foreign Income Verification Statement , is an information form. It doesn't create tax by itself. It tells the CRA what foreign investments you hold. Who must file You must file if you are a Canadian resident and the total cost of your specified foreign property was more than $100,000 at any time in the year. "At any time" matters: if you crossed $100,000 for one week, you file, even if you cashed out before December 31. "Cost" generally means what you paid, not today's value. A flat bought for a large price with a small down payment still counts at its full cost. For property you owned when you first became a resident, the cost is its fair market value on the day you became a resident. For inherited or gifted property, it is the value when you received it. Good to know: You don't file T1135 for the year you first became a resident of Canada. The rules apply from your second tax year here. What counts Money held outside Canada, such as Indian savings accounts, NRO and NRE accounts and fixed deposits Shares of foreign companies, even if you hold them through a Canadian broker Indian mutual funds (a fund based outside Canada counts, even though its own holdings are not listed) Real estate outside Canada that you rent out or hold as an investment Money owed to you by people or companies outside Canada, such as foreign bonds or loans What doesn't count Personal-use property, such as a home in India used mainly (more than half the time) by you for personal use. A flat that is mostly rented out for profit does count. Property used only in an active business you run Investments inside your RRSP, TFSA or other registered plans Canadian mutual funds, even if they invest in foreign shares Simplified or detailed Part A (simplified): if your total cost was more than $100,000 but under $250,000 throughout the year, you tick the type of property you hold, the countries, and report your total income and gains. Part B (detailed): if your total cost reached $250,000 or more at any time, you list each property. When it's due T1135 is due on the same day as your tax return. For 2026, that is April 30, 2027 , or June 15, 2027 if you or your spouse or common-law partner ran a business. You can file it electronically along with your return. Penalties, and what to do if you missed past years T1135 penalties Filing late: $25 a day for up to 100 days, with a minimum of $100 and a maximum of $2,500 per year. Knowingly or through gross negligence (serious carelessness) not filing: $500 a month for up to 24 months (up to $12,000), rising to $1,000 a month (up to $24,000) if you ignore a CRA demand to file. After 24 months: an extra penalty of 5% of the cost of the foreign property can apply, minus penalties already charged. There's another cost. If you didn't report income from foreign property and didn't file T1135 on time, the CRA gets three extra years to reassess (review and change) that year's return. If you missed income or T1135 in past years Many people only learn about these rules years after arriving. The fix is to correct the past years, ideally before the CRA contacts you. The CRA's Voluntary Disclosures Program (VDP) lets you correct errors or omissions. If you qualify, the CRA may cancel penalties and part of the interest. You still pay the tax owed. The program was changed on October 1, 2025. To qualify, you must meet all five conditions the CRA lists today: You apply before an audit or investigation has started about the information you are disclosing. You include all the information and documents for the years involved. The error or omission carries interest or penalties. The information is at least one year past its due date. You pay the estimated tax owing, or ask for a payment arrangement. The CRA gives more relief to people who come forward on their own than to those who act after being contacted. Information that is less than a year overdue doesn't qualify for the VDP, so it is usually fixed by changing the return instead. Talk to a professional about which route fits. Checklist List every Indian account, deposit, property, share and mutual fund you own, with what you paid for each. Collect interest certificates, rent records, sale papers and TDS certificates for both Indian years that overlap the Canadian year. Rebuild your income for January to December , including FD interest that has built up but not been paid. Convert each amount to Canadian dollars with Bank of Canada rates, and use the same rate for the related Indian tax. Report the full amount before Indian tax, then claim the credit on T2209 and T2036 . Check whether India withheld more than the treaty allows, and ask India for a refund of any extra. Add up the cost of your specified foreign property. If it went over $100,000 at any time, file T1135 with your return. File by April 30, 2027 for the 2026 year (June 15, 2027 if you or your spouse ran a business). Keep all records, with translations where needed. Missed earlier years? Get advice on fixing them before the CRA contacts you. Have income or property in India? title: Ride-share and delivery drivers in B.C.: income, GST and expenses
description: Tax basics for Uber, Lyft, DoorDash and other app drivers in B.C.: reporting income, GST rules for ride-share vs delivery, vehicle costs and CPP.
text: Guides · Small business Ride-share and delivery drivers in B.C.: income, GST and expenses Driving for Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart or another app makes you a small business owner in the CRA's eyes. This guide explains how to report your earnings, when you must charge GST (ride-share and delivery have different rules), what you can deduct, and what B.C.'s rules for app-based workers mean for you. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 7, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short Most app drivers are self-employed: report all fares, tips and bonuses on Form T2125, and deduct platform fees as an expense. Ride-share drivers must register for GST from their first fare; delivery-only drivers usually register once sales pass $30,000. Since the 2024 tax year, apps report what they paid you to the CRA, and must send you a copy by January 31. Deduct the business share of your vehicle costs, backed by a logbook of business kilometres. For 2026, you pay both halves of CPP: 11.9% up to $8,460.90, plus up to $832 of CPP2. File your 2026 return by June 15, 2027, but pay any balance by April 30, 2027. On this page You're running a small business Reporting your income: fares, tips and bonuses GST/HST: ride-share and delivery follow different rules GST returns, input tax credits and the quick method Vehicle costs and your logbook CPP, instalments and deadlines B.C. rules for app-based drivers Common mistakes and a year-end checklist You're running a small business If you drive for Uber or Lyft, or deliver for DoorDash, Uber Eats, Skip, Instacart or Amazon Flex, the CRA (Canada Revenue Agency) generally sees you as self-employed . That means you run your own small business. No one takes tax off your pay, so you are responsible for reporting your income, paying your own tax and CPP, and, in many cases, charging GST. The CRA says you are usually self-employed if you own your vehicle, or lease it for a flat fee or a share of your fares. If you aren't sure about your status, you can ask the CRA for a ruling with Form CPT1. You may have heard that B.C. now treats app-based drivers as "employees." That change is for the province's Employment Standards Act , the law on minimum pay and other work rules. It gives you some protections (see below), but it doesn't turn your app income into a regular job with a T4 slip and tax taken off. You report your driving business on Form T2125 , the Statement of Business or Professional Activities. It goes with your personal tax return. For ride-share, the CRA says to use industry code 485310 (taxi service). If you run your driving through a corporation, the rules are different; see our guide on sole proprietor vs incorporation in B.C. Reporting your income: fares, tips and bonuses The CRA's rule is simple: report all your income, including tips . In practice, that means: the full fare or delivery fee before the platform takes its cut, tips, whether paid in the app or in cash, bonuses, incentives, promotions and any distance pay the app gives you. The fees and commissions the platform keeps are not lost. The CRA says they can be claimed as a business expense . So start with your gross earnings, then deduct the fees. Don't just report the amount that landed in your bank account. Platforms now report to the CRA Under the Reporting Rules for Digital Platform Operators , apps must collect information about the people who earn money through them and report it to the CRA once a year. The CRA's guidance lists "transportation and delivery" work as a type of personal service covered by these rules. The rules started with the 2024 calendar year, and the first reports were due January 31, 2025. What this means for you: The CRA gets your name, address, tax number, what the app paid you and the fees it kept. The platform must give you a copy of the information by January 31 each year. Check it against your own records. If the app asks for your tax identification number, give it. The CRA can charge a $500 penalty each time you fail to provide it. If you missed reporting app income in past years, you can fix it by changing your returns or through the CRA's Voluntary Disclosures Program. GST/HST: ride-share and delivery follow different rules GST is the 5% federal Goods and Services Tax. In B.C., there's no HST (the combined federal and provincial sales tax used in some other provinces), so the rate on B.C. rides is 5%. The big question is whether you must register , which means getting a GST account with the CRA and charging GST to customers. Most small businesses don't have to register until they become larger than a small supplier : total taxable sales of $30,000 or less over four calendar quarters in a row. Ride-share drivers are the big exception. Since July 1, 2017, the CRA counts ride-share as a taxi business , and taxi businesses must register no matter how little they earn. Ride-share (Uber, Lyft) Delivery (food, groceries, parcels) When you must register From your first fare, at any income level Once taxable sales go over $30,000 over four calendar quarters Can you register earlier by choice? Not optional; you must register Yes, to claim back GST on your costs GST on what you earn Charge 5% GST on all B.C. fares Only once registered Doing both? If your ride-share and delivery sales together are $30,000 or less, your GST registration can cover only the ride-share part. Once the total goes over $30,000, you must charge GST on all your taxable sales. The CRA gives an example of a ride-share driver who also earns $10,000 delivering for Uber Eats: with combined sales under $30,000, GST applies to the rides but not the food deliveries. Warning for new ride-share drivers: your GST registration should start on the day you charged your first fare, and the CRA asks you to apply within 30 days. If you've been driving longer than that without a GST number, you'll need to backdate your registration. Who actually collects the GST on fares? The rider pays GST as part of the fare. Ride-share companies can handle some of the GST work for you, but only if you have authorized them to. The CRA is clear that the responsibility stays with you either way: you must make sure GST is collected and sent in on all your fares. Check your app's tax settings and statements so you know what the platform has done on your behalf. For more on registering and filing, see our GST/HST and PST guide for B.C. small businesses . GST returns, input tax credits and the quick method Filing your GST return Once registered, you file GST returns to report the GST you collected. The CRA usually gives drivers an annual reporting period, but you can choose monthly or quarterly. For an individual with a December 31 year-end, the 2026 annual GST return is due June 15, 2027 , and any GST you owe must be paid by April 30, 2027 . Input tax credits An input tax credit (ITC) lets you get back the GST you paid on things you buy for your business. Examples include fuel, repairs, car washes, and the lease or purchase of your vehicle. If you also use the car personally, claim only the business share. You can't claim ITCs on car insurance or loan interest, because no GST is charged on them. The quick method The quick method is a simpler way to work out the GST you owe. Instead of adding up every ITC, you pay a fixed percentage of your sales, GST included. For a service business in B.C., that rate is 3.6% , and you can take off 1% of the first $30,000 of those sales each year. You can use it if your yearly sales, including GST, are $400,000 or less. You still claim ITCs on big purchases such as a vehicle. You sign up using Form GST74 or online, and you must stay with it for at least a year. Illustration only: say you collect $21,000 in B.C. fares in a year, including $1,000 of GST. Under the quick method, you'd send 3.6% × $21,000 = $756, minus 1% × $21,000 = $210, for a total of $546 . Under the regular method, you'd send $1,000 minus your ITCs. Note that the GST you keep under the quick method counts as income on your tax return. What about B.C. PST? B.C.'s 7% Provincial Sales Tax (PST) applies only to certain goods and services. Rides and deliveries aren't on the province's list of taxable services, so drivers don't normally charge PST. You will still pay PST on many things you buy, such as car repairs and maintenance. Vehicle costs and your logbook Your vehicle is your biggest business cost. You can deduct the business share of costs like fuel, insurance, repairs and maintenance, licence and registration, loan interest, lease payments and capital cost allowance (CCA, the tax version of depreciation). Parking for business trips is deductible in full. Our self-employed expenses guide explains vehicle rules, 2026 limits and CCA in detail. Your business share is your business kilometres divided by your total kilometres for the year. Illustration only: if you drive 30,000 km and 24,000 km are for the apps, your business share is 80%. With $10,000 of vehicle costs, you could claim $8,000. Keep a logbook To prove your business kilometres, keep a logbook. For each business trip, the CRA wants the date, destination, purpose and kilometres. Also record your odometer reading at the start and end of the year. After one full year of logbook records (your base year ), the CRA lets you keep a simplified logbook : a three-month sample in later years. You can use it as long as your business use stays within 10% of the base year. If your driving pattern changes a lot, start a new full-year log. Other costs drivers often forget: the business share of your phone and data plan, phone mounts and chargers, insulated delivery bags, and the platform fees mentioned above. CPP, instalments and deadlines CPP: you pay both halves Employees and their employers each pay half of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contribution. As a self-employed driver, you pay both halves when you file your tax return. For 2026: The base rate is 5.95% for each half, so 11.9% in total on net earnings between $3,500 and $74,600. The most you'll pay is $8,460.90 . A second layer, called CPP2, is 4% for each half, so 8% on earnings between $74,600 and $85,000. The most you'll pay is $832 . Illustration only: with $40,000 of net driving income in 2026, your CPP would be ($40,000 − $3,500) × 11.9% = $4,343.50 , on top of your income tax. Instalments Because no tax is taken off your app earnings, you may end up owing a large amount each spring. If your net tax owing is more than $3,000 in 2026, and was also more than $3,000 in 2024 or 2025, the CRA expects you to pay instalments , which are tax payments made during the year. In 2027, instalments are due March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15. Filing deadlines for the 2026 tax year File your income tax return by June 15, 2027 . Pay any balance owing by April 30, 2027 . Interest starts after that, even though you have until June to file. Tip: move a set share of every weekly payout into a separate savings account for income tax, CPP and GST. Then the spring bill won't come as a shock. B.C. rules for app-based drivers Since September 3, 2024 , B.C. has had minimum standards for app-based ride-hail and delivery workers. They don't change how you're taxed, but they affect what you're paid and how you're protected. Minimum pay: as of June 1, 2026, at least $21.89 an hour for "engaged time," which runs from when you accept an order or ride until you complete it or it's cancelled. Waiting time between jobs doesn't count, and tips don't count toward the minimum. Vehicle allowance: on top of that, at least 45 cents a km for ride-hail and 35 cents a km for delivery. Tips: you keep 100% of your tips. Pay statements every pay period, which are useful for your tax records. WorkSafeBC coverage: if you're hurt while working, you can claim workers' compensation benefits. The platform company registers you and pays the premiums. (If you also hire helpers of your own, see our WorkSafeBC guide .) The province reviewed these standards with workers and platforms from January to March 2026, so some details may change. Keep in mind that everything the app pays you, including the per-km allowance, is part of your business income. You then deduct your actual vehicle costs as explained above. Common mistakes and a year-end checklist Common mistakes Reporting only the deposits in your bank account instead of gross earnings and fees. Leaving out tips, cash tips or bonuses. Starting ride-share without a GST number, or registering late. Assuming delivery drivers must register for GST from day one, or forgetting to register once delivery and other sales pass $30,000. No logbook, so you can't prove your business kilometres. Claiming 100% of a car or phone you also use personally. Forgetting about CPP, which can be thousands of dollars. Filing on June 15 but paying after April 30, and being charged interest. Checklist before you file Annual tax summaries from every app you used, plus the platform reporting copy you get by January 31. Your own record of income, tips and fees, by month. Logbook and odometer readings for January 1 and December 31. Receipts for fuel, repairs, insurance, phone and other costs, with GST shown separately if you're registered. Your GST return, if you're registered, and any instalments you paid. Keep all records for six years from the end of the tax year they relate to. Clear digital copies are fine.
