title: GST, HST and PST for small businesses in BC: a plain-language guide
description: When a BC business must register for GST and PST, what to charge, input tax credits, the Quick Method, filing deadlines and common mistakes, in plain language.
text: Guides · GST/HST & PST GST, HST and PST for small businesses in BC: a plain-language guide Most BC businesses deal with two sales taxes: the federal GST and BC's own PST. Here's when you need to register for each, what to charge, how to get back the tax you pay, and how to stay on top of your returns. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short You must register for GST once your taxable sales go over $30,000 in one calendar quarter or over four quarters in a row; taxi and rideshare drivers must register from day one. BC has 5% GST plus a separate 7% PST; sales shipped to Ontario or the Atlantic provinces get HST at that province's rate. Zero-rated sales (like basic groceries) let you claim input tax credits; exempt sales (like long-term residential rent) do not. The Quick Method can simplify GST for businesses with up to $400,000 in sales; BC service businesses remit 3.6% of GST-included sales. BC PST has no input tax credits: your business pays PST on taxable items it uses, and must self-assess when a seller doesn't charge it. BC paused its planned PST expansion to accounting and other professional services in September 2026; no new date has been set. On this page How sales tax works in BC Do you need to register for GST? Charging GST: other provinces, zero-rated and exempt sales Input tax credits: getting back the GST you pay Filing and paying your GST/HST return The Quick Method: a simpler option for some BC PST: who registers, what's taxable and how it works Common mistakes, records and a checklist How sales tax works in BC If you run a business in British Columbia, you may deal with two separate sales taxes: GST (goods and services tax) : a 5% federal tax, run by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). PST (provincial sales tax) : BC's own sales tax, run by the BC government. The general rate is 7%. Some other provinces have combined the federal and provincial taxes into one HST (harmonized sales tax) . BC does not have HST, but you may need to charge it if you sell to customers in those provinces. Where Federal sales tax Provincial sales tax British Columbia GST 5% PST 7% (separate) Alberta, Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut GST 5% None Ontario HST 13% (combined) Included in HST Nova Scotia HST 14% (combined, since April 1, 2025) Included in HST New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island HST 15% (combined) Included in HST The key idea: you collect GST from customers and pass it on to the government. It is not your money, so keep it separate from your operating cash. Do you need to register for GST? Most businesses must register for GST once they stop being a small supplier . You are a small supplier if your worldwide taxable sales are $30,000 or less . Sales of financial services, capital property and goodwill on selling a business are left out of this total. Two ways to cross the $30,000 line In a single calendar quarter. If your sales go over $30,000 within one quarter (for example, July to September), you stop being a small supplier with the sale that pushes you over. You must charge GST on that sale and register right away. Over four calendar quarters in a row. If your total for the last four quarters goes over $30,000 (but no single quarter did), you stop being a small supplier at the end of the month after that quarter. You must register and start charging GST by your first sale after that date. Example: Priya runs a home bakery. Her sales were $6,000, $7,000 and $9,000 in three quarters, then $9,500 in the next quarter. Her four-quarter total is $31,500, so she is no longer a small supplier at the end of the following month and must begin charging GST from her next sale after that. After the date you are required to register, you have 29 days to apply. You can register online with the CRA's Business Registration Online service, or by mailing Form RC1. You will get a business number (BN) with a GST/HST account attached. Taxi and rideshare drivers must register from day one. If you drive a taxi or work for a ride-sharing app as a self-employed driver, the small supplier rule does not apply to you. You must register for GST from the day you start giving rides, even if you earn less than $30,000. Registering voluntarily If you are under $30,000, you can still choose to register. Your registration can usually start on the day you ask for it, or up to 30 days earlier. Pros: you can claim back the GST you pay on business costs (see input tax credits below), and business customers who are registered can claim back the GST you charge them, so it costs them nothing extra. Cons: you must charge GST to every customer, which can make you more expensive for consumers, and you must file returns on time, even when you have nothing to report. Voluntary registration often suits businesses that sell mainly to other businesses or have large start-up costs. Charging GST: other provinces, zero-rated and exempt sales Selling to customers in other provinces The rate you charge depends on where the sale is considered to happen, known as the place of supply . The full rules are detailed, but the basics are: Goods: charge the rate of the province where the goods are delivered. If you ship a product from Surrey to a customer in Ontario, you charge 13% HST, not 5% GST. Services: in most cases, charge the rate of the province where your customer's home or business address is, if you get that address as part of doing business. If you design a website for a Halifax company, you would generally charge Nova Scotia's 14% HST. Real property: charge the rate of the province where the property is located. Your GST registration also covers HST; no separate account is needed. Zero-rated vs exempt: not the same thing Some sales have no GST, but for two very different reasons: Zero-rated Exempt GST charged? Taxed at 0%, so no No, outside the GST system Can you claim input tax credits? Yes Generally no Common examples Basic groceries (milk, bread, vegetables), prescription drugs, some medical devices like hearing aids, feminine hygiene products, most exports Long-term residential rent (one month or more), resale of used homes, most medical and dental services, child care for children 14 and under, music lessons, most financial services such as loans and bank accounts, insurance So a grocer selling zero-rated food can still recover GST on its costs, but a landlord renting apartments long-term cannot. A business making only exempt sales cannot register at all. Input tax credits: getting back the GST you pay An input tax credit (ITC) is how a registered business recovers the GST or HST it pays on business purchases. On each return, you subtract your ITCs from the GST you collected and pay only the difference. Example: In a quarter you charge $2,000 in GST to customers and pay $600 in GST on supplies, software and equipment. You send the CRA $1,400. You can claim an ITC when you were registered when the GST was paid or became payable, the purchase is for your commercial (taxable) business activities, and the cost is reasonable, you have proper paperwork, and you claim within the time limit. For most small businesses this is about four years. What your receipts must show Purchase amount What the invoice or receipt needs Under $100 Supplier's name, date, total amount $100 to $499.99 All of the above, plus the GST/HST amount (or a note that it is included) and the supplier's GST/HST number $500 or more All of the above, plus your name, a short description of what you bought, and the payment terms Some purchases are restricted or not eligible: personal items, recreational club memberships, and anything used to make exempt sales. Only part of the GST on meals and entertainment can be claimed. Filing and paying your GST/HST return When you register, the CRA assigns you a reporting period : monthly, quarterly or annual, based on your sales. You can ask to file more often if that suits you, for example to get refunds faster. Monthly and quarterly filers: the return and payment are due one month after the period ends. A quarter ending September 30 is due October 31. Annual filers: generally due three months after your fiscal year-end. A corporation with a December 31 year-end files and pays by March 31. Sole proprietors with a December 31 year-end: if you are an individual with business income, your payment is due April 30 and your return is due June 15. For the 2026 year, that means paying by April 30, 2027 and filing by June 15, 2027. Also keep in mind: You must file a return for every period, even if you had no sales. This is called a nil return. All GST/HST registrants (other than charities and certain financial institutions) must file electronically. Paper filers can be charged a penalty. If a due date falls on a weekend or public holiday, you have until the next business day. Instalments for annual filers If you file annually and your net tax for the previous year was $3,000 or more, you may need to pay quarterly instalments during the year. Each instalment is due within one month after the end of each fiscal quarter. The Quick Method: a simpler option for some The Quick Method is an optional way to work out how much GST to send the CRA. You still charge customers the full 5% GST (or HST where it applies). But instead of tracking GST on every expense, you pay a set percentage of your GST-included sales and keep the difference. Who can use it Your annual worldwide taxable sales, including GST/HST, are $400,000 or less. You have been in business for at least the past 365 days, or you are newly registered and expect to stay under the limit. You are not in an excluded line of work. Accountants, bookkeepers, lawyers, tax preparers, financial consultants and some others cannot use it. Rates for a business based in BC For sales where 5% GST applies, a BC business remits: 3.6% of GST-included sales if you mainly provide services, or 1.8% if you mainly buy goods to resell (your cost of goods must be at least 40% of your taxable sales). You also get a credit of 1% on the first $30,000 of eligible sales each year. Example: A Surrey house-cleaning business has $50,000 in sales plus $2,500 GST, for $52,500. Under the Quick Method it remits 3.6% of $52,500, which is $1,890, minus the 1% credit on $30,000 ($300), for a total of $1,590. The trade-off: you cannot claim ITCs on everyday expenses or inventory, only on capital property such as computers and vehicles, so it tends to suit businesses with low expenses. To use it, you elect through your CRA business account or Form GST74. Annual filers must elect by the first day of the second fiscal quarter. BC PST: who registers, what's taxable and how it works PST is completely separate from GST. You register with the BC government, not the CRA, and you file separate PST returns. Who must register A business located in BC generally must register to collect PST if it: sells or leases taxable goods in BC, provides related services to taxable goods, such as repairs, installation or alterations, provides software, telecommunication services or legal services in BC, or sells accommodation in BC (with some exceptions). Small seller exemption: you may not need to register if you are located in BC, have no established business premises and do not regularly sell from a commercial location (including a home-based shop), and you had and expect $10,000 or less in gross revenue from eligible taxable sales in the past and next 12 months. Small sellers do not charge PST, but they pay PST on items they buy to resell. What PST applies to PST applies to most goods bought or leased in BC, plus software, related services, telecommunication, legal services and short-term accommodation. Many food items and personal services such as hairstyling are exempt. Recent changes. From October 1, 2026, PST applies to basic cable TV, residential landline and toll-free phone services, and to clothing and footwear services (basic laundry and dry cleaning stay exempt). BC had also planned to extend PST to accounting, bookkeeping, architectural, engineering, security and non-residential real estate services on that date, but in September 2026 the province paused that expansion and has not set a new date. If you registered only for those services, BC says to cancel your PST account. Returns and payments When you register, BC tells you your reporting period. PST is due by the last day of the month after each period ends. For example, PST for a period ending June 30 is due July 31. Registered collectors who file and pay on time can earn a small commission. When your business buys things Unlike GST, there are no PST input tax credits. If your business buys taxable items for its own use, such as computers, furniture, vehicles or software, it pays PST and cannot get it back. Goods you buy to resell are exempt from PST, but if you later take items out of inventory for your own use, PST applies. If a supplier does not charge PST on a taxable item (for example, an online seller outside BC), you must self-assess it: report it on your next PST return, or, if you are not registered, file a casual remittance return by the end of the following month. Common mistakes, records and a checklist Common mistakes to avoid Not watching the $30,000 total and missing the date you had to register and start charging GST. Charging 5% GST on goods shipped to an HST province. Spending the GST and PST you collected and coming up short at filing time. Claiming ITCs without proper receipts or on personal purchases. Skipping nil returns or filing on paper. Forgetting to self-assess PST on taxable software or equipment bought from outside BC. Checklist Track your taxable sales every quarter and add up the last four quarters. Register for GST within 29 days of crossing $30,000 (or from day one if you drive taxi or rideshare). Check whether you must register for BC PST, or whether the small seller exemption applies. Keep every receipt and invoice that supports an ITC. Decide whether the Quick Method would save you time or money. Put your GST and PST due dates in your calendar and file electronically. Keep GST/HST records (sales invoices, receipts supporting ITCs, copies of returns) for 6 years from the end of the year they relate to, and PST records for 5 years, at your business or home in Canada. Sales tax rules have many exceptions, so if you are unsure about a product or customer, a tax professional can help. Want help with GST and PST for your business? title: Hiring contractors in BC: T4A, T5018 and contractor vs employee
description: Paying contractors in BC? Check employee vs contractor status, T4A and T5018 slip rules and 2026 deadlines, GST/HST and WorkSafeBC clearance letters.
text: Guides · Business tax Hiring contractors in BC: T4A, T5018 and contractor vs employee Paying freelancers, trades or other independent contractors is simpler than running payroll, but it still comes with duties. You need to be sure the person really is a contractor, report what you paid them on the right slip, and protect your business from someone else's unpaid WorkSafeBC premiums. Here's how it works for 2026. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 12, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short Calling someone a contractor doesn't make them one; the CRA looks at control, tools, risk and chance of profit. Report service fees over $500 a year to a contractor in box 048 of a T4A slip, without GST/HST. Construction businesses report subcontractor payments on a T5018 instead, due six months after their reporting period ends. For 2026 payments, T4A slips are due February 28, 2027; since that is a Sunday, March 1, 2027 is on time. If you file more than 5 slips for a calendar year, you must file them electronically. Get a WorkSafeBC clearance letter before and after a contractor works for you. On this page First, is the person really a contractor? Before the work starts: collect the right details T4A slips: reporting fees for services T5018 slips: the rule for construction businesses T4A or T5018? Deadlines, e-filing and penalties GST/HST on contractor invoices WorkSafeBC: protect yourself with a clearance letter Common mistakes and a checklist First, is the person really a contractor? An independent contractor (also called self-employed or a subcontractor) runs their own business and sells you a service. An employee works for you under your direction. The label you put on the contract does not settle it. The CRA looks at the real working relationship in two steps: What did you both intend? A written agreement helps show this. Do the facts back it up? The CRA checks each of these factors on its own and then together: Control: who decides how, when and where the work is done. Tools and equipment: who supplies and pays for them. Helpers: whether the worker can hire assistants or send someone else to do the job. Financial risk: whether the worker pays their own costs and could lose money. Investment and management: whether the worker has put money into a business of their own. Chance of profit: whether the worker can earn more by pricing jobs well, taking other clients and keeping costs down. Illustration: a graphic designer who has several clients, sets their own hours, uses their own computer and software, and sends you invoices is likely a contractor. A helper who works the shifts you set, with your tools, at an hourly rate, looks more like an employee. Getting this wrong is costly. If the CRA later decides the person was an employee, you can owe both the employee and employer shares of CPP and EI that you should have deducted, plus penalties and interest. If you are unsure, you or the worker can ask the CRA for a CPP/EI ruling (an official decision on the person's status). Payers can ask through My Business Account, or anyone can mail Form CPT1. The deadline is June 29 of the year after the work was done. If the person turns out to be an employee, our guide to hiring your first employee explains payroll. Before the work starts: collect the right details A few minutes of paperwork at the start saves a scramble at year-end. For each contractor, keep: Their legal name and address , and whether they are a person, a partnership or a corporation. Their identifying number: a Social Insurance Number (SIN) for an individual, or a business number (BN) for a partnership or corporation. You need this for the year-end slip. Their GST/HST number , if they charge you GST. A written agreement that describes the work, the price and who supplies what. A WorkSafeBC clearance letter (explained below). Most Canadian-resident contractors are paid in full: you do not take CPP, EI or income tax off their invoices. Paying a contractor who lives outside Canada for work done in Canada follows different rules, including tax withheld at source, so get advice before you pay. Tip: ask for the SIN or BN when you first sign up a contractor, not in February. The CRA can charge a $100 penalty each time you don't make a real effort to get a SIN. If you truly can't get it, you still file the slip on time without it. T4A slips: reporting fees for services A T4A slip is a year-end form that reports certain payments other than salary. When your business pays another business or a self-employed person for services, the yearly total goes in box 048, "Fees for services" . When a slip is needed Under the CRA's administrative policy, you issue a slip when your total payments to that contractor in the calendar year are more than $500 , or if you deducted any tax from a payment. Do not include GST/HST or PST in the box 048 amount. Enter the recipient's SIN for an individual, or their business number for a partnership or corporation. You also file a T4A Summary , which totals all your slips. If you don't already have one, you need a CRA payroll (RP) program account to file. Illustration: you paid a freelance web designer $2,000 plus $100 GST in 2026. You would report $2,000 in box 048 of their T4A, not $2,100. Due date for 2026 payments Slips go to the CRA and to each contractor by the last day of February after the year. For 2026 payments, that is February 28, 2027. Because that day is a Sunday, the CRA treats slips received (or postmarked) by Monday, March 1, 2027 as on time. Good to know: the CRA says it is currently not charging penalties for problems with box 048, except for businesses in the trucking industry, which face penalties starting with 2025 slips. The duty to report has not gone away, and the CRA uses these slips to check that contractors report their income. T5018 slips: the rule for construction businesses If your business's main activity is construction , meaning more than half of your business income comes from it, you report payments to subcontractors on a T5018, Statement of Contract Payments , instead of a T4A. What to report: payments to Canadian-resident subcontractors for construction services, whether paid by cheque, cash, barter or offset. Payments for goods only are left out. Threshold: you don't need to report a subcontractor you paid $500 or less in the year (not counting GST/HST). On the slip itself, the amount reported includes GST/HST and PST, which is different from the T4A. Reporting period: you can report on a calendar year or on your business's fiscal year. Due date: six months after the end of the reporting period you chose. If you use the 2026 calendar year, that works out to June 30, 2027. Copies: you file with the CRA. You don't have to give subcontractors a copy, though you may. Only report subcontractors you hired directly. A business that does some construction on the side but whose main business is something else does not need to file T5018s; it uses the T4A for service fees instead. T4A or T5018? Deadlines, e-filing and penalties T4A (box 048) T5018 Who files Businesses paying for services, outside the construction rule Businesses whose main activity is construction Who it reports Contractors paid more than $500 in the year Subcontractors paid more than $500 for construction services GST/HST in the amount? No Yes (GST/HST and PST included) Period Calendar year Calendar year or fiscal year Due date Last day of February (for 2026: February 28, 2027, on time by March 1, 2027) Six months after the period ends Copy to the contractor? Yes, by the same date Not required Filing online If you file more than 5 slips for a calendar year, you must file electronically, for example through your accounting software or the CRA's online services. Filing on paper when you should have filed online carries its own penalty, starting at $125 for 6 to 50 slips. Late filing penalties The CRA can charge a penalty for a late T4A return. It starts at $100 and grows with the number of slips and the number of days late, up to $7,500. Separately, not giving T4A slips to recipients on time can cost $25 a day, from $100 up to $2,500. Interest can be added on top. GST/HST on contractor invoices Many contractors add GST to their invoices, but not all of them have to. A contractor is a small supplier if their taxable sales were $30,000 or less over the last four calendar quarters. Small suppliers don't have to register for GST/HST, although they can choose to. Once they go over $30,000, they must register and start charging GST. What this means for you: If your business is registered for GST/HST, you can usually claim back the GST you pay on contractor invoices for your business as an input tax credit (ITC) . That is a credit on your GST return for tax you paid on business costs. To claim it, keep invoices that show the contractor's GST/HST number. You can check that the number is real with the CRA's free GST/HST Registry , using the number, the business name and the invoice date. If a contractor charges GST but isn't registered, you can't claim an ITC for it. Most businesses must claim ITCs within four years. For more on charging and claiming sales taxes in B.C., see our GST/HST and PST guide . WorkSafeBC: protect yourself with a clearance letter WorkSafeBC provides workers' compensation insurance in B.C. Whether you must cover a contractor depends on how independent they are. Independent businesses (for example, they have several clients, advertise to the public and bring their own major equipment) are generally not treated as your workers. They handle their own WorkSafeBC registration. Labour-only contractors who don't run an independent business may count as your workers. In that case you are responsible for their coverage and must pay premiums for them. A sole proprietor or partner is not automatically covered for their own injuries. They can buy optional Personal Coverage. WorkSafeBC can't tell you whether they have it, so ask the contractor for proof. If you hire a contractor who is registered with WorkSafeBC but isn't paying their premiums, you could be held liable for the premiums tied to the work they did for you. A clearance letter confirms a business is registered and in good standing. Get one before and after the contractor works for you. Most letters are available through WorkSafeBC's online clearance letter tool using the firm's account number or exact name. The letter must be addressed to you to count. Our WorkSafeBC guide explains registration and premiums for your own business. Common mistakes and a checklist Common mistakes Calling someone a contractor when you control their hours, tools and duties like an employer. Waiting until February to ask for a SIN or business number. Including GST/HST in box 048 of the T4A. A construction business sending T4As instead of T5018s, or the other way around. Filing more than 5 slips on paper. Skipping the WorkSafeBC clearance letter for a contractor who works on your job. Claiming an ITC on GST from a contractor whose GST number you never checked. Checklist Confirm the person is really a contractor; ask the CRA for a ruling if unsure. Collect their legal name, address, SIN or BN, and GST/HST number. Put the work, price and responsibilities in a written agreement. Get a WorkSafeBC clearance letter before and after the work. Track payments to each contractor through the year, without GST/HST (with it, for T5018 amounts). Decide whether you file T4As (most businesses) or T5018s (construction businesses). For 2026 payments, file T4A slips and the summary, and give contractors their copies, by February 28, 2027 (on time by March 1, 2027). File online if you have more than 5 slips. Good records make all of this easier. Our guide to CRA letters, reviews and audits explains what to expect if the CRA asks questions later. Want help with contractor slips? title: Hiring your first employee in BC: payroll made simple
description: Set up payroll for your first BC employee: CRA payroll account, CPP and EI for 2026 and 2027, remittance deadlines, T4s, ROEs, WorkSafeBC and BC pay rules.
text: Guides · Payroll Hiring your first employee in BC: payroll made simple Hiring your first employee is a big step, and it comes with new duties: deducting and sending CPP, EI and income tax, following BC's employment rules, and filing slips at year-end. Here's what to do, in order. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short Check the worker is truly an employee; the CRA looks at control, tools, financial risk and chance of profit, not just the contract. Open a CRA payroll (RP) account before your first remittance is due, and register with WorkSafeBC when you hire. For 2026 you match the employee's CPP and pay 1.4 times their EI premium; the base CPP rate drops from 4.95% to 4.75% each on January 1, 2027. Most new employers remit by the 15th of the following month; late remittances over $500 carry penalties of 3% to 10%. BC requires at least $18.25 an hour (since June 1, 2026), pay at least twice a month, and 4% vacation pay after 5 days. File T4 slips by the end of February and issue a Record of Employment when someone leaves or stops being paid. On this page Employee or contractor? Get this right first Set up your accounts before the first payday Paperwork for a new employee Payroll deductions: CPP, EI and income tax Sending deductions to the CRA (remitting) BC employment standards basics Taxable benefits in brief Year-end slips and when someone leaves Records, common mistakes and a checklist Employee or contractor? Get this right first Before you set up payroll, make sure the person really is an employee. Calling someone a contractor does not make them one. The CRA looks at the whole working relationship in two steps. What did you both intend? A written contract helps show this, but it is not the final word. Do the facts match? The CRA looks at who controls the work and the hours, who supplies the tools and equipment, whether the worker can hire helpers, whether the worker takes on financial risk and has invested in their own business, and whether they can make a profit or loss. Example: A shop assistant who works the hours you set, uses your till and is paid by the hour is almost certainly an employee. A bookkeeper who serves several clients, sets their own schedule, uses their own software and sends you invoices is more likely self-employed. If you get it wrong, you may face penalties for not deducting CPP, EI and income tax. If you are unsure, you or the worker can ask the CRA for a ruling through your CRA account or with Form CPT1. The request must be made by June 29 of the year after the year in question. Set up your accounts before the first payday 1. A CRA payroll account You need a payroll program account with the CRA. It is attached to your business number (BN) and ends in "RP". If you already have a BN (for example, for GST), add the payroll account to it rather than getting a new BN. You can register online through the CRA's Business Registration Online service or by mailing Form RC1. You must open the payroll account before your first remittance is due. That is normally the 15th of the month after the month you first take deductions off a pay cheque. 2. WorkSafeBC In BC, if your business hires one or more workers, whether full-time, part-time, casual or on contract, you must register with WorkSafeBC for workers' compensation coverage. Our WorkSafeBC guide explains registration, premiums and reporting step by step. If you are a sole proprietor and your spouse works for you, note that they are not automatically covered. 3. BC Employer Health Tax (usually not yet) BC's Employer Health Tax only applies once your total BC payroll for the year is over $1,000,000 . A business hiring its first employee will almost always be below that, so you don't need to register. Keep it in mind as you grow. Paperwork for a new employee Social Insurance Number (SIN): the employee must give you their SIN within 3 days of starting work. Check that the name and number are correct, since mistakes can affect their future CPP benefits. You can be charged a $100 penalty if you don't make a reasonable effort to get it. Temporary SINs starting with 9: these are common for newcomers on work or study permits. They expire with the immigration document, so check the expiry date and ask for an updated document when needed. Form TD1 (federal): every new employee fills one out. It tells you which tax credits they are claiming, which affects how much tax you deduct. Form TD1BC (provincial): needed if the employee claims more than the basic personal amount. Keep the TD1 forms on file; do not send them to the CRA. If an employee doesn't give you a TD1, deduct tax as if they claim only the basic personal amount. Employees only need a new form when their credits change, and should give it to you within 7 days of that change. Also put the job offer, pay rate, hours and start date in writing. It avoids disagreements later. Payroll deductions: CPP, EI and income tax Each payday you take three main deductions off the employee's gross pay, and you add your own employer share on top. Canada Pension Plan (CPP) For 2026, the employee pays 5.95% of pensionable earnings above a $3,500 yearly basic exemption, up to the year's maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE) of $74,600. The most an employee pays is $4,230.45, and you pay the same amount again as the employer. CPP2 (the second additional contribution) applies to earnings between $74,600 and $85,000 in 2026, at 4% each for employee and employer. It only matters for employees earning more than $74,600. Employment Insurance (EI) For 2026, the employee rate is $1.63 per $100 of insurable earnings, up to maximum insurable earnings of $68,900. As the employer, you pay 1.4 times the employee's premium. Changes for 2027 2026 2027 Base CPP rate (each of employee and employer) 4.95% 4.75% YMPE (first CPP ceiling) $74,600 $76,700 YAMPE (CPP2 ceiling) $85,000 $87,400 EI employee rate per $100 $1.63 $1.64 EI maximum insurable earnings $68,900 $70,800 The cut to the base CPP rate, from January 1, 2027, was passed into law in 2026. Check the CRA's CPP page for the full 2027 rates and maximums, and make sure your payroll software or calculator is updated for January. Income tax You also deduct federal and BC income tax, based on the employee's pay and their TD1 forms. The easiest way is the CRA's free Payroll Deductions Online Calculator (PDOC) , which works out CPP, EI and federal and provincial tax for each pay. Payroll software does the same. Use the current version: BC's tax withholding changed part-way through 2026, from July 1. Example: If your employee earns $2,000 in a pay period, you deduct their CPP, EI and income tax from that $2,000 and pay them the rest. You then send the CRA those deductions plus your matching CPP and your EI share (1.4 times theirs). Sending deductions to the CRA (remitting) The money you deduct belongs to the government. You hold it in trust and must send it, with your employer share, by the due date. Regular remitters: due by the 15th of the month after you paid the employee. Wages paid in March are due April 15. New small employers: if your payroll account has been open less than 12 months, your monthly withholdings are under $1,000, and you have a perfect compliance record on all your payroll and GST/HST accounts, you can remit quarterly: by April 15, July 15, October 15 and January 15. Check your CRA statement of account for the schedule that applies to you. If a due date falls on a weekend or public holiday, payment is on time if it arrives the next business day. Penalties Late remittances over $500 attract a penalty based on how late they are: How late Penalty 1 to 3 days 3% 4 or 5 days 5% 6 or 7 days 7% More than 7 days, or not remitted 10% Repeated late payments in the same year that are knowing or grossly negligent can face 20%. Separately, if you fail to deduct CPP, EI or tax at all, the CRA can charge 10% of what you should have deducted. Interest, compounded daily, is added too. Tip: remit when you run payroll rather than waiting for the deadline. A missed quarterly payment can also cost you quarterly remitting status. BC employment standards basics BC's Employment Standards Act sets minimum rules for most employees. The key ones for a new employer: Minimum wage: the general minimum wage is $18.25 an hour since June 1, 2026. It goes up each year in line with BC inflation. Paydays: pay employees at least twice a month, and within 8 days after the end of each pay period. A pay period can be no longer than 16 days. Vacation pay: after 5 calendar days of employment, employees earn vacation pay of at least 4% of their total wages, rising to 6% after 5 consecutive years. They also earn 2 weeks of vacation after 12 months, and 3 weeks after 5 years. Vacation pay is due at least 7 days before the vacation, or on each pay cheque if you both agree in writing. Statutory holidays: BC has 11: New Year's Day, Family Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, B.C. Day, Labour Day, National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Thanksgiving, Remembrance Day and Christmas Day. An employee qualifies for stat holiday pay (an average day's pay) after being employed for 30 calendar days and working or earning wages on 15 of the 30 days before the holiday. There are other rules on overtime, breaks, leaves and ending employment. If something is unclear, check the BC Employment Standards Branch. Taxable benefits in brief Pay isn't only wages. If you give an employee something of personal value, it may be a taxable benefit that you must add to their income on payroll and on their T4. Common examples: personal use of a company car, free or cheap housing, and allowances or reimbursements for personal expenses. Cash benefits (paid by cheque or direct deposit) are subject to CPP, EI and income tax. Non-cash benefits are generally subject to CPP and income tax, but not EI. Reasonable reimbursements of business travel costs are generally not taxable. A cell phone you own and provide for work is not a taxable benefit, but paying for the employee's own phone is. The CRA's Guide T4130 covers the details for each type of benefit. Year-end slips and when someone leaves T4 slips After each calendar year, prepare a T4 slip for each employee showing their pay and deductions, and a T4 Summary of the totals. File them with the CRA and give each employee their copy. The deadline is the last day of February. For 2026 pay, that is February 28, 2027, which is a Sunday, so filing by Monday, March 1, 2027 is on time. If you have more than 5 slips, you must file electronically. Record of Employment (ROE) When an employee stops working for you or has an interruption of earnings (generally 7 days in a row with no work and no pay, such as a layoff or quitting), you must issue a Record of Employment to Service Canada. They use it to decide EI benefits. Issue one even if the employee doesn't plan to apply for EI. Electronic ROE (through ROE Web or payroll software): for weekly, every-two-weeks or twice-a-month pay, within 5 calendar days after the end of the pay period in which the interruption happened. Paper ROE: within 5 calendar days of the interruption, or of when you learn about it. Records, common mistakes and a checklist Records to keep Keep payroll records (hours, pay, deductions, TD1 forms, remittances, T4s and ROEs) for at least 6 years after the year they relate to, at your business or home in Canada. BC's Employment Standards Act also requires payroll records for each employee. Common mistakes to avoid Treating a worker as a contractor when the facts point to employment. Forgetting the employer share of CPP and EI when budgeting for a new hire. Paying remittances late, even by a day or two. Using an out-of-date calculator or tables after rates change on January 1. Paying only once a month, which breaks BC's twice-a-month rule. Forgetting vacation pay or stat holiday pay. Not registering with WorkSafeBC once you hire. Checklist for your first hire Confirm the worker is an employee, not a contractor. Open a CRA payroll (RP) account and register with WorkSafeBC. Collect the SIN, TD1 and (if needed) TD1BC. Choose payroll software or use PDOC, and set at least twice-monthly paydays. Pay at least BC minimum wage, plus vacation and stat holiday pay. Remit deductions plus your share by the 15th of the next month (or quarterly, if eligible). Issue T4s by the end of February and an ROE when employment ends. If you'd rather not handle payroll yourself, a tax professional can help set it up correctly from the first pay. Want help setting up payroll? title: International students and work-permit holders: taxes and benefits in Canada
description: How tax residency works on a study or work permit, your SIN, work limits, scholarships, the tuition credit, benefits you can get, B.C. MSP and filing.
text: Guides · Newcomers International students and work-permit holders: taxes and benefits in Canada Studying or working in Canada on a temporary permit? You may owe tax here, and you may also be able to get benefits. This guide covers what is different for international students and temporary workers in B.C., from your SIN and work hours to tuition slips and filing your return. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 6, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short Your tax residency depends on your ties to Canada, such as a home here, not on your permit type. Eligible students can work up to 24 hours a week off campus during classes, and without a weekly limit in scheduled breaks. Full-time students usually pay no tax on scholarships, and unused tuition amounts can be carried forward to a year you owe tax. Tax residents 19 and older can get the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit by applying with Form RC151 and filing each year. Temporary residents can get the Canada child benefit after 18 months in Canada, with a valid permit in the 19th month. File your 2026 return by April 30, 2027, even with little or no income. On this page Are you a Canadian resident for tax? Your SIN, work limits and payroll deductions Scholarships, tuition and money from home Benefits you may be able to get B.C. health coverage for students Filing your return Common mistakes to avoid Are you a Canadian resident for tax? Your study permit or work permit decides whether you can study or work here. It does not decide how Canada taxes you. For tax, what counts is your residency status , which the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) works out from your residential ties : the links between your daily life and Canada. Significant ties are a home in Canada, a spouse or common-law partner in Canada, or dependants (such as children) in Canada. Secondary ties include a car or furniture here, a Canadian bank account or credit card, a B.C. driver's licence, memberships in local clubs or religious groups, and provincial health coverage. Many international students and most work-permit holders who rent a place and live here year-round become residents for tax. A resident reports world income (income from every country) from the day they settled here. The CRA notes that a student who goes home for long stretches, or lives abroad when not in classes, may not have set up significant ties. The four possible results Resident: you have significant ties, even if you lived here only part of the year. Non-resident: no significant ties and fewer than 183 days in Canada in the year. You are taxed only on certain Canadian income, such as pay for work done here. Deemed resident: no significant ties, but 183 days or more in Canada in a calendar year (and not treated as a resident of your home country under a tax treaty). You report world income for the whole year and pay a federal surtax (an extra federal tax) instead of B.C. tax. You can't claim B.C. credits. Deemed non-resident: you have ties here, but a tax treaty (an agreement between two countries that decides which one taxes you) says you are a resident of the other country. Non-resident rules then apply. Not sure which applies? You can send the CRA Form NR74 , Determination of Residency Status (entering Canada) , for its opinion. The opinion isn't binding, so the CRA can look at your situation again later. If you are a resident, our first-year guide for newcomers explains your first return, your entry date and property you brought with you. Your SIN, work limits and payroll deductions Your Social Insurance Number You need a Social Insurance Number (SIN) , a nine-digit number from Service Canada, to work and to file a tax return. A SIN given to a temporary resident always starts with 9 and expires on the same date as your permit . When you get a new permit with a later date, update your SIN record. If your SIN expires while you are waiting for IRCC to decide on your permit extension, you can keep working until the decision. How much students can work off campus Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) sets the work rules, not the CRA. As of its page updated April 15, 2026: Eligible full-time students can work up to 24 hours a week off campus during an academic session, counting all jobs together. This applies even if your permit still says 20 hours, as long as you meet the other conditions. During a scheduled break set by your school (such as summer, winter break or reading week), there is no weekly limit. If your program has no scheduled breaks, the 24-hour limit applies all year. Your study permit must show work conditions, and you can't work off campus while on an authorized leave from studies. Check IRCC's rules before you take extra shifts. Working more than you're allowed is an immigration problem, not a tax one, and it can affect your permit. Paying tax on the income doesn't make the work allowed. What comes off your pay cheque When you start a job, you fill in a TD1 form so your employer knows how much income tax to hold back. Your employer also deducts Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contributions (from age 18) and Employment Insurance (EI) premiums, and adds its own matching share. Being on a temporary permit doesn't exempt you from these. By the end of February, your employer must give you a T4 slip showing your pay and deductions for the year. If too much tax was held back, you get it back when you file. Running your own business, or hiring help, works differently: see our payroll guide for B.C. employers . Scholarships, tuition and money from home Scholarships and bursaries Scholarships and bursaries from your school are reported on a T4A slip (box 105). If you are a full-time student in a qualifying post-secondary program, they are usually not taxable at all . For part-time students, the tax-free part is limited to tuition and required program materials, plus a $500 basic exemption. Research grants and postdoctoral fellowships follow different rules. The tuition tax credit and your T2202 Your college or university gives you a T2202 , the Tuition and Enrolment Certificate , usually through your student account. It shows the eligible tuition you paid in the calendar year. Fees paid to each school must be more than $100 . You claim the amount on Schedule 11 of your return. The tuition amount is a non-refundable credit : it lowers tax you owe, but it doesn't pay you cash if you owe nothing. Many international students earn little while studying, so they don't need the credit right away. In that case you can: Carry it forward to a later year when you owe tax, such as your first year of full-time work. You must use it in the first year you owe tax. Transfer up to $5,000 of the current year's federal amount (less what you used yourself) to a spouse or common-law partner, parent or grandparent. This only helps if that person files a Canadian return and owes Canadian tax, so it rarely helps parents who live abroad. Once an amount is carried forward, it can't be transferred later. File every year, even with no income. The CRA says that if you are carrying tuition forward and skip filing a return for a year, the amount won't carry forward and you lose it. Each return also keeps your benefits flowing. Illustration (made-up numbers): Mei pays $20,000 of tuition in 2026 and earns $8,000 from a part-time job. She owes no tax, so her tuition amount is carried forward. In 2028 she starts a full-time job and uses the carried-forward amount to cut her tax that year. Moving costs If your T2202 has an amount in box C (full-time attendance), you may be able to deduct moving costs. For a move to attend school, the deduction only reduces the taxable part of scholarships, bursaries and research grants. Your new home must be at least 40 kilometres closer to the school or new job. Money your family sends you Most gifts and inheritances aren't taxed in Canada, so money your parents send for fees and rent isn't income. But interest or other income you earn on that money is taxable once you are a resident. If you have bank deposits or investments abroad, see our newcomers guide for foreign income and the T1135 form. Benefits you may be able to get Benefits are paid by the CRA based on your tax return. Being a temporary resident doesn't rule you out, but each benefit has its own rules. Benefit Can students and temporary workers get it? How Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (formerly the GST/HST credit) Yes, if you are a tax resident, 19 or older, and your income is low or modest Form RC151 in your first year, then file a return every year Canada child benefit (CCB) Yes, for children under 18, once you have lived in Canada for 18 months and hold a valid permit in the 19th month Forms RC66 and RC66SCH B.C. family benefit Yes, if your child is registered for the CCB Automatic, paid with the CCB Canada carbon rebate No. It is closed, and it was never paid in B.C. Not applicable B.C. climate action tax credit No. B.C. cancelled it, with the final payment in April 2025 Not applicable Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (CGEB) The CGEB is a tax-free payment made four times a year to people with low and modest incomes. It replaced the GST/HST credit. You must be a resident for tax at the end of the month before, and at the start of the month of, each payment. For the current period, payments are scheduled for July 5, 2026 , October 5, 2026 , January 5, 2027 and April 5, 2027 , based on your 2025 return. In the year you become a resident, apply with Form RC151 . After that, filing your return each year is how you keep getting it. Budget 2026, tabled on November 5, 2026, proposes a one-time extra CGEB payment in early 2027; see our Budget 2026 article . Canada child benefit and the B.C. family benefit The Canada child benefit (CCB) is a tax-free monthly payment for children under 18. If you or your spouse is a temporary resident, you qualify only after living in Canada for the previous 18 months , and you must hold a valid permit in the 19th month . A permit marked "does not confer status" doesn't count. Once your child is registered for the CCB, the B.C. family benefit is added to the same monthly payment. Our CCB and B.C. family benefits guide has the details. If you are not a resident of Canada for tax, you can't get the CGEB. B.C. health coverage for students B.C.'s Medical Services Plan (MSP) is the provincial health insurance that pays for doctor visits and hospital care. It isn't a tax, but it is a monthly cost that many students don't plan for. If your study permit is valid for six months or longer and you are in B.C. for at least six months of the year, enrolling in MSP is mandatory . Each international student pays a health fee of $75 a month , whatever their income. Coverage starts after a waiting period: the rest of the month you arrive plus two more months. Keep private health insurance until then. A spouse without their own study permit doesn't pay the student fee. A family member with their own study permit of six months or more pays it too. Apply as soon as you arrive. Work-permit holders should check their own MSP eligibility, as the student fee rules apply to study permit holders. Filing your return Your 2026 return is due on April 30, 2027 , and any balance owing is due the same day. If you or your spouse or common-law partner are self-employed, you have until June 15, 2027 to file, but tax owing is still due April 30, 2027. File even if you earned little or nothing. A return is how you: get back extra tax your employer held back; keep CGEB payments and child benefits coming; record your tuition amount so it can be carried forward. Gather your T4 slips, T4A slips, your T2202, and records of any income from outside Canada. The CRA aims to send your notice of assessment (its summary of your return) about two weeks after you file online, or about eight weeks for paper. Save a copy, as you may be asked for it later. Our guide to often-missed tax credits lists other amounts worth checking. When you finish your studies or leave Moving from a study permit to a work permit doesn't change your tax status by itself: your ties to Canada do. If you leave Canada for good, you may stop being a resident on your departure date. You'll file a final return and tell the CRA, so benefits stop on time. Our guide to leaving Canada covers the steps. Common mistakes to avoid Assuming a temporary permit means you're not a tax resident. Your ties decide it, not your permit. Not filing because your income was low. You can miss benefits and refunds, and the CRA warns you can lose tuition carried forward. Forgetting the T2202. Download it from your school's student portal every year. Expecting your parents abroad to use your tuition transfer. It only helps someone who owes Canadian tax. Letting your SIN lapse. Update your SIN record whenever you get a new permit. Working past your permitted hours. Check IRCC's current rules, especially between breaks and classes. Applying for child benefits too early, or not at all. Note the date you'll pass 18 months in Canada and apply then. Leaving out income from abroad. Once you are a resident, interest, rent or other income earned outside Canada belongs on your return. Studying or working in Canada on a permit? We help international students and temporary workers confirm their residency status, apply for benefits, claim tuition and scholarship amounts correctly and file on time each year. title: Leaving Canada? What happens to your taxes
description: Becoming a non-resident, your final return, departure tax, T1161 and T1244, withholding on Canadian income, and what happens to your RRSP, TFSA and FHSA.
text: Guides · Personal tax Leaving Canada? What happens to your taxes Moving abroad changes how Canada taxes you, and the year you leave has its own rules and forms. Here's what to sort out before and after you go. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 In short You become a non-resident when you cut your residential ties, usually on the latest of when you leave, when your family leaves, or when you become resident elsewhere. Your final return reports world income up to your departure date and only certain Canadian income after it. Most property is treated as sold at market value when you leave, but Canadian real estate and registered plans like RRSPs and TFSAs are not. File Form T1161 if your property is worth over $25,000; you can defer departure tax with Form T1244. After you leave, Canadian payers usually withhold 25% on income like rent, pensions and RRSP withdrawals, unless a treaty lowers it. Stop TFSA contributions once you are a non-resident, and repay any HBP or LLP balance within 60 days of leaving. On this page When you stop being a Canadian resident Your departure date Your final (departure-year) tax return Departure tax: the deemed sale of your property Canadian income after you leave Your RRSP, TFSA, FHSA, HBP and LLP Benefits, banks and other loose ends Checklist before and after you leave When you stop being a Canadian resident Canada taxes people based on residency , not citizenship. You become an emigrant for tax when you leave Canada to live in another country and cut your residential ties , the links between your life and Canada. Significant ties: a home in Canada, a spouse or common-law partner in Canada, and dependants in Canada. Secondary ties: personal property such as a car or furniture, social ties, economic ties such as bank accounts and credit cards, a Canadian driver's licence, and provincial health insurance. Cutting ties usually means selling or giving up your Canadian home, setting up a permanent home abroad, having your spouse and children move too, and moving your personal and social life to the new country. Three ways the CRA may see you Status What it means Factual resident You live or work abroad but keep significant ties here, such as a home or family in Canada. You are still treated as a resident of Canada for tax. Deemed non-resident You still have ties to Canada, but under a tax treaty you are a resident of the other country. You are treated like an emigrant. Non-resident (emigrant) You have cut your significant ties. Canada taxes only certain Canadian income. A separate rule can make a person a deemed resident : someone without significant ties who stays in Canada for 183 days or more in a year. If your situation is unclear, you can ask the CRA for its opinion using Form NR73 , Determination of Residency Status (leaving Canada) . It is optional. Your departure date Your departure date is the day you become a non-resident. It is usually the latest of these dates: the day you leave Canada; the day your spouse or common-law partner and dependants leave Canada; the day you become a resident of your new country. Example: you fly to your new country on June 1, but your spouse and children stay to finish the school year and join you on July 15. Your departure date is usually July 15. Exception: if you lived in another country before and are going back there, you generally become a non-resident on the day you leave, even if your spouse stays behind for a while to sell your home. If you don't need to file a return for the year you leave, still tell the CRA your departure date as soon as you can. Your final (departure-year) tax return In the year you leave, you file a return that covers two periods, with your departure date on page 1. Use the BC forms if you lived in BC on your departure date. Before you left: report your world income (Canadian and foreign) in Canadian dollars. After you left: report only certain Canadian income, such as pay for work done in Canada. Other Canadian income, like interest and rent, is usually handled by withholding at source (see below). Credits and deductions Your federal non-refundable credits, such as the basic personal amount, are generally limited to the part of the year you were a resident. BC credits may be limited too. Most deductions still apply. Moving expenses for a move abroad generally aren't deductible, except for certain full-time students. BC refundable credits are generally not available unless you were a resident on December 31. Due dates The return is due April 30 of the year after you leave, or June 15 if you or your spouse carried on a business. Any balance owing is due by April 30 either way. For example, if you leave in 2026, the usual deadline is April 30, 2027. Departure tax: the deemed sale of your property When you leave, the CRA treats you as if you sold most of your property at its fair market value (FMV) , the price it would fetch on the open market, on your departure date, and bought it straight back. This is a deemed disposition , often called "departure tax." You pay tax on any gain even though you sold nothing. Example: you bought shares in a non-registered account for $20,000 and they are worth $50,000 when you leave. You report a $30,000 capital gain on your final return. Property that is not deemed sold Canadian real estate , such as your house, condo or rental property, and Canadian resource and timber property. It stays taxable in Canada when you actually sell it later. Property of a business you carry on through a permanent establishment in Canada. Registered plans and pensions: RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, RESPs, RDSPs, pension plans, annuities, most employee stock options taxed in Canada, and Canadian life insurance (other than segregated funds). Short-term residents: if you lived in Canada for 60 months or less in the 10 years before leaving, property you owned when you last arrived (or inherited after arriving) is not deemed sold. The forms Form T1243 calculates the gains and losses from the deemed sale. You then report them on Schedule 3 of your return. Form T1161 , the list of properties, is required if the FMV of everything you own is more than $25,000 when you leave. Leave out cash and bank deposits, registered plans, and personal-use items (household goods, clothing, cars) worth under $10,000. It is due by your filing due date even if you don't otherwise need to file a return. The late-filing penalty is $25 a day , at least $100 and up to $2,500 . Deferring the tax: Form T1244 You can choose to put off paying departure tax until you actually sell the property, with no interest , by filing Form T1244 by April 30 of the year after you leave. If the federal tax you are deferring is more than $16,500 , you must give the CRA adequate security (a guarantee of payment), and you may need security for provincial tax too. Contact the CRA before April 30 to arrange it. Get values on your departure date. Save statements and valuations showing what each investment was worth the day you left. If you later move back, you may be able to elect to undo the deemed sale on property you still own, and you will need these numbers. Canadian income after you leave Withholding tax (Part XIII) Once you are a non-resident, Canadian payers must hold back non-resident tax (called Part XIII tax) on income such as dividends, rent, pensions, OAS, CPP, RRSP and RRIF payments and annuities. The usual rate is 25% , unless a tax treaty between Canada and your new country lowers it. You get an NR4 slip showing what was paid and withheld. This is usually your final Canadian tax on that income, so you generally don't file a return for it. The section 217 election If most of your income is Canadian pension-type income, such as CPP, OAS, workplace pensions, RRSP or RRIF payments, or EI, you can choose to file a Canadian return under section 217 . You are then taxed at normal resident rates and may get back some or all of the 25% withheld. The CRA only applies the election if it helps you, and the return must be filed on time. Keeping a Canadian rental property Your tenant or property manager must withhold 25% of the gross rent and send it to the CRA. With an approved Form NR6 , filed with a Canadian agent (a resident who acts for you) on or before January 1 each year or before the first rent payment is due, the 25% is withheld on the net rent (rent minus expenses) instead. Under section 216 you can file a separate return for your rental income to pay tax on the net profit and get back extra tax withheld. If you used an NR6, you file this return by June 30 of the next year. Without an NR6, you generally have two years from the end of the year to file it. Selling Canadian property later When a non-resident sells taxable Canadian property , such as Canadian real estate, you must tell the CRA within 10 days of the sale (or before a proposed sale) using Form T2062 , along with payment or security for the tax. The CRA then issues a certificate of compliance . Without one, the buyer may hold back 25% of the price (50% for some property). Late notice costs $25 a day, at least $100 and up to $2,500. You must also file a return for the year of sale by April 30 of the next year. Your RRSP, TFSA, FHSA, HBP and LLP Account What happens when you leave RRSP / RRIF Not deemed sold. You can keep it. Withdrawals after you leave have 25% non-resident tax withheld (less if a treaty applies). A section 217 election may lower the tax. TFSA You can keep it, and its income and withdrawals aren't taxed in Canada. No new room builds for any full year you are a non-resident. Withdrawals are added back to your room only if you become a resident again. FHSA You can keep it, but you can't make a tax-free qualifying withdrawal for a home while you are a non-resident. Taxable withdrawals have 25% withheld, unless a treaty lowers it. Home Buyers' Plan (HBP) Repay the remaining balance by the earlier of when you file your return for the year you leave, or 60 days after you become a non-resident. Anything not repaid is added to that year's income. Lifelong Learning Plan (LLP) Same deadline: repay the balance, or it is added to your income for the year you leave. Don't contribute to your TFSA after you leave. A contribution made while you are a non-resident is taxed at 1% for each month it stays in the account, until you withdraw it or move back. Your new country may also tax TFSA income, so check its rules. Benefits, banks and other loose ends Benefits stop. As a non-resident you are generally not eligible for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit or the Canada child benefit (or related provincial payments such as the B.C. family benefit). Tell the CRA your departure date. If payments keep arriving after you leave, contact the CRA right away. Tell your banks and payers. Let every Canadian bank, brokerage, pension plan and other payer know you are now a non-resident, so they withhold the right tax and issue NR4 slips. Update your address with the CRA and keep access to My Account. You will still need it for NR4 slips, rental returns and correspondence. Keep records of your departure date, property values and returns for at least six years. Checklist before and after you leave Decide your departure date and keep proof (tickets, lease or sale documents, new-country residence papers). Consider whether you are cutting your ties; use NR73 if you want the CRA's view. Get the fair market value of investments and other property on your departure date. Complete T1243 and, if your property is worth over $25,000, T1161 . Decide whether to defer departure tax with T1244 (by April 30 of the next year), and arrange security if federal tax is over $16,500. Repay any HBP or LLP balance within 60 days of leaving, or plan for the tax. Stop TFSA contributions from your departure date. If you keep a rental, appoint a Canadian agent and file NR6 before rent starts. Tell the CRA, your banks and other payers that you are a non-resident. File your final return by April 30 of the year after you leave. Leaving Canada with investments, a home or registered plans involves several one-time decisions, and a tax professional can help you plan them before you go. Planning a move abroad? We can help you confirm your departure date, calculate departure tax, prepare your final return with T1243, T1161 and T1244, and set up NR6 and section 216 filings for a Canadian rental you keep. title: New to Canada? Your first-year tax guide
description: When tax residency starts, benefits to apply for, your first return, property you bring, T1135, and TFSA and RRSP room for newcomers to Canada.
text: Guides · Newcomers New to Canada? Your first-year tax guide Your first year in Canada brings a new tax system, new forms and new benefits. This guide walks you through what to do, from the day you arrive to your first tax return and beyond. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short For most newcomers, tax residency starts the day you settle in Canada with ties such as a home or family here. Apply for benefits like the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit and Canada child benefit right away, without waiting for a tax return. On your first return, report world income only from your residency date, and expect some credits to be reduced for the part year. Property you own on arrival gets a new cost equal to its value that day, so keep proof of that value. You don't file Form T1135 in your first year, but from the second year you must if your foreign assets cost more than $100,000. TFSA room starts from your residency date ($7,000 for 2026), and RRSP room builds once you report Canadian earned income. On this page When you become a Canadian resident for tax Your SIN, or a temporary tax number Apply for benefits before your first tax return Filing your first tax return Property you owned when you arrived Reporting foreign assets: Form T1135 TFSA and RRSP room for newcomers Notices of assessment and CRA scams Your first-year checklist When you become a Canadian resident for tax For tax, what matters is your residency , not your immigration status. Your permit or PR card shows whether you can live, work or study here. Your tax residency decides what Canada can tax. For most newcomers, tax residency starts on the first day you live in Canada. The CRA looks at your residential ties , the links between your life and Canada: Significant ties: a home in Canada, a spouse or common-law partner in Canada, and dependants (such as children) in Canada. Secondary ties: personal property like a car or furniture, social ties, economic ties such as a Canadian bank account or credit card, a Canadian driver's licence, and provincial health insurance. This applies to permanent residents, work and study permit holders, and protected persons alike. A student or worker on a temporary permit can still be a full tax resident if they have set up their life here. Someone who has no significant ties but stays in Canada for 183 days or more in a year can be a deemed resident . If you are unsure of your status, you can ask the CRA for its opinion using Form NR74 , Determination of Residency Status (entering Canada) . Most people with a home and family here won't need it. Your SIN, or a temporary tax number A Social Insurance Number (SIN) is a nine-digit number you need to work, get benefits and credits, and open most bank accounts. You apply through Service Canada. Keep it private: only give it to employers, banks and government when they truly need it. If Service Canada can't give you a SIN, the CRA can issue a temporary tax number (TTN) . You send your benefit application or tax return without a SIN, attach a letter explaining why, and you can include certified copies of identity documents to speed things up. A TTN lets you apply for benefits, file returns and register for a CRA account. Once you have a SIN or TTN, register for a CRA account (My Account). It shows your benefits, notices and limits, and lets you send information online. Apply for benefits before your first tax return Many newcomers miss months of payments because they wait for their first tax return. You don't have to wait. You can apply as soon as you are a resident. Which form to use Your situation What to send No children RC151 web form online, for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit Children under 19, not applying for CCB Paper RC151 by mail to your tax centre, with proof of birth for each child Children under 18 and eligible for the Canada child benefit RC66 plus RC66SCH (status in Canada and income). RC66 also covers the groceries benefit, so you don't need RC151 Getting CCB with a spouse or partner who was a non-resident for part or all of the year Their income through the online Statement of Income, or Form CTB9 The benefits Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (CGEB): a tax-free payment made four times a year to people with low and modest incomes. It replaced the GST/HST credit in July 2026. Only one application is needed per household. Canada child benefit (CCB): a tax-free monthly payment for children under 18. You or your spouse must be a citizen, permanent resident, protected person (with a positive decision from the Immigration and Refugee Board) or temporary resident. Temporary residents can qualify from the 19th month after living in Canada for the previous 18 months, with a valid permit in that 19th month. Refugee claimants who hold only a Refugee Protection Claimant Document aren't eligible. B.C. family benefit: once your child is registered for the CCB and you file returns, BC automatically pays this benefit together with your CCB each month. No separate application is needed. Reporting your income from before you arrived Benefits are based on family income, so the CRA asks for your (and your spouse's) world income for up to two years before you became a resident . You report it on a Statement of Income (SOI) , even if the amount was zero. Convert amounts to Canadian dollars using the Bank of Canada exchange rate on the date you received the income. You can send it online through My Account (it updates right away), by mail or by phone. Reporting this income doesn't mean Canada taxes it. Income you earned abroad before becoming a resident isn't subject to Canadian tax. Have these ready: marital status, date of entry, immigration documents, proof of birth for children, and income details. Documents not in English or French need a copy of the original and an acceptable translation. Keep your payments going. If you are on a temporary permit, send the CRA your new permit before the current one expires, or proof that you applied to extend it. Tell the CRA right away about changes, such as a child moving out. Filing your first tax return When it's due You file your first return for the year you arrive, by the usual deadline in the following spring. For example, someone who arrived in 2025 filed their 2025 return by April 30, 2026. The deadline is April 30 of the next year, or June 15 if you or your spouse is self-employed (any tax owing is still due April 30). File every year after that, even with no income: it keeps your benefits flowing. Your date of entry On page 1 of the return, you enter the date you became a resident for tax. Example: if you arrived and set up significant ties on June 8, you enter it as month and day, "0608". What income to report After you became a resident: your world income , from Canada and every other country, in Canadian dollars. That includes rent from a flat back home, interest on a foreign bank deposit and foreign dividends. Before you became a resident: only certain Canadian income, such as pay for work done in Canada, business income from a business carried on in Canada, and taxable gains on taxable Canadian property. Protected persons generally don't report money received from a charity or individual while they were non-residents, but wages from a charity are taxable. Credits are reduced for a part year Many non-refundable credits, such as the basic personal amount (the income you can earn before paying federal tax), are cut in proportion to the days you were a resident. The formula is days resident divided by 365. If you became a resident on July 1, you get roughly half the full amount. Some credits aren't reduced for the resident period. These include CPP and EI contributions, the Canada employment amount, tuition, medical expenses, donations, student loan interest and the home buyers' amount. For your months before arrival, extra credits apply only if your Canadian income was at least 90% of your net world income for that time. Avoiding double tax Foreign tax credit: if another country also taxed income you report in Canada, you may claim a federal foreign tax credit on Form T2209 . Provinces have similar credits. Tax treaties: Canada has tax treaties with many countries that decide which country can tax which income. Some foreign income that a treaty exempts (certain pensions, for example) is still reported, then deducted on line 25600. Other first-year points You use the BC tax forms if you lived in BC on December 31. Moving expenses to Canada generally aren't deductible, except for certain full-time students with taxable Canadian scholarships. Spousal or child support you pay may be deductible even if the recipient lives abroad. Keep receipts and records for at least six years after you file. Property you owned when you arrived When you become a resident, the CRA treats most property you already own, such as shares, jewellery, paintings or collections, as if you sold it and bought it back at its fair market value (FMV) on the day your residency started. FMV is the price it would sell for between unrelated people. That value becomes your cost base for Canadian tax. When you later sell, give away or lose the property, Canada taxes only the gain after you arrived. Example: you bought shares abroad for $10,000. They were worth $30,000 when you arrived, and you sell them years later for $40,000. For Canadian tax, your gain starts from $30,000, so it is $10,000, not $30,000. Get proof of value now. Save broker statements, bank balances and, for property like real estate, a valuation as of your arrival date. Finding these years later is hard, and without them you may be taxed on gains made before you came. Reporting foreign assets: Form T1135 Form T1135 , the foreign income verification statement, tells the CRA about money and investments you hold outside Canada. Not in your first year. You don't file T1135 for the tax year you first became a resident. From the second year, you must file it if the total cost of your specified foreign property was more than $100,000 at any time in the year. For property you owned on arrival, the cost is its FMV on the day you became a resident. What counts: foreign bank accounts and deposits, shares of foreign companies (even held through a Canadian broker), foreign rental property, and land held as an investment. What doesn't count: property used mainly for personal use (such as a family home abroad you use yourself), personal items like jewellery and art, and investments inside your RRSP or TFSA. Example: a $75,000 fixed deposit abroad plus $35,000 of foreign shares totals $110,000, so T1135 is required, even if you cashed some out before December 31. T1135 is due with your tax return. Penalties can apply for filing late or leaving things out, so don't skip it. TFSA and RRSP room for newcomers Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) Your TFSA room starts building on the day you become a resident, if you are 18 or older. You get the full yearly limit for the year you arrive, even for a part year, but no room for years before you lived here. For 2026, the limit is $7,000. So an adult who became a resident in September 2026 has $7,000 of room for 2026, not the total since 2009. Over-contributing is costly, so check your room in My Account before you put in large amounts. Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) RRSP room comes from earned income (mainly salary and self-employment income) reported on a Canadian return: generally 18% of the previous year's earned income, up to a yearly maximum. Because you have no Canadian return yet, you generally can't deduct RRSP contributions in your first year of filing. Your room appears after your first return is assessed. Notices of assessment and CRA scams Keep every notice of assessment After you file, the CRA sends a notice of assessment (NOA) , a summary of your return and any refund or balance. Banks, landlords and immigration programs often ask for it, and it shows your RRSP limit. Save a PDF copy each year from My Account. Watch for scams Newcomers are frequent targets of fake "CRA" calls and texts. The real CRA will never: threaten to arrest or deport you, or send you to prison; demand immediate payment by Interac e-transfer, gift cards, prepaid credit cards or cryptocurrency; send refunds or benefits by e-transfer or text message; contact you through WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger or other messaging apps; ask for personal or financial information by email or voicemail. If in doubt, hang up. Sign in to My Account, or find the CRA's phone number on canada.ca and call yourself. Report scams to your local police and the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. Your first-year checklist Note your date of arrival and when you set up ties (home, family, bank account). Get your SIN (or a TTN) and register for My Account . Apply for benefits: RC151 , or RC66 and RC66SCH if you have children. Report your world income for the two years before arrival (Statement of Income or CTB9). Record the value of everything you owned on arrival, with proof. Keep records of foreign income and foreign tax paid after you arrived. File your first return by April 30 of the next year, with your entry date. From the second year, check whether your foreign assets cost more than $100,000 (T1135). Check TFSA and RRSP room in My Account before contributing. Save every notice of assessment, and ignore threatening "CRA" calls. A newcomer's first return is one of the trickier ones to get right. A tax professional can help, especially if you have income or property abroad. Just arrived in Canada?
