title: Tax credits and deductions BC families often miss
description: Medical expenses, disability and caregiver credits, tuition, child care, donations, B.C. renter's credit and more, plus how to fix a past return.
text: Guides · Personal tax Tax credits and deductions BC families often miss Every year, families leave money on the table by missing claims they're entitled to. Here are the credits and deductions we most often find missing on B.C. returns, how they work, and how to fix a past return if you missed one. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 · Figures for 2025 tax year In short A deduction lowers your income; a credit lowers your tax directly, and refundable credits are paid even if you owe nothing. Medical expenses count once they pass 3% of net income or $2,834 (2025), whichever is less, and one spouse can claim for the family. The disability tax credit unlocks other help, including the child disability benefit and the RDSP. Pool both spouses' donations on one return: gifts above $200 earn a much higher credit rate. B.C. renters may get up to $400 a year through the renter's tax credit on Form BC479. You can ask the CRA to fix a past return, but refunds aren't issued for requests made more than 10 years after the tax year. On this page Credits and deductions: what's the difference? Medical expenses: the claim families miss most Disability tax credit and caregiver amounts Child care, moving and work costs Students and recent graduates Homes, renovations and donations Working families, renters and seniors Missed something? How to fix a past return Checklist before you file Credits and deductions: what's the difference? A deduction lowers your income before tax is worked out. Its value depends on your tax rate: the higher your income, the more a deduction saves. Child care, moving expenses and union dues are deductions. A non-refundable tax credit lowers the tax you owe. Most federal credits are worth the lowest federal tax rate times the claim: 14.5% for 2025 and 14% for 2026 . So a $1,000 credit amount saves $145 of federal tax on a 2025 return. If you owe no tax, a non-refundable credit gives you nothing back, although some can be transferred or carried forward. A refundable credit is paid to you even if you owe no tax. The Canada workers benefit and the B.C. renter's tax credit work this way. B.C. has its own version of many credits, so one claim often saves both federal and provincial tax. Figures below are for the 2025 tax year (the return filed in spring 2026) unless we say otherwise. Medical expenses: the claim families miss most Many people assume their medical bills are too small to matter. Often the threshold is lower than they think. How the threshold works You claim the part of your eligible expenses that is above the lower of: 3% of your net income , or $2,834 (for 2025). Example: your net income is $40,000, so 3% is $1,200. If your family paid $3,000 in eligible expenses, you can claim $1,800. At 14.5%, that's about $261 off your federal tax, plus a B.C. credit on top. Rules that work in your favour Any 12-month period. You don't have to use the calendar year. For a 2025 return you can pick any 12 months ending in 2025, as long as those expenses weren't claimed for 2024. Choose the window with the most expenses. One spouse claims for the family. You can group expenses for yourself, your spouse or common-law partner, and your children under 18. The spouse with the lower net income often gets the bigger claim. Other relatives. You can also claim for adult children, grandchildren, parents, grandparents and some other relatives who depended on you for support. Each one is worked out separately, using 3% of their net income. Common eligible expenses Dental work by a dentist or other practitioner (not purely cosmetic work) Prescription drugs recorded by a pharmacist (not over-the-counter medicines or vitamins) Prescription glasses and contact lenses Premiums you paid for a private health or dental plan Travel to get care not available near home: transit or car costs if you went at least 40 km each way, and meals, parking and lodging too if you went at least 80 km Low-income workers with high medical costs may also get the refundable medical expense supplement . Disability tax credit and caregiver amounts Disability tax credit (DTC) The DTC is for people with a severe and prolonged impairment, one that has lasted or is expected to last at least 12 months and markedly restricts daily activities. Many people who would qualify never apply. It covers impairments in mental functions as well as physical ones, and type 1 diabetes is treated as meeting the life-sustaining therapy test. How to apply: you fill in Part A of Form T2201 (online in your CRA account, by phone or on paper), and a medical practitioner, such as a doctor, nurse practitioner, psychologist, optometrist or occupational therapist, completes Part B. Amount for 2025: $10,138 for an adult, plus a supplement of up to $5,914 for a person under 18. Transfer: if the person doesn't need the full credit, a spouse, parent or other supporting relative may be able to claim the unused part. Back years: on the form you can ask the CRA to adjust earlier returns. Once you're approved, the CRA reworks the years that apply automatically. Why the DTC matters beyond the credit: approval opens the door to the child disability benefit (up to $284.25 a month per child, paid with the Canada child benefit), the registered disability savings plan (RDSP), the Canada disability benefit for ages 18 to 64, the disability supplement of the Canada workers benefit, and the home accessibility and home buyers' claims below. Canada caregiver credit If you support a spouse or relative who depends on you because of a physical or mental infirmity, you may be able to claim the Canada caregiver amount. For 2025: Up to $8,601 for each adult relative (such as a parent, adult child or sibling) with an infirmity who depends on you, if their net income is under $28,798. $2,687 added to the amount for a spouse, an eligible dependant or a child under 18 who has an infirmity. Keep a signed statement from a medical practitioner in case the CRA asks (not needed if the person is approved for the DTC). Child care, moving and work costs Child care expenses (deduction) You can deduct amounts paid so that you could work, run a business or go to school, for a child under 16 (or older, with an infirmity). Daycare centres, day camps and caregivers generally count. Leisure fees, such as tennis lessons or Scouts registration, don't. Who claims: usually the spouse with the lower net income , even if that's zero. The higher-income spouse can claim only in specific cases, for example if the other spouse was in school, in hospital or unable to care for children because of an infirmity. The caregiver can't be the child's parent or a relative under 18. Moving expenses (deduction) If you moved for a new job, to run a business or to study full-time at a post-secondary school, and your new home is at least 40 km closer (by the shortest public route) to the new work or school, you may deduct costs such as movers, travel, up to 15 days of temporary meals and lodging, lease-cancellation costs, and real estate commissions and legal fees on selling your old home. You deduct them against employment or self-employment income earned at the new location (students: against taxable scholarships and similar awards). Any amount you can't use carries forward to next year. Use Form T1-M. Union and professional dues (deduction) Union dues are usually in box 44 of your T4. Also deductible: dues you must pay to keep a professional status recognized by B.C. law, such as a licensing body, and required professional liability insurance. If you paid dues directly, don't forget the receipt. Initiation fees don't qualify. Students and recent graduates Tuition credit: use it, transfer it or keep it Eligible tuition shown on your T2202 slip gives you a credit. Students often earn too little to use it, but it isn't lost: After using what you need to bring your own tax to zero, you can transfer up to $5,000 of the current year's federal tuition amount to a spouse, a parent or a grandparent (yours or your spouse's). Whatever is left carries forward to future years, when you're working and paying tax. Keep filing. The CRA says that if you skip filing a return in a year you're carrying tuition forward, that amount isn't carried forward. File every year, even with little or no income, and include Schedule 11. Interest on student loans Interest you paid on a government student loan (Canada student loan or a provincial loan such as B.C.'s) gives you a credit. Bank loans, lines of credit, loans from abroad, and student loans combined with other debt don't count. You can claim interest paid in the year or in any of the previous five years that you haven't already claimed. Only the student who owes the loan can claim it, even if a parent made the payments. Homes, renovations and donations Home buyers' amount If you bought your first home, you can claim up to $10,000 (worth up to $1,450 in federal tax for 2025). Generally you're a first-time buyer if neither you nor your spouse or partner lived in a home either of you owned in the year of purchase or the four years before. Spouses can split the claim, but the total can't go over $10,000 for the home. A person who qualifies for the DTC may be able to claim without being a first-time buyer. Home accessibility expenses Eligible renovations to the home of someone who is 65 or older at the end of the year, or who qualifies for the DTC, can be claimed up to $20,000 a year . The person can claim it, and so can a spouse or a supporting relative in many cases. Materials and work by contractors count; your own labour doesn't. Routine repairs, appliances and work done mainly to raise the home's value don't count. An expense that is also a medical expense can be claimed as both. Donations Gifts to registered charities and other qualified donees earn a credit at two levels: Part of your total gifts Federal credit rate First $200 Lowest tax rate (14.5% for 2025, 14% for 2026) Above $200 29%, or 33% on gifts that match your taxable income above the top bracket ($253,414 for 2025) Because the rate jumps after $200, it usually pays for one spouse to claim both spouses' donations , which the CRA allows. You can also carry donations forward for up to five years and claim them in a year when your total is bigger. Claims are generally capped at 75% of net income. Working families, renters and seniors Canada workers benefit (CWB) The CWB is a refundable credit for people with low working income. For 2025 the basic amount is up to $1,633 for a single person and $2,813 for a family , reduced once adjusted net income passes $26,855 (single) or $30,639 (family). People approved for the DTC may get a disability supplement of up to $843. You generally must be 19 or older (or live with a spouse or child) and a Canadian resident all year. Part of the CWB is paid in advance in July, October and January. B.C. renter's tax credit B.C. renters can get up to $400 a year , paid as a refundable credit through your return on Form BC479. You need to have rented an eligible home in B.C. for at least six months of the year and be 19 or older (or a parent, or living with a spouse) on December 31. The credit shrinks once adjusted family income passes $64,764 for 2025 and is gone at $84,764 (for 2026: $66,189 and $86,189). Only one spouse can claim it, but roommates who aren't a couple can each claim their own. Pension amount and pension splitting Pension income amount: up to $2,000 of eligible pension income gives a credit. Pension from a workplace plan counts at any age; RRIF and annuity income generally counts from 65. CPP and OAS don't count. Pension splitting: you can move up to 50% of eligible pension income to your spouse's or partner's return. This can lower the couple's total tax. Both of you must sign and file Form T1032 with your returns by the filing deadline. Missed something? How to fix a past return Missed a claim in an earlier year? After you get the notice of assessment for that year, you can ask the CRA to change it: Change my return in your CRA account online. The CRA's current target is about two weeks. ReFILE through certified tax software or your tax preparer, if the original return was filed electronically. Form T1-ADJ by mail, with supporting documents. This takes much longer (the CRA's target is about 20 weeks), and very old years can only be changed this way. Time limit: the CRA can't issue a refund for a change you ask for more than 10 calendar years after the end of the tax year. A request made in 2026 can usually still reach back to 2016. Don't wait. A few things can't be added through a change request, such as making or changing certain elections, so some fixes need a different form. One example worth checking: the digital news subscription credit ended after 2024, but if you paid for a qualifying subscription between 2020 and 2024 and never claimed it, you can still claim up to $500 for each of those years. Checklist before you file Added up the whole family's medical and dental receipts, and picked the best 12-month period and the right spouse to claim them. Considered whether anyone in the family might qualify for the disability tax credit, and whether you support a relative with an infirmity. Claimed child care on the lower-income spouse's return, with receipts. Checked moving expenses if you moved 40 km or more closer to a new job or school. Students: claimed tuition and decided whether to transfer up to $5,000 or carry it forward; claimed government student loan interest. Claimed the home buyers' amount or home accessibility expenses if they apply. Pooled both spouses' donations on one return, or carried them forward. Checked the Canada workers benefit and the B.C. renter's tax credit (Form BC479). Seniors: claimed the pension amount and looked at pension splitting with Form T1032. Checked past returns for missed claims (10-year limit). Think you've missed a claim? We can review your family's returns, spot credits and deductions that were missed, and request changes for past years where it makes sense. title: Paying yourself from your corporation: salary, dividends and shareholder loans
description: How BC owner-managers can pay themselves: salary vs dividends, CPP and RRSP room, T4 and T5 slips, and the one-year rule for shareholder loans.
text: Guides · Small business Paying yourself from your corporation: salary, dividends and shareholder loans Once your business is incorporated, the money it earns belongs to the company, not to you. To get it into your own pocket, you need to choose how: a salary, dividends, or (carefully) a shareholder loan. Each one is taxed differently and comes with its own paperwork. This guide explains the options in plain language for owners of small BC corporations. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 9, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short Company money isn't yours: every withdrawal should be recorded as salary, a dividend or a loan. Salary is deductible to the company, needs payroll and a T4, pays both halves of CPP and creates RRSP room. Dividends come from after-tax profit, need a T5, and build no CPP pension or RRSP room. Most dividends from small-business profit are non-eligible: grossed up 15%, then reduced by the dividend tax credit. A shareholder loan not repaid within one year after the company's year-end can be added to your income. T4 and T5 returns are due by the last day of February; an accrued bonus must be paid within 180 days of year-end. On this page First, the basics: the company's money isn't yours Option 1: Paying yourself a salary Bonuses and "accrued" salary: the 180-day rule Option 2: Paying yourself dividends Salary vs dividends at a glance Using a mix of salary and dividends Shareholder loans: borrowing from your company Paperwork and year-end timing Common mistakes First, the basics: the company's money isn't yours When you incorporate, the corporation becomes a separate legal "person." You own it as a shareholder , which means you hold shares in it. If you also run it day to day, you are an owner-manager . Most small BC companies are Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) : private companies controlled by Canadian residents. Because the company is separate from you, the money in its bank account belongs to the company. You can't simply move it to your own account the way a sole proprietor takes "drawings." Every dollar you take out needs a label. The three most common are: Salary or bonus : you are paid as an employee of your company. Dividends : you are paid as a shareholder, out of the company's after-tax profit. Shareholder loans : you borrow from the company and pay it back. Each one is taxed differently, has its own paperwork and affects things like your Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and RRSP room. If you're still deciding whether to incorporate, start with our guide to sole proprietorship vs incorporation in BC . Option 1: Paying yourself a salary With a salary, your company treats you like any other employee. It runs payroll, takes deductions off each pay and sends them to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). At year-end it gives you a T4 slip , the form that shows your employment income and deductions. What the company must do Open a payroll account with the CRA and deduct income tax and CPP from each pay. Our guide to hiring your first employee walks through the set-up. Send the deductions on time. Most new employers are "regular remitters," with remittances due on the 15th of the month after you were paid. File the T4 return by the last day of February after the year ends. CPP: you pay both halves CPP is the public pension plan. Employees and employers each pay the same amount. When you own the company, both halves come out of money you control. For 2026: The employee and employer each pay 5.95% on earnings between $3,500 and $74,600, up to a maximum of $4,230.45 each. On earnings between $74,600 and $85,000, each also pays a second contribution (often called CPP2) of 4%, up to $416 each. That is a real cost today, but it also builds your future CPP pension. Employment Insurance (EI) is different. The CRA says a job is generally not insurable when the employee controls more than 40% of the company's voting shares. So many owner-managers don't pay EI premiums, and they also can't collect regular EI benefits from that job. Why owners choose salary It's a business expense. A reasonable salary lowers the company's taxable income. It creates RRSP room. RRSP room is the amount you can put into a registered retirement savings plan and deduct. It's generally 18% of last year's "earned income," up to a yearly maximum. Salary counts as earned income. The maximum is $33,810 for 2026 and $35,390 for 2027. It shows steady income , which can help when you apply for a mortgage or other loan. Bonuses and "accrued" salary: the 180-day rule Some owners wait until the company's year-end, see how much profit there is, and then declare a bonus . The company can record the bonus as an expense for that year even if it's paid a little later. This is called an accrued bonus. There is a time limit. Under the Income Tax Act, if salary or a bonus is still unpaid 180 days after the end of the company's tax year, the company can't deduct it in that year. It can only deduct it in the year it's actually paid. Illustration only: Your company's year ends on December 31, 2026. It records a $20,000 bonus for you. To deduct it in 2026, the company needs to actually pay it (with payroll deductions sent to the CRA) within 180 days after December 31, 2026. Tip: An unpaid bonus isn't money in your pocket yet. Count the days from your company's year-end, and make sure payroll deductions on the bonus are remitted on time too. Option 2: Paying yourself dividends A dividend is a share of the company's profit paid to its shareholders. It comes out of profit the company has already paid tax on. The company reports dividends on a T5 slip and must file the T5 return, and give you your copy, by the last day of February after the year ends. A slip isn't needed if one person's total for the year is under $50. What's different about dividends Not a business expense. Dividends don't lower the company's taxable income. No payroll. No CPP is paid, so there's no CPP pension built on that income. There are no source deductions, so you may owe tax when you file your own return. No RRSP room. Dividends aren't on the CRA's list of earned income. Gross-up and dividend tax credit The tax system tries to avoid taxing the same profit twice, once in the company and again in your hands. It does this in two steps: Gross-up: you report more than you actually received. This "grossed-up" figure is called the taxable amount . Dividend tax credit: you then get a credit that lowers your tax, to make up for the tax the company already paid. Eligible vs non-eligible dividends There are two kinds of dividends: Non-eligible dividends (the CRA calls them "other than eligible") usually come from profit taxed at the low small-business rate. Most dividends from a small owner-managed company are this kind. They are grossed up by 15%. Eligible dividends generally come from profit taxed at the higher general rate. A CCPC tracks this in its general rate income pool (GRIP) , and it can pay eligible dividends only up to that pool without extra tax. They are grossed up by 38%. Illustration only: You receive a $10,000 non-eligible dividend in 2026. You report a taxable amount of $11,500. Your federal dividend tax credit is 9.0301% of that, about $1,038. The BC credit for 2026 is 1.96% of the taxable amount, about $225. Your actual tax depends on your other income. Watch out for family dividends: Paying dividends to a spouse or adult children who don't work in the business can trigger the tax on split income (TOSI) , a special tax on some income from a family business. Some exceptions apply, so check before you set up family shareholders. Salary vs dividends at a glance Feature Salary or bonus Dividends Slip you receive T4 T5 Deductible for the company? Yes, if reasonable No, paid from after-tax profit Payroll deductions Yes: income tax and CPP, sent monthly for most new employers None CPP Both halves paid; builds your pension None paid; no pension built EI (owner with over 40% of voting shares) Generally not insurable Not applicable Creates RRSP room? Yes No Personal tax Taxed like any job income Gross-up, then dividend tax credit Paperwork Payroll account, remittances, T4 by end of February Directors' resolution, T5 by end of February Using a mix of salary and dividends Many owner-managers take some salary and some dividends. There's no single right answer. The best mix depends on how much cash you need, whether you want CPP and RRSP room, your other income, and how much profit you'd like to leave in the company. It helps to know how the company itself is taxed. A CCPC can claim the small business deduction , which lowers the tax rate on its active business income up to a "business limit" of $500,000 a year. For BC companies, that means a combined rate of 11% (9% federal plus 2% BC) on income up to the limit, and 27% (15% plus 12%) above it. The limit is shared between associated companies and shrinks once the company's investment income goes over $50,000 a year. A few general points to discuss with your accountant: Salary lowers company profit. Paying a salary can keep the company's income within the small-business limit. Retirement goals matter. If you want RRSP room or a larger CPP pension, some salary helps. Cash flow matters. Dividends avoid monthly payroll remittances, but you may need to set money aside for tax in April, or make tax instalments. Personal expenses aren't a third option. If the company pays your personal bills, the CRA can treat that as a shareholder benefit that you must add to your income, and the company can't deduct it. See our guide to business expenses and deductions for what counts as a real business cost. Shareholder loans: borrowing from your company Your accountant keeps a shareholder loan account (sometimes called a shareholder account) in the company's books. It tracks money moving between you and the company: If you put your own money in, or pay company bills personally, the company owes you . You can usually take that money back without tax. If you take out more than the company owes you, you owe the company . That's a shareholder loan. The one-year repayment rule Under section 15(2) of the Income Tax Act, a loan from a corporation to a shareholder is generally added to the shareholder's income. But there is an important exception: the rule doesn't apply if the loan is repaid within one year after the end of the company's tax year in which you borrowed it. Illustration only: Your company's year ends on December 31. You borrow $15,000 in March 2026. The loan arose in the company's 2026 tax year, so you'd need to repay it by December 31, 2027. If you don't, the $15,000 can be added to your 2026 income. The repayment must be genuine. The Act says the exception doesn't apply if the repayment is part of a "series of loans or other transactions and repayments," for example repaying just before year-end and borrowing the same money back right after. Keep bank records that show the money actually moved back to the company. The deemed interest benefit Even a loan you repay on time can create a small taxable amount. If the loan carries no interest, or low interest, you're treated as receiving a benefit equal to interest at the CRA's prescribed rate , minus any interest you actually pay to the company no later than 30 days after the end of the year. The prescribed rate for this purpose is 3% for October 1 to December 31, 2026. The CRA sets it every three months. Exceptions, briefly Some loans made to someone because they are an employee , not because they own shares, are treated differently, for example a loan to help buy a home or a car used for work. There must also be real repayment terms. These exceptions are narrow and rarely help an owner who borrows because they control the company. Warning: A shareholder loan is not a way to avoid tax. If it isn't repaid in time, you pay tax on the full amount, and you can't fix it with a journal entry. Plan repayment before you borrow. Paperwork and year-end timing Good records protect you if the CRA asks questions. Keep these in your company's minute book or files: Directors' resolutions for dividends. A resolution is a short written decision by the company's directors. It should state the amount, the date, which class of shares, and whether any part is an eligible dividend. Payroll records : pay stubs, remittance confirmations and T4s. A shareholder loan schedule : dates and amounts of every amount borrowed or repaid, with bank proof, and any loan agreement. Timing matters too. A few weeks before your company's year-end, review profit, decide whether to declare a bonus or dividend, and check any shareholder loan balance against its repayment date. Remember the slips: T4 and T5 returns for a calendar year are due by the last day of February, even if the company's tax year ends at a different time. Common mistakes Taking money with no label. Transfers that aren't recorded as salary, dividends or a loan repayment end up in the shareholder loan account and can become taxable. Missing the one-year repayment deadline on a shareholder loan, or repaying and re-borrowing in a pattern. Paying a bonus late. Unpaid after 180 days, the company loses the deduction for that year. Skipping payroll on salary. Salary needs source deductions, CPP and a T4. Late remittances are charged interest. Forgetting the T5. Dividends need a T5 slip by the last day of February. Not saving for personal tax on dividends. No tax is withheld, so set money aside. Running personal bills through the company. These can become shareholder benefits that the company can't deduct. Paying family dividends without checking TOSI. Want help planning how to pay yourself? title: Renting out a suite, condo or room: how rental income is taxed
description: Renting a basement suite, laneway home, condo or room in B.C.? What to report, what you can deduct, CCA and your principal residence, explained simply.
text: Guides · Personal tax Renting out a suite, condo or room: how rental income is taxed Renting a basement suite, laneway home, condo or spare room is common across Metro Vancouver. Here's how the rent is taxed, which expenses you can deduct, and how to protect the tax-free status of your home. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 In short Report rent and expenses on Form T776 with your return; co-owners each report their own share. Repairs are deducted right away, but improvements are capital costs claimed over time through capital cost allowance (CCA). If you live in the home, deduct only the rented share of whole-house costs, based on floor area or rooms. Claiming CCA on part of your own home can make part of your gain taxable when you sell. Renting to family below market rent means you can't claim a rental loss. Non-compliant short-term rentals lose their expense deductions, and long-term residential rent is generally GST-exempt. On this page Is it rental income or business income? How to report rental income What you can deduct: current vs capital expenses Renting part of the home you live in Capital cost allowance (CCA) in plain language Why claiming CCA on your home can cost you later Short-term rentals, GST and B.C. housing taxes If you move away and keep renting Records to keep and common mistakes Is it rental income or business income? Most landlords earn rental income , which the CRA treats as income from property. The key question is how many services you provide. Rental income: you provide the space plus basic services such as heat, light, parking and laundry. This is the usual case for a basement suite, laneway home, condo or rented room. Possibly business income: you also provide extra services such as cleaning, security or meals. The more services you add, the more likely it's a business, reported on Form T2125 instead. This guide covers ordinary rental income. How to report rental income You report rental income and expenses on Form T776, Statement of Real Estate Rentals , filed with your personal return. The CRA's guide T4036 explains each line. Calendar year. Report rent for January 1 to December 31. Accrual method. Generally, report rent in the year it's earned and expenses in the year they're incurred, even if paid later. You may use the cash method only if the result would be almost the same. Co-owners each report their share. If you and your spouse own the house 50/50, each of you reports half the rent and half the expenses. Owning a property together as an investment isn't a partnership. Reasonable expectation of profit. If there's no reasonable expectation of making a profit, you can't claim the expenses. Renting to family below market rent Many families rent a suite to a parent, adult child or sibling for less than market rent. The CRA treats this as cost-sharing, not a business of renting, so you can't claim a rental loss . If you charge the same rent you'd charge a stranger and expect a profit, normal rules apply. Small amounts a relative chips in for groceries or upkeep aren't rental income. What you can deduct: current vs capital expenses Rental expenses fall into two groups, and the difference matters. Current expenses keep the property running or restore it to how it was. You deduct them in full in the year. Capital expenses give a lasting benefit or improve the property beyond its original condition. You can't deduct them all at once. Instead, you claim capital cost allowance over several years (see below). Current (deduct now) Capital (claim CCA over time) Repainting the outside of the house Putting vinyl siding on a wooden house Repairing worn wooden steps Replacing wooden steps with concrete ones Fixing the roof back to its original state Buying a new fridge for the suite Common deductible current expenses Mortgage interest on money borrowed to buy or improve the rental (not the principal) Property taxes and insurance (a premium covering three years is deducted one year at a time) Repairs and maintenance Utilities you pay for the tenant Advertising, legal and accounting fees, and property management fees What you can't deduct Repayments of mortgage principal The cost of land (it's never depreciated) The value of your own time and labour Land transfer (property transfer) tax, which is added to the property's cost instead Interest on money borrowed for personal use, even if the loan is secured by the rental Renting part of the home you live in If you live upstairs and rent the basement, or rent a room, you can deduct: 100% of costs that apply only to the rented part (for example, advertising the suite or repairing its bathroom), and a reasonable share of costs for the whole house, such as property taxes, insurance, mortgage interest and shared utilities. The CRA accepts splitting whole-house costs by floor area or by number of rooms . Example: your house has 2,400 square feet and the basement suite is 800, so one-third of the house is rented. If property tax is $4,500 and home insurance is $1,800 for the year, you can deduct $1,500 and $600 for the suite. For a single room rented to a lodger, use the share of rooms rented, plus a fair share of rooms you both use, like the kitchen. Capital cost allowance (CCA) in plain language Capital cost allowance (CCA) is the tax version of depreciation. It lets you deduct the cost of the building and items like appliances a little at a time, because they wear out over many years. Classes and rates. Assets are grouped into classes, each with a yearly rate. Rental buildings are commonly in class 1 (4%) . Other assets, such as appliances, go in their own classes with different rates. Declining balance. The rate applies to what's left in the class each year, so the claim shrinks over time. Building only. Land can't be depreciated, so split the purchase price between land and building. Separate class. Each rental property that cost $50,000 or more goes in its own class. First-year rules. Normally the half-year rule lets you claim only half the usual CCA in the year you buy. For many properties bought after November 20, 2018, an accelerated incentive replaces this with a larger first-year claim, and further changes have been proposed for property bought after 2024. Check the rules for your purchase year. Optional. You can claim any amount from zero up to the maximum. No losses. CCA can't create or increase a rental loss. When you sell: recapture and terminal loss CCA isn't free money. If you sell the building for more than its remaining undepreciated balance, the CCA you claimed is generally added back to your income (called recapture ). If you sell for less and no property is left in the class, you may deduct the difference as a terminal loss . Why claiming CCA on your home can cost you later For most Metro Vancouver homeowners, the biggest tax break is the principal residence exemption , which can make the gain on selling your home tax-free. Renting part or all of your home can affect it. Renting part of your home The CRA usually treats the whole home as still your principal residence if all three are true: the rental use is small compared with your own use, you made no structural changes to rent it, and you claim no CCA on it. Renting a room in your house is a typical example. If you claim CCA on the rented part, or convert part of the house into a self-contained suite, the CRA may treat that part as sold and bought back at market value when the rental started (a change in use ). Part of your gain on a later sale could then be taxable. Tip: claiming CCA on part of your own home saves a little tax now but can cost far more when you sell. Many homeowners choose not to claim it. Talk it through before you do. Turning your whole home into a rental If you move out and rent your home, you're normally treated as selling it at market value on that date. You can file a subsection 45(2) election (a signed letter with your return for that year) so no sale is treated as happening then. You can then keep designating the home as your principal residence for up to four years while it's rented, if you remain a Canadian resident. But you can't claim CCA during that time; doing so cancels the election. Moving back into a former rental If a rental becomes your home, a subsection 45(3) election can postpone the deemed sale until you actually sell. It isn't available if CCA was claimed on the property after 1984. Since March 19, 2019, both elections can also apply when only part of a property changes use. Short-term rentals, GST and B.C. housing taxes Short-term rentals B.C.'s short-term rental rules limit hosts, in communities where the rule applies, to renting their own principal residence plus one secondary suite or accessory unit on the same property. Since May 1, 2025, hosts must register with the provincial registry and show the registration number on their listings. The federal tax rules add a cost to breaking these rules. For income tax, a short-term rental is one rented or offered for less than 90 consecutive days. If the province or city doesn't allow your short-term rental, or you lack a required licence or registration, it's non-compliant and the CRA denies the expenses for the non-compliant days. GST/HST Long-term residential rent, where a tenant lives in the unit for a month or more, is generally exempt from GST/HST . You don't charge GST on it. Short stays of less than a month can be taxable if you're a GST/HST registrant. B.C. speculation and vacancy tax Owners of residential property in the taxable areas of B.C. who get a declaration letter must declare every year before March 31, even if they're exempt. Living in the home as your principal residence, or renting it out for at least six months of the year, are the main exemptions. Federal Underused Housing Tax This mainly affected owners who aren't Canadian citizens or permanent residents. No return or tax is required for 2025 and later years, but returns and tax for 2022 to 2024 still apply. If you move away and keep renting Many families keep a Metro Vancouver condo or house as a rental after moving abroad. Once you're a non-resident: Your tenant or property manager must withhold 25% of the gross rent and send it to the CRA by the 15th of the following month. You and your Canadian agent can file Form NR6 so the 25% is withheld on net rent (after expenses) instead. File it by January 1 each year, or before the first rent payment is due. You can file a section 216 return (Form T1159) to pay tax on net rental income, which can lower your tax or bring a refund. It's generally due within two years after the year-end, or by June 30 of the next year if you filed an NR6. Records to keep and common mistakes Records to keep Leases, rent ledger and bank deposits Receipts and invoices for every expense Purchase documents showing the split between land and building Your floor-area or room calculation, if you live in the home Your CCA history, year by year Keep them for six years from the end of the tax year. Don't send them with your return, but have them ready if the CRA asks. Common mistakes to avoid Not reporting rent from a suite or room because it's paid in cash or by a relative. Deducting capital costs such as a new kitchen or appliances as repairs. Deducting mortgage principal , or claiming 100% of whole-house costs when you live there too. Claiming a loss on a below-market rental to family. Claiming CCA on your own home without weighing the effect on the principal residence exemption. Splitting income wrongly between co-owners instead of by ownership share. Running a non-compliant short-term rental , which costs you your expense deductions for those days. Forgetting the 25% withholding after moving abroad. Want help with your rental income? We prepare T776 rental statements, work out the right expense split and CCA for your situation, and help you weigh the effect on your principal residence exemption before you claim. title: RESPs and education grants for your children
description: How an RESP works, how to get the Canada Education Savings Grant, Canada Learning Bond and B.C.'s $1,200 grant, and what happens when the money comes out.
text: Guides · Family finances RESPs and education grants for your children A registered education savings plan (RESP) is one of the few places where the government adds free money to your savings. For B.C. families, that can mean a 20% federal grant on what you put in, extra help for lower-income families, and a one-time $1,200 provincial grant. Here's how it all works in plain language, with 2026 figures. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 5, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short The Canada Education Savings Grant adds 20% to your RESP contributions, up to $500 a year and $7,200 per child over a lifetime. Families with lower or middle incomes get an extra 10% or 20% on the first $500 they contribute each year (2026 income bands). The Canada Learning Bond pays up to $2,000 to children from low-income families, with no contribution needed. B.C. children can get a one-time $1,200 grant, but only if you apply between their 6th birthday and the day before they turn 9. The lifetime contribution limit is $50,000 per child, and going over costs 1% a month in tax. Your contributions come back tax-free; grants and growth are taxed to the student, who often pays little or no tax. On this page What an RESP is How to open an RESP The Canada Education Savings Grant (CESG) The Canada Learning Bond (CLB) B.C. Training and Education Savings Grant (BCTESG) Contribution limits and overcontributions How the money comes out If your child doesn't go to school Checklist and common mistakes What an RESP is A registered education savings plan (RESP) is a special savings account for a child's education after high school. That can include university, college and other designated schools in Canada, and many schools outside Canada. The money inside grows without being taxed each year. Government grants are paid straight into it. A few words you will see often: Subscriber: the person who opens the RESP and puts money in. Any adult can do this, including parents, grandparents, other relatives and friends. Beneficiary: the child (or adult) the savings are for. Promoter: the company that offers the RESP, such as a bank, credit union, financial planner or group plan dealer. Types of plans Family plan: can have more than one beneficiary, which is handy if you have several children. Each beneficiary must be related to the subscriber by blood or adoption, and must be under 21 when added. Individual plan: has one beneficiary. The subscriber doesn't have to be related to the child. Group plan: sold by group plan dealers (sometimes called scholarship plan dealers). The government warns that these plans may charge fees if you stop making regular payments, so read the terms carefully. Whichever type you choose, ask the promoter about fees for opening, managing or closing the plan, any penalties, and which government grants they offer. Not every promoter offers every grant. How to open an RESP Get a Social Insurance Number (SIN) for your child. A SIN is the nine-digit number the government uses to identify you. The child needs one before they can be named on an RESP. The subscriber needs one too. Choose a promoter. Most banks and credit unions offer RESPs. Compare fees and ask which grants they offer. Open the plan and name your child. Many promoters let you do this online, by phone or by mail. You don't need a bank account to open an RESP. Apply for the grants at the same time. Your promoter helps you fill in the application for the Canada Education Savings Grant and the Canada Learning Bond, plus the B.C. grant if your child is the right age. Contribute if you want the main grant. The Canada Education Savings Grant only matches money you put in. The Canada Learning Bond needs no contribution at all. Grants are deposited automatically once approved. The federal grant usually arrives about 6 to 8 weeks after your contribution is processed. New to Canada? See our newcomers tax guide for getting set up with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). The Canada Education Savings Grant (CESG) The Canada Education Savings Grant (CESG) is the federal government's main RESP grant. Every family can get it, whatever their income. The basic grant The government adds 20% of the first $2,500 you contribute each year, so up to $500 a year . The most one child can receive over their lifetime is $7,200 . The additional grant for lower and middle incomes On the first $500 you contribute each year, some families get an extra amount. It depends on adjusted family net income , which is roughly the total net income of the child's main caregiver and their spouse or common-law partner. Adjusted family net income (2026) Extra grant on first $500 Most CESG per year Less than $58,523 20% ($100) $600 $58,523 to $117,045 10% ($50) $550 More than $117,045 None $500 Catching up on missed years Each child who lives in Canada builds up grant room every year from birth to 17: $500 a year since 2007. If you don't use it, it carries forward. In a year when you have unused room, you can get up to $1,000 of basic grant, which means contributing up to $5,000 that year. Illustration only: a family that starts saving when their child is 5 puts in $5,000 in one year. The government adds $1,000 (20% of $5,000), using up that year's room plus one missed year. Rules for 16- and 17-year-olds Contributions can earn the grant up to the end of the calendar year the child turns 17. But a child who is 16 or 17 only qualifies if, before the end of the year they turned 15, at least one of these happened: at least $2,000 in total was contributed and not taken out, or at least $100 was contributed (and not taken out) in any four years. Year-end tip: grant room works by calendar year. If you want the 2026 grant, make your contribution by December 31, 2026 . Check your promoter's cut-off date, since processing can take a few days. The Canada Learning Bond (CLB) The Canada Learning Bond (CLB) is free money for children from low-income families. You don't have to contribute anything to get it. You only need an RESP to receive it. $500 for the first year the child qualifies, plus $100 for each later year they qualify, up to and including the year they turn 15. The most a child can get is $2,000 . The child must be born on or after January 1, 2004 . The government also pays $25 into the RESP that gets the first $500, to help with the cost of opening it. Who qualifies It depends on the adjusted family income of the child's main caregiver and the number of children. For July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027 , the limits are: 1 to 3 children: $58,523 or less 4 children: less than $66,036 5 children: less than $73,577 This is one more reason both parents should file a tax return every year, even with little or no income. Our Canada child benefit guide explains why filing matters for family benefits. Missed years are paid too The CLB is retroactive , meaning it pays for past years the child qualified, not just the current one. The main caregiver can ask for it until the day before the child turns 18. After that, the young person can apply themselves from age 18, but must do so before turning 21. Coming: automatic RESPs The federal government says that starting in April 2028 it will automatically open an RESP for eligible children born in 2024 or later who don't already have one by age 4, so they get the CLB. Families will be able to opt out starting in 2027. The government says more details are still to come, so treat this as planned rather than final. B.C. Training and Education Savings Grant (BCTESG) The B.C. Training and Education Savings Grant (BCTESG) is a one-time $1,200 grant from the Province of British Columbia, paid into your child's RESP. No contribution needed. The province does not ask you to match it. Age window: you can apply from the child's 6th birthday until the day before they turn 9 . Residency: both the child and the parent or guardian must live in B.C. when you apply, and the child needs a valid SIN. How to apply: through a financial institution that offers the grant. If your current RESP provider doesn't, you can open a new RESP with one that does. Don't miss the window: once your child turns 9, the chance to apply for the $1,200 is gone for good. Put a reminder in your calendar for your child's 6th birthday. Contribution limits and overcontributions There is no yearly limit on how much you can put into an RESP. There is a lifetime limit of $50,000 per child , counting every RESP for that child, no matter who opened it. Only contributions count toward the $50,000. Grants and investment growth don't. If total contributions go over $50,000, that's an overcontribution . Each subscriber pays a tax of 1% per month on their share of the extra amount until it is taken out. Overcontributions often happen by accident, for example when grandparents open a separate RESP for the same child. Talk to family members so everyone knows what has already been saved. How the money comes out When your child enrols in a qualifying program, the money comes out in two parts that are taxed differently: Part of the RESP Who gets it Taxed? Your contributions You (or you can pay it to the student) No Grants, bonds and growth (paid as an EAP) The student Yes, as the student's income An educational assistance payment (EAP) is a payment from the grants and investment growth. It counts as the student's income, but students often have low income, so they may pay little or no tax on it. What counts as a qualifying program Full-time in Canada: at least 3 weeks in a row, with at least 10 hours a week of classes or work. Part-time in Canada: at least 3 weeks in a row, with at least 12 hours a month of classes. Full-time outside Canada: at least 13 weeks, or 3 weeks for a university program. Limits on EAPs Full-time: up to $8,000 in the first 13 weeks in a row of study. After that, there's no set limit while the student keeps qualifying. Part-time: up to $4,000 for each 13-week period. The student must show official proof of enrolment. EAPs can still be paid for up to 6 months after studies end, if the plan allows it. If your child doesn't go to school You have several options, and you don't have to decide right away: Wait. The plan can stay open for many years, in case your child goes back to school later. Change the beneficiary to another child, such as a brother or sister. The CESG can be shared with a sibling who still has grant room. Close the plan. Your contributions come back to you tax-free. The CESG and CLB go back to the government. The CLB can only be used for education. What happens to the investment growth The growth can be paid to the subscriber as an accumulated income payment (AIP) . This is generally allowed after the year of the plan's 9th anniversary, once every beneficiary is at least 21 and not eligible for EAPs. An AIP is taxed at your regular rate plus an extra 20% . You can avoid much of that tax by moving up to $50,000 of the growth (over your lifetime) into your RRSP or your spouse's RRSP, if you have enough RRSP contribution room. If your child qualifies for the disability tax credit, the growth may be able to move to their registered disability savings plan (RDSP) instead. Checklist and common mistakes Checklist Get a SIN for your child as early as possible. Open an RESP and apply for the CESG and CLB at the same time. Contribute by December 31 each year to use that year's grant room. Apply for the $1,200 BCTESG between your child's 6th and 9th birthdays. File tax returns every year so the government can check your income for the extra grant and the CLB. Keep track of every RESP for each child so no one goes over $50,000. Common mistakes Not opening an RESP because you can't afford to contribute. The CLB and BCTESG need no contributions. Missing the B.C. grant because the child turned 9. Starting to save only at 16 and finding the child doesn't qualify for the CESG. Signing a group plan without understanding the fees for stopping payments. Letting relatives open a second RESP for the same child without checking the $50,000 total. For other money families often miss, see our guide to often-missed tax credits . Want help planning for your child's education? We can check which grants your family qualifies for, make sure both parents' returns are filed so the extra grants and the Canada Learning Bond flow, and help with the tax side when RESP money comes out. title: Retirement income in Canada: OAS, CPP, RRIFs and pension splitting
description: How OAS, GIS, CPP and RRIFs work in 2026, the OAS clawback, RRIF minimum withdrawals and how couples save tax by splitting pension income.
text: Guides · Retirement Retirement income in Canada: OAS, CPP, RRIFs and pension splitting Old Age Security, the Canada Pension Plan and your RRSP or RRIF savings each follow their own rules on timing and tax. Here's how they work in 2026, how to avoid the OAS clawback, what you must do with your RRSP at 71, and how couples can split pension income to pay less tax. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 4, 2026 · Figures for 2026 (OAS and GIS: October to December 2026) In short The maximum OAS pension for October to December 2026 is $762.50 a month at 65 to 74 and $838.75 at 75 and older. For 2026, OAS starts to be clawed back at 15% of net income over $95,323. You can start CPP between 60 and 70: it drops 0.6% a month before 65 and rises 0.7% a month after 65. By the end of the year you turn 71, you must turn your RRSP into a RRIF, an annuity or cash, and RRIFs have a yearly minimum withdrawal. Couples can move up to 50% of eligible pension income to each other using Form T1032, but CPP and OAS can't be split this way. On this page The main pieces of retirement income Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement The OAS clawback (recovery tax) The Canada Pension Plan: when to start From RRSP to RRIF: the age-71 deadline and minimum withdrawals Pension income splitting, the pension income amount and the age amount Checklist and common mistakes The main pieces of retirement income Most retirees live on a mix of government pensions and their own savings. Each piece has its own rules. Old Age Security (OAS): a monthly federal pension for people 65 and older. It is based on how long you have lived in Canada, not on your work history. Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS): an extra monthly payment on top of OAS for seniors with low income. Canada Pension Plan (CPP): a monthly pension based on what you paid into CPP from your work pay over the years. Registered retirement income fund (RRIF): an account that pays your own savings back to you as income, usually after you move money from your registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) into it. Workplace pensions: monthly payments from a pension plan you belonged to at work. OAS, CPP, RRIF payments and workplace pensions are all taxable . That means they count as income on your tax return. GIS is not taxable. This guide uses figures for 2026 , and for OAS and GIS, the October to December 2026 quarter. Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement Who can get OAS To get OAS while living in Canada, you must be 65 or older, a Canadian citizen or legal resident when your application is approved, and have lived in Canada for at least 10 years since turning 18. If you live outside Canada, you need at least 20 years of residence in Canada after age 18. A full pension is based on 40 years in Canada after age 18. With fewer years, you get a partial pension : your years in Canada divided by 40. So 20 years in Canada after 18 gives about half. How much you can get (October to December 2026) Payment Maximum per month OAS, age 65 to 74 $762.50 OAS, age 75 and older $838.75 GIS, single person (yearly income under $23,112, not counting OAS) $1,138.90 The higher amount at 75 comes from a permanent 10% increase that starts the month after your 75th birthday. OAS amounts are reviewed every January, April, July and October to keep up with the cost of living. They went up 1.4% for October to December 2026, and they don't go down when prices fall. Delaying OAS You can put off your first OAS payment for up to 5 years after 65. For each month you wait, your pension goes up by 0.6% , up to 36% more if you start at 70. GIS and the B.C. Senior's Supplement GIS amounts depend on your income and your spouse's income. Couples have different limits from single people. GIS is recalculated every July using your net income from the year before, so filing your tax return on time matters. In B.C., low-income seniors who get OAS and GIS may also get the Senior's Supplement from the province: up to $99.30 a month for a single senior and up to $220.50 a month for a couple. You don't need to apply; it is paid automatically to people who qualify. The OAS clawback (recovery tax) If your income is high, you may have to pay back some or all of your OAS. The official name is the OAS pension recovery tax , but most people call it the clawback . For 2026 , the clawback starts when your individual net income is over $95,323 . (For 2025 income, it was $93,454.) You repay 15% of your income above that threshold. Based on Service Canada's figures for October to December 2026, your OAS is fully clawed back at about $155,320 of income if you are 65 to 74, and about $161,320 if you are 75 or older. Net income is the amount on line 23600 of your tax return: your total income after deductions such as RRSP contributions. It includes your OAS, CPP, pensions, RRIF withdrawals and investment income. Illustration only: if your 2026 net income ends up $10,000 over the threshold, you would repay 15% of $10,000, or $1,500. The repayment is taken out of future OAS payments. For example, the amount based on 2025 income comes off payments from July 2026 to June 2027, spread over 12 months. Tip: Because the clawback looks at your own net income, not your family's, pension income splitting (explained below) can sometimes lower or remove it. A large one-time RRIF or RRSP withdrawal can do the opposite and push you over the line for that year. The Canada Pension Plan: when to start You can start your CPP retirement pension any time from age 60 to age 70 . The age you pick changes your monthly amount for life: If you start Change to your monthly pension Before 65 Goes down 0.6% for each month before 65 (up to 36% less at 60) At 65 Your standard amount After 65 Goes up 0.7% for each month after 65 (up to 42% more at 70) There is no gain from waiting past 70, because the increase stops then. For a pension starting at 65 in January 2026, the most anyone could get is $1,507.65 a month . Most people get less, because it depends on how much and how long you contributed. The average for new retirees starting at 65 was $858.34 a month in July 2026. Your My Service Canada Account shows an estimate based on your own record. Starting early means more years of smaller payments; starting late means fewer years of bigger ones. Your health, savings and work plans all matter, so there is no single right answer. CPP pension sharing CPP has its own way to share income with a spouse or common-law partner, called pension sharing . If you live together and at least one of you gets (or has applied for) a CPP retirement pension, you can ask Service Canada to split it between you. This can lower your combined tax. You apply through My Service Canada Account or on form ISP1002. It is separate from the tax-return pension splitting covered below, because CPP cannot be split on your tax return. CPP payments are reported on your tax return from your T4A(P) slip. From RRSP to RRIF: the age-71 deadline and minimum withdrawals December 31 of the year you turn 71 is the last day you can put money into your own RRSP. In that year, you must choose what to do with your RRSP savings: cash it out (the whole amount is taxed as income that year, which can be very costly); move it to a RRIF ; or buy an annuity , a contract that pays you a set income, often for life. No tax is taken off when money moves straight into a RRIF or is used to buy an annuity. Minimum withdrawals A RRIF must pay you at least a minimum amount every year, starting the year after you open it. The minimum for the first year is zero. Each year, the minimum is the RRIF's value on January 1 multiplied by a percentage set by your age at the start of the year: Under 71: 1 divided by (90 minus your age). At 65, that is 1/25, or 4%. 71 and older: a fixed percentage from the CRA's table, for example 5.28% at 71, 5.82% at 75, 6.82% at 80, 8.51% at 85, 11.92% at 90 and 20% at 95 or older. Illustration only: a RRIF worth $200,000 on January 1, for someone who is 71 at that date, must pay out at least $200,000 × 5.28% = $10,560 that year. If your spouse or common-law partner is younger, you can choose to base the minimum on their age, which gives a lower minimum. You must make this choice before you receive any payments from that RRIF, and you can't change it later. Watch the tax: Your RRIF carrier doesn't withhold tax on the minimum amount, but it must withhold tax on anything you take above it. Withholding is only a prepayment. You may still owe tax in April. Talk to your carrier or accountant early so a tax bill doesn't catch you off guard. For comparison, a cash withdrawal from an RRSP has 10% withheld on amounts up to $5,000, 20% from $5,000 to $15,000 and 30% over $15,000 (outside Quebec), and that is often less than the tax you really owe. Pension income splitting, the pension income amount and the age amount Pension income splitting Canada taxes each person on their own income, and tax rates rise as income goes up. So a couple usually pays less tax when their incomes are close together. Pension income splitting lets you move up to 50% of your eligible pension income to your spouse or common-law partner on your tax returns. No money actually changes hands; it is only a tax calculation. What counts as eligible pension income depends on the age of the person transferring it: Any age: the taxable part of lifetime payments from a workplace pension plan. 65 or older at the end of the year: also RRIF payments (including payments from a life income fund , or LIF, which is a special kind of RRIF) and annuity payments from an RRSP. Never eligible: OAS, CPP, and U.S. individual retirement account (IRA) income. To split, you and your partner both fill out and sign Form T1032 , Joint Election to Split Pension Income , and each of you files it with your own return by the filing deadline. The information on both forms must match. Any tax withheld on the pension moves with it in the same proportion. You can choose a different percentage each year. You can't split if, at the end of the year, you had been living apart because your relationship broke down for 90 days or more. Both of you must also be Canadian residents on December 31. If you forgot to split in an earlier year, you can generally ask the CRA to accept a late election within three years after that year's filing due date. Illustration only: Asha, 68, has a $40,000 workplace pension. Her husband has $10,000 of income. Asha could move up to $20,000 to him. Moving $15,000 would leave them with about $25,000 each, which often means less tax in total. The pension income amount The pension income amount is a federal tax credit on up to $2,000 of eligible pension income a year (the CRA's figure for 2025). If one spouse has no eligible pension income, splitting even a small amount can let that spouse claim this credit too. The age amount If you are 65 or older on December 31, you can claim the age amount , a federal tax credit of up to $9,208 for 2026. It starts to shrink once your net income is over $46,432 (2026). If you can't use all of it, you may be able to transfer some to your spouse or common-law partner. Splitting changes each spouse's net income, so it can also change how much of the age amount each of you keeps. Our guide to often-missed tax credits covers other credits seniors can claim. Checklist and common mistakes Checklist Checked your CPP estimate in My Service Canada Account and thought about when to start (60 to 70). Applied for OAS, or decided to delay it, around age 65. If your income is low, made sure you are getting GIS (and the B.C. Senior's Supplement follows automatically). Planned what to do with your RRSP before December 31 of the year you turn 71. If your spouse is younger, considered using their age for your RRIF minimum before the first payment. Arranged enough tax withholding on RRIF and pension payments to avoid a surprise bill. Filed Form T1032 with both returns if splitting pension income. Common mistakes Trying to split CPP or OAS on the tax return. CPP uses Service Canada's separate pension sharing instead, and OAS can't be split. Splitting RRIF income when the person transferring it is under 65. Taking a big RRIF or RRSP withdrawal in one year and triggering the OAS clawback. Assuming the tax withheld on RRIF payments covers all the tax owed. Forgetting about foreign pensions. A pension from India or another country usually has to be reported on your Canadian return. If you are thinking of moving abroad in retirement, see our leaving Canada tax guide . title: RRSP vs TFSA vs FHSA: which account is right for you?
description: A plain-language comparison of the RRSP, TFSA and FHSA for 2026: who can open each, contribution limits, tax treatment, pros and cons, and which to use first.
text: Guides · Savings & tax RRSP vs TFSA vs FHSA: which account is right for you? Canada has three main tax-advantaged accounts for saving. Each one works differently, and choosing the right one, or the right mix, can save you thousands. Here's how they compare, in plain language. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated October 31, 2026 · Figures for 2026 On this page The short version Side-by-side comparison TFSA: Tax-Free Savings Account RRSP: Registered Retirement Savings Plan FHSA: First Home Savings Account Buying your first home: using all three Which should you use first? Common mistakes to avoid The short version TFSA Flexible, any goal No tax deduction when you put money in, but all growth and withdrawals are tax-free. Take money out any time, for anything. RRSP Retirement Contributions lower your taxes today. Money grows tax-deferred, and you pay tax when you take it out, ideally in retirement when your income is lower. FHSA Your first home The best of both: contributions are tax-deductible and withdrawals for your first home are tax-free. Only for first-time buyers. In all three accounts you can hold the same kinds of investments: savings deposits, GICs, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs and stocks. The account is just the tax "wrapper" around them. Side-by-side comparison Comparison of TFSA, RRSP and FHSA Feature TFSA RRSP FHSA Best for Any goal: emergency fund, car, travel, extra retirement savings Retirement Buying your first home Who can open Canadian residents 18+ with a SIN Anyone with earned income who files a return, until the end of the year they turn 71 Canadian residents 18 to 71 who are first-time home buyers 2026 limit $7,000 a year (up to $109,000 total if eligible since 2009) 18% of last year's earned income, up to $33,810, minus any pension adjustment $8,000 a year, $40,000 lifetime Unused room Carries forward with no limit Carries forward with no limit Up to $8,000 carries forward (only after the account is open) Tax deduction for contributions? No Yes Yes Investment growth Tax-free Tax-deferred Tax-free Withdrawals Tax-free, any time, any reason Taxed as income (tax withheld at source) Tax-free for a qualifying first-home purchase; otherwise taxed Withdrawal adds room back? Yes, on January 1 of the next year No (except HBP and LLP repayments) No Affects government benefits? No, withdrawals aren't income Yes, withdrawals count as income Qualifying withdrawals aren't income Time limit None Must close by the end of the year you turn 71 Must close within about 15 years, or by age 71 Over-contribution penalty 1% per month on the excess 1% per month on excess above a $2,000 buffer 1% per month on the excess TFSA: Tax-Free Savings Account How it works You contribute money you've already paid tax on. Everything it earns, whether interest, dividends or capital gains, is never taxed, and you can take money out at any time without paying tax. Who can open one You must be a Canadian resident, at least 18 years old, with a valid Social Insurance Number. You start building room in the year you turn 18. Newcomers start building room from the year they become residents (if 18 or older). Room isn't backdated for years before you lived in Canada. Limits 2026 limit: $7,000. The CRA hasn't announced the 2027 limit yet; it's usually published in November. Total room: someone who was 18 or older and living in Canada every year since 2009, and has never contributed, has $109,000 of room in 2026. Unused room carries forward forever. Anything you withdraw is added back to your room on January 1 of the following year . Pros All growth and withdrawals are tax-free Withdraw any time, for any reason Withdrawals don't reduce income-tested benefits like the Canada Child Benefit, GST/HST credit or Old Age Security No age limit and no need to have earned income Withdrawn amounts can be re-contributed later Cons No tax deduction for contributions Easy access can tempt you to spend your savings Re-contributing in the same year you withdrew can trigger an over-contribution penalty Contributions made while you're a non-resident are penalized RRSP: Registered Retirement Savings Plan How it works Your contributions are deducted from your income, which lowers the tax you pay this year. The money grows without tax until you withdraw it, and then the withdrawal is taxed as income. The idea is to get the deduction while you're earning a higher income and pay the tax later, in retirement, when your income and tax rate are usually lower. Who can contribute Anyone with RRSP room, which comes from earned income (mainly employment and self-employment income) reported on a tax return. You can contribute to your own RRSP until December 31 of the year you turn 71 . You can still contribute to a spousal RRSP after that, until the end of the year your spouse or common-law partner turns 71. Limits Your new room each year is 18% of the previous year's earned income , up to an annual maximum: $33,810 for 2026 and $35,390 for 2027 . If you're in a workplace pension plan, your room is reduced by your pension adjustment. Unused room carries forward. Your exact limit is printed on your Notice of Assessment and shown in your CRA account. Contributions made in the first 60 days of the year can be deducted on the previous year's return. For the 2026 tax year, the deadline is March 1, 2027 . You can over-contribute up to $2,000 without penalty. Beyond that, the excess is taxed at 1% per month. Withdrawals Withdrawals are added to your income, and your bank withholds tax at the source: 10% on amounts up to $5,000, 20% on $5,000 to $15,000, and 30% over $15,000 (outside Quebec). The withholding often isn't the full tax, so you may owe more at tax time. Unlike a TFSA, the room you used is gone for good. By the end of the year you turn 71, you must convert your RRSP to a RRIF (Registered Retirement Income Fund), buy an annuity , or withdraw it as cash. Spousal RRSP You can contribute to your spouse's or partner's RRSP using your own room and claim the deduction yourself. In retirement, the money is taxed in their hands, which can split income between you. If they withdraw it within about three years of your contributions, the withdrawal may be taxed back to you. Pros Contributions reduce your taxes now, often creating a refund Growth is tax-deferred for decades Higher limits than a TFSA for higher earners Spousal RRSPs help couples split retirement income Can be used for your first home (HBP) or education (LLP) Cons Withdrawals are fully taxable, with tax withheld up front Withdrawals can reduce income-tested benefits such as OAS and the GST/HST credit Room used on a withdrawal is lost Less useful when your income is low and you pay little tax Must be converted by the end of the year you turn 71 RRSP programs for homes and school Home Buyers' Plan (HBP): first-time buyers can withdraw up to $60,000 from their RRSPs tax-free to buy or build a home, and repay it over 15 years. Normally repayments start in the second year after the withdrawal. For a first withdrawal made between January 1, 2026 and December 31, 2028, repayments are deferred to start in the fifth year (for example, a 2026 withdrawal starts repayments in 2031). Missed repayments are added to your income. Lifelong Learning Plan (LLP): withdraw up to $10,000 a year , and $20,000 in total, to pay for full-time education or training for you or your spouse, then repay over 10 years. FHSA: First Home Savings Account How it works The FHSA combines the best parts of the RRSP and TFSA. Contributions are tax-deductible like an RRSP, and withdrawals to buy your first home are tax-free like a TFSA. Who can open one You must be a Canadian resident, at least 18 (19 in provinces where that's the age of majority, including BC), and no older than 71 at the end of the year you open it. You must be a first-time home buyer : in the current year and the four previous calendar years, you didn't live in a home you owned or jointly owned. If you have a spouse or common-law partner, the same applies to a home they owned that you lived in. Limits $8,000 a year , up to $40,000 in your lifetime . Room only starts once you open the account . Up to $8,000 of unused room carries forward, so the most you can contribute in one year is $16,000. Unlike the RRSP, contributions must be made by December 31 to count for that year. You don't have to deduct your contributions right away. You can carry the deduction forward to a year when your income, and the tax saving, is higher. Withdrawals A withdrawal is tax-free if it's a qualifying withdrawal: you're still a first-time buyer, you have a written agreement to buy or build a qualifying home in Canada before October 1 of the following year, and you plan to live in it as your main home within one year. The account must be closed by December 31 of the earliest of: the 15th anniversary of opening your first FHSA, the year you turn 71, or the year after your first qualifying withdrawal. If you don't buy a home, you can transfer the money to your RRSP tax-free without using any RRSP room, or withdraw it as taxable income. Pros Tax deduction going in and tax-free coming out for a home Unlike the HBP, nothing has to be paid back Can be combined with the Home Buyers' Plan for the same home If plans change, it rolls into your RRSP without using RRSP room The deduction can be saved for a higher-income year Cons Only for first-time buyers Room doesn't build until you open the account, so open it early Lower limits: $8,000 a year and $40,000 for life Non-qualifying withdrawals are fully taxable Must be closed within about 15 years Buying your first home: using all three First-time buyers can combine accounts for the same home. Per person, that's up to: $40,000 of FHSA contributions plus any growth, withdrawn tax-free and never repaid $60,000 from RRSPs through the Home Buyers' Plan, repaid over 15 years Whatever you've saved in your TFSA , withdrawn tax-free A couple who are both first-time buyers can each do this, which can add up to $200,000 or more toward a down payment before counting TFSAs. Which should you use first? There's no single right answer, but these are common starting points: Planning to buy your first home Open an FHSA now, even with a small deposit, so your room starts building. Max it out before anything else, then use your RRSP (with the HBP) and TFSA. Lower income (roughly under $55,000) Usually TFSA first . Your RRSP deduction would save little tax, and RRSP withdrawals later could reduce benefits. Save the RRSP room for when your income rises. Higher income The RRSP often comes first, because the deduction saves tax at a higher rate. Put your refund into your TFSA to make it work twice. Building an emergency fund A TFSA , since you can take money out at any time without tax and get the room back next year. Self-employed or variable income Use the TFSA in lower-income years and the RRSP in higher-income years to get the most from each deduction. New to Canada Your TFSA room starts the year you arrive (if 18 or older), and RRSP room starts once you have Canadian earned income and file a return. Check whether you qualify as a first-time buyer for an FHSA , and remember to report any foreign property over $100,000. The income levels above are rough guides. The best mix depends on your tax bracket now and in retirement, your goals and your benefits. Common mistakes to avoid Over-contributing to a TFSA by withdrawing and putting money back in the same year. The room only comes back on January 1. Guessing your limits. Check your CRA account or Notice of Assessment. Bank records don't show contributions you made at other institutions. Waiting to open an FHSA. No room builds until the account exists. Leaving cash uninvested. A registered account holding cash earning nothing wastes its tax advantage. Choose investments that suit your timeline and risk. Missing HBP repayments, which are added to your taxable income. Contributing while living abroad to a TFSA, which is penalized every month. US citizens: TFSAs and FHSAs may not be tax-sheltered under US tax rules. Get advice before contributing. Not sure which account is right for you? We'll look at your income, goals and tax situation, check your available room, and help you decide where your savings should go. As part of your tax return, we'll also make sure your RRSP and FHSA deductions are claimed in the best year.
