title: Self-employed? What you can deduct on Form T2125
description: What freelancers, contractors and ride-share drivers can deduct on Form T2125: home office, vehicle, meals, phone, CCA, plus CPP and deadlines.
text: Guides · Small business Self-employed? What you can deduct on Form T2125 When you work for yourself, every legitimate business expense lowers the tax you pay. This guide explains what you can claim on Form T2125, the rules for home offices and vehicles, and the records you need to back it all up. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short You can deduct reasonable expenses you incur to earn business income, but only the business share of anything you also use personally. A home office qualifies only if it's your main place of business, or used only for business and regularly to meet clients, and it can't create a loss. Vehicle costs are claimed by business kilometres, so keep a logbook; for 2026, the class 10.1 cost limit for passenger vehicles is $39,000 plus tax. Meals and entertainment are usually only 50% deductible, and big purchases are claimed over time through capital cost allowance. For 2026, self-employed people pay both halves of CPP: 11.9% up to a maximum of $8,460.90, plus CPP2. File by June 15, 2027 for the 2026 tax year, but pay any balance by April 30, 2027. On this page The basic test: what makes an expense deductible Common deductible expenses Business use of your home Car and vehicle expenses Bigger purchases: capital cost allowance What you can't deduct GST/HST and keeping records CPP, instalments and deadlines Common mistakes and a year-end checklist The basic test: what makes an expense deductible If you're a sole proprietor, freelancer, contractor, or ride-share or delivery driver, you report your business income and expenses on Form T2125 , the Statement of Business or Professional Activities, which goes with your personal tax return. You pay tax only on your net income : what you earned minus your allowable expenses. Two questions decide whether an expense counts: Did you spend it to earn business income? The CRA describes a business expense as a cost incurred "for the sole purpose of earning business income." Personal costs don't qualify. Is the amount reasonable? You can generally deduct reasonable current expenses. A $5,000 dinner with one client, or paying your teenager $40 an hour to file papers, would raise questions. When something is used for both business and personal life, like a car, a phone or your home, you deduct only the business part . And if you're registered for GST/HST, you deduct each expense net of any input tax credit you claim (more on that below). Common deductible expenses These are the everyday costs most self-employed people can claim, as long as they're for the business: Advertising: website, online ads, business cards, flyers. Supplies used up in your work, and office expenses such as stationery, postage and printer ink. Professional fees: accounting, bookkeeping and legal fees for the business. Business taxes, licences and dues: a municipal business licence, professional association fees. Insurance for the business, such as liability insurance. Interest and bank charges on business loans, business credit cards and your business account. Rent for an office, workshop or storage unit. Delivery and freight costs. Travel costs for business trips. Salaries and wages paid to employees, including your spouse or child if they really do the work, you actually pay them, and the pay is what you'd pay a stranger for the same job. You must issue them T4 slips. Meals and entertainment are deductible, but usually only 50% of the lesser of what you spent and a reasonable amount. So a $100 client lunch gives a $50 deduction. A few exceptions exist, for example if you bill the meal to a client and show it on the invoice. Couriers and rickshaw drivers can claim a flat $23 a day for the extra food they need on an eight-hour working day, as long as they keep a logbook. Phone and internet: a separate business phone line is fully deductible. For your cellphone, claim the business percentage of your plan. The basic monthly rate of a personal home landline isn't deductible, but business long-distance calls are. Apply the same business-share idea to your internet. Business use of your home Working from home can let you claim part of your household costs, but only if your workspace meets one of these conditions: it's your main place of business , or you use it only to earn business income, and you use it regularly and on an ongoing basis to meet clients , customers or patients. What you can include Homeowners: a share of heating, electricity, home insurance, cleaning materials, maintenance, property taxes and mortgage interest (not the principal part of your payment). Renters: a share of your rent and any expenses that relate to the workspace. How to work out your share Use a reasonable method, usually floor area. If your office is 150 square feet in a 1,500-square-foot home, your business share is 10%. If annual eligible costs are $24,000, you could claim $2,400. If the room is also used by the family, multiply further by the hours it's used for business. For example, a room used for business 8 hours a day gives 8 ÷ 24 = one-third of that room's share. If you run the business for only part of the year, reduce the claim to match. Limits to know Home office expenses can't create or increase a business loss . You can claim them only up to your business income after other expenses. Any amount you can't use carries forward to next year, under the same conditions. You can also claim capital cost allowance (CCA, the tax version of depreciation) on the business part of a home you own, but this is usually a bad idea: when you sell, capital gains and recapture rules can apply to that business part of your home. Car and vehicle expenses If you use your vehicle for business, you can deduct the business share of its costs. That's especially important for ride-share, delivery and trades workers. What you can claim Fuel, or electricity for an electric vehicle, oil changes, maintenance and repairs, insurance, licence and registration, interest on a car loan, lease payments, and CCA if you own the vehicle. Parking for business trips and extra business insurance are deductible in full. Business share = business kilometres ÷ total kilometres Example: you drive 20,000 km in the year, and 15,000 km are for business. Your business share is 75%. If your vehicle costs (not counting CCA) total $8,000, you can claim $6,000. Keep a logbook For each business trip, record the date, destination, purpose and kilometres. Write down your odometer reading at the start and end of the year. After you've kept a full logbook for one year, the CRA allows a simpler option: a three-month sample logbook in later years, as long as your business use stays within 10% of that base year. Limits on passenger vehicles for 2026 Most cars count as "passenger vehicles" (Guide T4002 has a chart to classify yours, based on seating and how it's used). For passenger vehicles, these 2026 limits apply: Limit 2026 amount Cost you can depreciate (CCA class 10.1), for vehicles bought on or after January 1, 2026 $39,000 plus tax Cost you can depreciate for a zero-emission passenger vehicle (class 54) $61,000 plus tax Deductible car loan interest (new loans) $350 a month Deductible lease cost (new leases) $1,100 a month plus tax The CRA's per-kilometre rate isn't for you. For 2026, the federal government set 73 cents a km for the first 5,000 km and 67 cents after that in the provinces. Those rates limit tax-free allowances that employers pay employees. As a self-employed person, you claim your actual costs times your business-use share, backed by receipts and a logbook. Bigger purchases: capital cost allowance Some costs give you a benefit for many years, like a laptop, tools, furniture or a vehicle. These are capital expenses , and you usually can't deduct them all at once. Instead, you claim capital cost allowance (CCA) , a set percentage each year. Day-to-day costs and repairs that just restore something to how it was are current expenses and are deducted in full. Some common CCA classes: Class 50 (55%): computers and related hardware. Class 8 (20%): furniture, equipment and tools costing $500 or more. Class 12 (100%): small tools and kitchen utensils costing less than $500, plus most application software. Class 10 (30%): motor vehicles, and passenger vehicles that cost $39,000 or less (for 2026 purchases). Class 10.1 (30%): passenger vehicles that cost more than the limit. Each one goes in its own class, and you can only depreciate up to the limit. In the year you buy something, the half-year rule usually lets you claim CCA on only half the cost. You don't have to claim the maximum CCA; you can claim less in a low-income year and save the balance for later. A temporary rule that let unincorporated business owners write off some purchases right away ("immediate expensing") applied only to property that became available for use before 2025 , so it doesn't help with purchases made now. The CRA's guide also describes proposed rules for a larger first-year claim on some property; ask before relying on them. What you can't deduct Personal and living expenses, such as your groceries, family trips, gym membership, or the personal share of your car, phone and home. Money you pay yourself. Your own "salary" or drawings from a sole proprietorship aren't an expense. Most fines and penalties, including parking and speeding tickets, even on a business trip. Interest and penalties on your income tax. Donations and political contributions. Most life insurance premiums. The full cost of capital items in one year (use CCA instead). Clothing is a grey area. The CRA's lists of business expenses don't include everyday clothing, and personal costs can't be deducted, so ask before claiming any. GST/HST and keeping records GST/HST input tax credits You must register for GST/HST once your taxable sales go over $30,000 in a single calendar quarter or over four consecutive quarters. Taxi and ride-share drivers must register no matter how much they earn. Once registered, you can usually claim back the GST/HST you paid on business expenses as input tax credits (ITCs) . If you do, deduct the expense on your T2125 without the GST/HST you got back, so you don't claim it twice. Records and receipts Keep receipts, invoices and bank and credit card statements. Receipts should show the seller's name and the date. Keep your records for at least six years after the end of the last tax year they relate to. Digital copies are fine if they are clear and easy to read. Keep your vehicle logbook and your home-office measurements with your records. Tip: a separate bank account and credit card for the business makes record keeping much easier, and makes it simple to show the CRA which costs were business costs. CPP, instalments and deadlines CPP for the self-employed Employees pay half of their Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contributions and their employer pays the other half. When you're self-employed, you pay both halves , calculated on your net self-employment income when you file your return. For 2026: 11.9% on net earnings between $3,500 and $74,600, up to a maximum of $8,460.90 . A second layer (CPP2) of 8% on earnings between $74,600 and $85,000, up to $832 . Example: with $50,000 of net self-employment income, your 2026 CPP is ($50,000 − $3,500) × 11.9% = $5,533.50 . There's some relief: the "employer" half of the base contributions, plus all the enhanced (extra) contributions, are deducted from your income. The other half of the base contributions gives you a non-refundable tax credit. Instalments If your net tax owing is more than $3,000 for this year, and was also over $3,000 in either of the two previous years, the CRA expects you to pay tax in instalments during the year. For 2027, the due dates are March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15. Filing and payment deadlines For the 2026 tax year, self-employed people (and their spouses or common-law partners) have until June 15, 2027 to file. But any balance owing must be paid by April 30, 2027 , or interest starts. Common mistakes and a year-end checklist Common mistakes Claiming 100% of a car or phone that's also used personally. No logbook, so the business share of driving can't be proven. Claiming meals in full instead of 50%. Deducting a laptop or vehicle in full instead of using CCA. Using home office expenses to create a loss. Claiming GST/HST as an expense and also as an input tax credit. Filing on June 15 but paying late, and being charged interest from April 30. Forgetting to set money aside for CPP, which can be a large bill for the self-employed. Checklist before you file Total income from all sources: invoices, platform statements and T4A slips. Receipts sorted by category, with the GST/HST paid shown separately if you're registered. Vehicle logbook and odometer readings for January 1 and December 31. Home office measurements and the year's utility, insurance, property tax, mortgage interest or rent bills. List of equipment bought or sold during the year, with dates and costs. Any instalments paid, and money set aside for tax and CPP. Want help getting your business expenses right? We prepare T2125 statements for freelancers, contractors and drivers every year. We can sort your receipts, work out your home office and vehicle claims, and set up simple record keeping for next year. title: Separation and divorce in BC: how your taxes and benefits change
description: Separating or divorcing in BC? Learn the CRA's 90-day rule, how your benefits change, how child and spousal support are taxed, and how to split property.
text: Guides · Personal tax Separation and divorce in BC: how your taxes and benefits change A separation changes a lot more than your living arrangements. It changes your marital status for tax purposes, the benefits you receive, how support payments are taxed and how your shared property and savings can be divided. Getting the tax side right early can protect your benefit payments and save you from a bill later. Here is a plain-language overview for people in British Columbia. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 13, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short For tax purposes, you count as separated once you have lived apart because of a relationship breakdown for at least 90 days. After the 90 days, tell the CRA by the end of the month after your status changed so your benefits are recalculated correctly. Child support under an order or agreement made after April 1997 is not taxable or deductible; spousal support usually is. Register any order or agreement that includes spousal support with the CRA on Form T1158. RRSP and TFSA savings can move to a former partner without tax if done as a direct transfer under a court order or written agreement. If neither parent can agree who claims the eligible dependant amount for a child, neither parent can claim it. On this page When does the CRA treat you as separated? Telling the CRA about your new status How your benefits change Child support and spousal support: who pays tax? The eligible dependant credit and legal fees Dividing property, savings and pension credits Checklist and common mistakes When does the CRA treat you as separated? Your marital status is how the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) describes your relationship on your tax return: married, living common-law, separated, divorced, widowed or single. It matters because many credits and benefits are based on your family net income , which is your income plus your partner's. A common-law partner is someone you live with in a marriage-like relationship who is not your legal spouse. For tax purposes, that usually means you have lived together for 12 months in a row, or you share a child by birth or adoption. The 90-day rule You are separated when you have lived apart from your spouse or common-law partner because your relationship broke down, for at least 90 days. Once you reach 90 days, your separation counts from the first day you lived apart, not from day 90. Living apart for other reasons, such as work, school, health or time in prison, does not make you separated. You are divorced only once the divorce is legally final. Until then, a married person who has lived apart for 90 days is separated. Illustration: Sam and Alex stop living together on March 1 because their relationship has ended. They are still apart on May 30, 90 days later, so the CRA treats them as separated from March 1. B.C. family law uses a different test Tax rules and family law rules are not the same. Under B.C.'s Family Law Act , unmarried partners must have lived together in a marriage-like relationship for at least two years before the property and debt division rules apply. A couple with a child together can qualify for spousal support with less time than that. Telling the CRA about your new status Wait for the 90 days. Do not report a separation until you have been apart for at least 90 days. Then report it quickly. The CRA asks you to report a change by the end of the month after the month your status changed. How to report: update your status in CRA My Account (the fastest way), call the CRA's benefits line at 1-800-387-1193, or mail Form RC65, Marital Status Change . If you already filed: if you filed as a couple before reaching 90 days apart, and you then stay apart past 90 days, update your status and file a change (an amended return ) to fix amounts you claimed as a couple. Reporting on time matters. Your benefits are recalculated on your new family income, and late reporting can lead to overpayments that you have to pay back. Both of you should keep filing a tax return every year, even with no income. The CRA needs each return to work out benefits such as the Canada child benefit. If you are leaving an abusive situation: the CRA says you do not need your partner's signature on any benefit form, and you never need to contact an abusive person to get your benefits. If you can't get the usual documents, a letter from a shelter or a copy of a police report can be used instead. You can update your address right away, without waiting 90 days. How your benefits change Canada child benefit (CCB) The CCB is a tax-free monthly payment for families with children under 18. After a separation is reported, the CRA recalculates it using your new status and your own family income. The new amount starts with the month after the month your status changed. Only one parent in a household gets the CCB for a child. When a child lives with a mother, the CRA usually treats her as the parent mainly responsible for the child. If the other parent is actually mainly responsible, they can apply with a signed letter from the mother saying so. Shared custody means the child lives with each parent about equally, which the CRA treats as 40% to 60% of the time with each. In that case, each parent gets half of what they would get if the child lived with them full-time. Each parent should tell the CRA about a new custody arrangement right away, through My Account or Form RC66. Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (formerly the GST/HST credit) In July 2026, the GST/HST credit was renamed the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit . It is a tax-free payment, made four times a year, for people with low or modest incomes. After a separation, each of you is assessed separately from the date you started living apart, and the CRA sends a notice showing the new amount. In shared custody, each eligible parent may get half of the amount for the child. B.C. family benefit The B.C. family benefit is a provincial payment for families with children under 18. The CRA pays it with your CCB in one monthly deposit, using the same application, so you do not apply separately. The CRA lists a separate amount for the first child in a single-parent family (up to $41.66 a month for July 2026 to June 2027), so your payment can change when you become a single parent. Our CCB and B.C. family benefit guide explains how the amounts are worked out. Child support and spousal support: who pays tax? Support payments are regular amounts one person pays to help support a former partner, their children, or both. Child support is for the children. Spousal support is only for the former spouse or common-law partner. For the CRA to treat a payment as support, it generally must be: set out in a court order or written agreement , with a specific amount; paid on a periodic (regular) schedule, such as monthly, as the order or agreement sets out; paid while you live apart because the relationship broke down (for a former partner); and money the recipient can use however they choose. Child support Spousal support Order or agreement made after April 1997 Not deductible for the payer and not taxable for the recipient Usually deductible for the payer and taxable for the recipient Payer reports it on Line 21999 (total paid) Line 21999 (total) and line 22000 (deductible part) Recipient reports it on Line 12799 (total received) Line 12799 (total) and line 12800 (taxable part) Register with the CRA? Not if the order covers child support only Yes, on Form T1158 Older orders and agreements made before May 1997 can follow the old rules, where child support is also taxable and deductible. That changes if the child support amount was later changed, or if both parents sign Form T1157 to move to the newer rules, a choice that can't be undone. Rules that catch people out Spousal support counts only if child support is fully paid. When an order covers both, payments are applied to child support first. Spousal support is deductible only when all child support owed for the year and earlier years has been paid. Payments before the paperwork. Support paid before the order or agreement is signed, in the same year or the year before, counts only if the order or agreement says so. Register spousal support. Send Form T1158 for each order or agreement that includes spousal support. Do not attach the agreement to your return, but keep proof of every payment, such as bank statements or cancelled cheques. Illustration: Jordan pays $1,000 a month in child support and $500 a month in spousal support under a 2026 separation agreement. Over a full year Jordan would report $18,000 on line 21999 and deduct $6,000 on line 22000. Her former partner reports $18,000 on line 12799 and $6,000 on line 12800. Warning about lump sums: a one-time payment is usually not support for tax purposes, even if the agreement calls it deductible. A lump sum paid to settle future support is neither deductible nor taxable. Paying overdue support in one amount is treated differently. Get advice before agreeing to a lump sum. The eligible dependant credit and legal fees Amount for an eligible dependant (line 30400) This non-refundable tax credit (a credit that lowers the tax you owe but does not create a refund on its own) can help single parents. A separated or divorced parent may be able to claim it for a child under 18 who lives with them in a home they keep up. Key rules: Only one claim is allowed per household, and the amount can't be split between two people. A parent who must pay child support for a child generally can't claim this amount for that child. The other parent may be able to. If both parents are clearly required to pay support for the same child, or custody is shared, you must agree who claims. If you can't agree, neither of you can claim. Using both parents' incomes to work out child support does not, by itself, mean both are paying. In the year you separate, if you paid support, you can choose either this credit or the deduction for your support payments, whichever helps you more. Our guide to often-missed tax credits covers other credits single parents should check. Can you deduct legal fees? Not deductible for anyone: fees to get a separation or divorce, or to set custody or parenting time. Not deductible for the payer: fees to set, fight or reduce support. Deductible for the recipient: fees to collect overdue support, to set the amount of support, or to try to increase it. Fees to try to make child support non-taxable are also deductible. Dividing property, savings and pension credits Transfers between partners: the rollover Normally, when you give away an investment or property that has gone up in value, you pay tax on the capital gain (the increase in value). Between spouses or common-law partners, a special rule called a rollover applies instead. The property moves at its original cost, so there is no tax at the time of the transfer. The person receiving it takes over that original cost and pays the tax when they later sell. You can choose to opt out of the rollover and transfer at market value, but that triggers tax right away. Attribution rules are anti-income-splitting rules. Normally, if a spouse sells property you gave them, the gain can be taxed back to you. If you are living apart because the relationship broke down, you can file a signed election with your return so the gain is not taxed to you. RRSPs and TFSAs RRSP: money can move from one partner's RRSP to the other's without tax if it is a direct transfer under a court order or written agreement dividing property, and you are living apart because of the breakdown. The financial institution uses Form T2220 . TFSA: a direct transfer between institutions under a court order or written separation agreement, while you live apart, does not affect either person's TFSA room. Withdrawing the cash and handing it over is different, and could put the receiving person over their limit. Your home The principal residence exemption can remove the capital gain on your home when you sell it. A family unit can only name one home per year. Your spouse or partner stays in your family unit for a year unless, for that whole year, you lived apart under a court-ordered (judicial) separation or a written separation agreement. If you sell, you must report the sale on your return using Form T2091(IND). See our guide to capital gains and selling a home . CPP credit splitting The pension credits you each built up in the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) while living together can be split between you. You must have lived together for at least 12 months in a row. Separated married couples and former common-law partners must also have lived apart for at least 12 months in a row. Former common-law partners must apply within 48 months of starting to live apart. Either of you can apply to Service Canada, online or on Form ISP1901. The split is permanent. Our retirement income guide explains CPP in more detail. Checklist and common mistakes Checklist Note the first day you and your partner lived apart. After 90 days apart, update your marital status in My Account or on Form RC65, by the end of the following month. Report any new custody arrangement for the CCB right away. Make sure your support terms are in a written agreement or court order, with clear amounts for child and spousal support. Register any agreement that includes spousal support on Form T1158. Keep proof of every support payment. Agree in writing which parent will claim the eligible dependant amount for each child. Move RRSP and TFSA money by direct transfer, not by withdrawing it. Decide how CPP credits will be split and apply to Service Canada. Keep filing your tax return every year, on time. Common mistakes Reporting a separation before 90 days, or forgetting to report it at all. Paying "spousal support" without a written agreement, then trying to deduct it. Deducting spousal support while child support is still owing. Both parents claiming the eligible dependant amount for the same child. Cashing out an RRSP to pay a former partner, instead of a tax-free transfer. Trying to deduct the legal costs of getting a divorce. Going through a separation? Calcitax Advisors can help you update your status with the CRA, check your benefits, work out how support payments affect your taxes, and prepare your return for the year you separate. title: Sole proprietor or corporation? Choosing a structure in BC
description: Should your BC business stay a sole proprietorship or incorporate? Costs, tax rates, paying yourself, liability and signs it's time to switch.
text: Guides · Small business Sole proprietor or corporation? Choosing a structure in BC Most small businesses in BC start as sole proprietorships, and many later wonder whether to incorporate. Here's how the two structures compare on cost, tax, liability and paperwork, so you can weigh the factors for your own business. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short A sole proprietor is taxed on all business profit personally, on Form T2125; a corporation files its own T2 return and pays its own tax. A small Canadian-controlled private corporation pays about 11% combined federal and BC tax on its first $500,000 of active business income. The lower rate mainly defers tax on profit left in the company; you pay personal tax when you take it out. Salary builds CPP and RRSP room; dividends don't, but they're taxed with a dividend tax credit. Limited liability doesn't cover personal guarantees or unremitted payroll deductions. A corporation costs more to set up and run: BC fees, a T2 return, an annual report and more formal bookkeeping. On this page Sole proprietorship or corporation: what's the difference? Setting up in BC: registration, names and costs How each one is taxed Paying yourself from a corporation: salary or dividends Liability protection and the extra work of a corporation Side-by-side comparison Signs it may be time to incorporate Common mistakes to avoid Sole proprietorship or corporation: what's the difference? A sole proprietorship is the simplest way to run a business. You and the business are the same person in the eyes of the law. You keep all the profit, you make all the decisions, and you carry all the risk. If the business owes money, the CRA notes that the risk can reach your personal property and assets. A corporation (a company) is a separate legal "person." It can own property, sign contracts, borrow money and pay tax in its own name. You own it through shares, so you're a shareholder , and you usually act as its director (the person who manages it) too. The company keeps existing even if the shares change hands. Neither one is "better." Many businesses start as sole proprietorships and incorporate later, once profits grow. The right choice depends on how much you earn, how much you need to live on, the risks in your line of work, and how much paperwork you're ready to take on. Setting up in BC: registration, names and costs Sole proprietorship If you do business under your own legal name (for example, "Priya Sharma"), you don't need to register the business or request a name with the province. If you use any other name (for example, "Fraser Valley Cleaning"), you must first get the name approved and then register the business with BC Registries. Government fees: $30 for a name request ($100 for priority service), then $40 to register online through the BC Business Registry or in person at Service BC. Register within 56 days of the name being approved, or the approval expires. BC corporation Reserve a name for $30 (it must end with a word like Inc. or Ltd.), or skip the name and use a numbered company such as "0123456 B.C. Ltd." Prepare the company's articles (its rule book) and apply to incorporate. The provincial fee for most companies is $350 . Every year, file a BC annual report within two months of your incorporation anniversary. The fee is $43.39 . Missing it two years in a row can lead to the company being dissolved. Federal corporation Incorporating federally with Corporations Canada costs $200 online and protects your name across Canada. The federal annual return is $12 online. If you operate in BC, a federal company must also register in BC as an "extraprovincial" company ( $350 ) and file BC annual reports as well. These are government filing fees only. Legal help with articles and share structure, accounting set-up and a municipal business licence (from Surrey, Vancouver or your own city) are separate costs. How each one is taxed Sole proprietor: on your personal return You report the business's income and expenses on Form T2125 and include the profit on your personal T1 return. It's added to any other income you have and taxed at your personal rates. For 2026, the combined federal and BC rate on each extra dollar is 28.2% once your taxable income is between $58,523 and $100,728, and it climbs from there. A business loss can reduce your other income, such as a part-time job, in the same year. Corporation: its own return and its own rates The company files a T2 corporate return every year, within six months of its year-end, even if it owes no tax. A Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) earning active business income can claim the small business deduction , which lowers the tax rate on its first $500,000 of active business income each year (the "business limit"). Federal rate with the small business deduction: 9% . BC small business rate: 2% . Combined: about 11% on income up to the $500,000 limit, compared with 27% (15% federal plus 12% BC) on income above it. The $500,000 limit is shared between associated companies (for example, two companies owned by the same person) and shrinks if the company's investment income goes over $50,000 a year. Losses stay inside the company: you can't use them on your personal return. The "tax deferral" idea Here's a simple illustration with round numbers. Say your business makes $150,000 of profit and you need $90,000 a year to live on. As a sole proprietor, all $150,000 is taxed on your personal return this year. The last $60,000 is taxed at combined 2026 rates that range from 28.2% up to 40.7% as your income rises. With a corporation, you could pay yourself $90,000 and leave the other $60,000 in the company. At about 11%, the company pays roughly $6,600 of tax on it, leaving about $53,400 to reinvest in the business or save. Deferral isn't the same as saving. When you later take that money out as a dividend, you pay personal tax on it. The benefit comes mainly from timing : it helps most when you don't need all the profit for living costs. If you take out everything the business earns each year, incorporating may save little or nothing once extra costs are counted. Paying yourself from a corporation: salary or dividends A sole proprietor simply takes money out of the business. Those "drawings" aren't a deduction, and you're taxed on the profit whether you take it out or not. With a corporation, the money belongs to the company, so you need a proper way to pay yourself. The two main options: Salary (or bonus) The company runs payroll, deducts tax, and issues you a T4 slip . The company deducts CPP contributions from your pay and also pays a matching employer share, so both halves of CPP are paid, which builds your future CPP pension. Salary counts as earned income , so it creates RRSP room (18% of the previous year's earned income, up to the yearly maximum). Salary is an expense for the company, which lowers its taxable income. Dividends The company pays dividends out of its after-tax profit and reports them on a T5 slip . Dividends aren't employment earnings, so no CPP is paid on them. That saves cash now, but it also means no CPP pension built on that income. Dividends don't count as earned income, so they create no RRSP room . On your personal return, dividends are "grossed up" and then reduced by the dividend tax credit . There are two kinds, "eligible" and "other than eligible" dividends, with different gross-ups (38% and 15%) and credits. Many owners use a mix of both. The best mix depends on your income needs, retirement plans, RRSP and CPP goals, and whether family members work in the business. This is an area where a tax professional can help you run the numbers each year. Liability protection and the extra work of a corporation How much protection does a company really give? In general, shareholders aren't responsible for a corporation's debts, so a supplier or customer with a claim against the business usually can't come after your house. But there are important limits: Personal guarantees. Banks and landlords often ask a small company's owner to personally guarantee a loan or lease. If you sign, you owe that debt if the company can't pay. Directors' liability. Directors can be personally liable for payroll deductions, CPP and other amounts the company was required to withhold or remit but didn't. Extra costs and filings A T2 return every year, with financial statements, due six months after year-end. Any tax owing is usually due three months after year-end for a CCPC claiming the small business deduction (two months otherwise). The BC annual report (and the federal annual return if federally incorporated). A separate business bank account and proper bookkeeping, since the company's money isn't yours. Payroll filings and T4 slips if you pay salary, and T5 slips if you pay dividends. Minute book and company records kept at the registered office. Higher accounting fees than for a simple T2125. Selling your business one day Owners who sell shares of a qualifying small business corporation may be able to shelter a large capital gain with the lifetime capital gains exemption . The CRA's guidance for 2025 shows a limit of $1,250,000 , describes that figure as a proposed change, and says the limit is indexed to inflation. The conditions are strict and need planning years ahead. A sole proprietor selling a business can't use this exemption on shares, because there are no shares to sell. GST/HST applies either way Whether you're a sole proprietor or a corporation, you must register for GST/HST once your taxable sales (together with associated businesses) go over $30,000 in a single calendar quarter or over four consecutive quarters. Taxi and ride-share drivers must register no matter how much they earn. Incorporating doesn't change this. Side-by-side comparison Feature Sole proprietorship Corporation Legal status You and the business are the same Separate legal entity BC set-up fees None under your own name; $30 name + $40 registration otherwise $30 name (optional) + $350 (BC); or $200 federal + $350 BC registration Yearly government filing None to the registry BC annual report ($43.39); federal return extra Tax return T1 with Form T2125 T2 corporate return, plus your own T1 Tax rate on business profit Your personal rates About 11% combined on the first $500,000 of active business income Business losses Can reduce your other income Stay in the company Paying yourself Drawings (not deductible) Salary (T4) and/or dividends (T5) CPP Both halves on net self-employment income Both halves on salary; none on dividends Liability Unlimited personal liability Generally limited, but not for personal guarantees or unremitted payroll Bookkeeping Simpler More formal; separate records and bank account GST/HST Register over $30,000 Register over $30,000 Signs it may be time to incorporate There's no single income level where incorporating becomes right. These are the factors to weigh: You're earning more than you spend. If profit is well above what you need to live on, and you'd leave the extra in the business, the lower corporate rate can help you grow faster. Your business carries real risk. Contracts, employees, a lease, or customers who could sue may make limited liability worth having, keeping in mind its limits. You need to raise money. A corporation can usually raise larger amounts of capital, for example by selling shares to an investor. You might sell one day. Selling shares of a qualifying company may let you use the lifetime capital gains exemption. Family members are involved. Paying a spouse or adult child, or making them shareholders, adds options but also special tax rules, so get advice before you set things up. On the other side, staying a sole proprietor often makes sense when you're just starting, expect losses in the early years (which can reduce your other income), need all the profit to live on, or want to keep paperwork and costs low. Common mistakes to avoid Mixing personal and business money. Paying groceries from the company account, or company bills from your own card, makes bookkeeping messy and can create tax problems. Use a separate account and card. Treating company money as your own. Money you take out of a corporation that isn't salary, a dividend or a repaid expense becomes a shareholder loan . If it's not repaid within one year after the end of the company's tax year (and isn't part of a pattern of borrowing and repaying), it can be added to your personal income. Incorporating only for the "11% rate". If you take out every dollar each year, the deferral advantage mostly disappears, while the extra costs remain. Forgetting the annual report. Two missed years can get the company dissolved. Not registering a business name. In BC, a sole proprietor using any name other than their own legal name must get it approved and register it. Assuming a company protects everything. Personal guarantees and unpaid payroll remittances can still land on you. Ignoring GST/HST. The $30,000 threshold applies either way, and ride-share drivers must register from day one. Thinking about incorporating your business? title: Tax instalments for individuals: who pays, when and how much
description: Plain-language guide to CRA tax instalments: the $3,000 rule, the four due dates, the three ways to work out payments, and how to avoid interest.
text: Guides · Personal tax Tax instalments for individuals: who pays, when and how much If you earn money with no tax taken off, such as self-employment, rental or investment income, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) may ask you to pay part of your tax during the year instead of all of it in the spring. These advance payments are called instalments. This guide explains who has to pay them, the four due dates, how to work out the amounts, and how to avoid interest charges. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 10, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short You must pay 2026 instalments if your net tax owing is more than $3,000 for 2026 and was also more than $3,000 in 2025 or 2024. Instalments are due March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15 (farmers and fishers pay once, on December 31). The CRA sends reminders in February and August, but they are not a bill: you can choose another calculation option if your income changed. Late or short payments are charged interest at the CRA's prescribed rate, 7% compounded daily for October to December 2026. Having more tax withheld from a pension, CPP, OAS or a job can reduce or remove the need for instalments. Budget 2026 proposes raising the threshold to $7,500 from 2028, but this is not law yet. On this page What tax instalments are and why they exist Who has to pay: the $3,000 rule The four due dates How much to pay: the three options Paying and keeping track Interest and penalties if you pay late or too little Ways to reduce or avoid instalments Common mistakes and a quick checklist What tax instalments are and why they exist When you have a job, your employer takes income tax off every paycheque and sends it to the CRA. This is called tax withheld at source . By the time you file your return, most of your tax is already paid. Some income has little or no tax taken off. The CRA lists these common examples: self-employment income, such as a small business, consulting or gig work rental income investment income, such as interest, dividends and capital gains certain pension payments income from more than one job, where each employer withholds too little If you have this kind of income, you could owe a large bill in the spring. Instalments are payments you make during the year to cover that tax as you go, a bit like having tax withheld from a paycheque. They are not an extra tax. Every dollar you pay counts toward your final tax bill, and you claim it on your return. Instalments for one year are paid during that same year. For example, 2026 instalments are paid in 2026 toward the tax on your 2026 income. Who has to pay: the $3,000 rule Whether you must pay depends on your net tax owing . In simple terms, this is your total federal and provincial income tax for the year, minus the tax that was already withheld at source. It is roughly the balance you would owe when you file if you made no instalments. If you live anywhere in Canada except Quebec, you must pay instalments for 2026 when both of these are true: your net tax owing for 2026 will be more than $3,000 , and your net tax owing was more than $3,000 in either 2025 or 2024 . For Quebec residents the threshold is $1,800. The province you live in on December 31 is the one that counts. Here is how the two-part test works, using simple made-up numbers for someone in B.C.: Person 2024 2025 Expected 2026 Instalments for 2026? Amrit $2,000 $4,000 $5,000 Yes: over $3,000 in 2026 and in 2025 Lisa $1,000 $2,500 $6,000 No: 2024 and 2025 were both $3,000 or less Tom $5,000 $5,000 $2,000 No: 2026 will be $3,000 or less Notice Lisa: even with a big jump in 2026, she does not have to pay instalments this year. She will still owe the full $6,000 when she files. If her income stays high, she will likely have to start instalments in 2027. If your main source of income is farming or fishing, different rules apply, and you may also have to pay instalments. The four due dates Instalments for individuals are due on: March 15 June 15 September 15 December 15 If a due date falls on a weekend or a public holiday the CRA recognizes, your payment counts as on time if the CRA receives it on the next business day. A few people have different rules: Farmers and fishers whose main income is from self-employment in farming or fishing have one instalment due date each year: December 31 . The CRA sends them a reminder in November. When someone dies, instalments due on or after the date of death do not have to be paid. Tip: Put the four dates in your phone calendar with a reminder a week ahead. Online payments can take a few business days to show up, so don't leave it to the last day. How much to pay: the three options The CRA lets you choose one of three ways to work out your instalments. You can pick the one that gives the lowest payments, as long as you pay on time. Option How it works Best when No-calculation The CRA works out the amounts from your latest assessed return and prints them on your reminder. You just pay those amounts. Your income, deductions and credits stay about the same each year. Prior-year You base the year's total on last year's (2025) return, using the CRA's calculation chart. 2026 looks like 2025, but 2024 was quite different. Current-year You estimate your 2026 net tax owing, plus any CPP contributions and voluntary EI premiums, using the same chart. 2026 will be quite different from both 2025 and 2024, for example if your income dropped. With the prior-year or current-year option, the CRA says it won't charge instalment interest or a penalty if you pay the full amounts by the due dates, unless your figures turn out to be too low. The current-year option carries the most risk: if you underestimate, you can be charged interest on the shortfall. Instalment reminders The CRA sends an instalment reminder (form INNS1) to people it expects will need to pay. The February reminder covers the March and June payments, and the August reminder covers September and December. You can also see them in your CRA account. A reminder is a suggestion, not a bill. If you received a 2026 reminder but your 2026 net tax owing will be $3,000 or less, you don't have to pay 2026 instalments. Example (made-up numbers): Priya earns consulting income and rent from a basement suite. Her net tax owing was about $6,000 in both 2024 and 2025, and she expects about the same in 2026. The no-calculation option is simplest for her: she pays the amounts on her reminders and doesn't need to do any maths. Paying and keeping track You can pay online, using one of the payment options listed on the CRA's website. If you pay in person or by mail, use your instalment remittance voucher (form INNS3), which comes with your reminder, so the money goes to the right account. You can also download a voucher from your CRA account. People who pay by pre-authorized debit don't receive a voucher. The CRA doesn't send a receipt right away, so: keep your own proof of payment, such as your bank confirmation check your CRA account under "Accounts and payments" after about 3 business days for online payments, or 10 business days for cheques and money orders In February, the CRA sends an instalment payment summary (form INNS2) listing what you paid for the year. When you file, you claim your total instalments on line 47600 of your return. If a payment is missing from the summary, add it yourself. If the summary shows a wrong amount, call the CRA at 1-800-959-8281. Watch out: Don't send an instalment as a payment toward last year's balance by mistake. If a payment lands in the wrong place, you can ask the CRA to move it through "Transfer payment(s)" in your CRA account, or by phone. Interest and penalties if you pay late or too little If you were required to pay instalments, received a reminder showing an amount to pay, and then paid late, paid too little or didn't pay, the CRA charges instalment interest . It is calculated at the CRA's prescribed interest rate , which can change every three months and is compounded daily. For October 1 to December 31, 2026, the rate on overdue taxes is 7% . The CRA compares the interest on the payments you should have made with the interest on the payments you actually made. You are charged the difference only if it is more than $25 . The instalment penalty A separate penalty applies only if your instalment interest for the year is more than $1,000 . The CRA takes the higher of $1,000 or 25% of the interest you would have owed if you had paid no instalments at all. It subtracts that from your actual instalment interest and charges half of what is left. Example (made-up numbers): Your actual instalment interest is $3,000. If you had paid nothing, it would have been $8,000. 25% of $8,000 is $2,000, which is higher than $1,000. So: $3,000 minus $2,000 = $1,000, divided by 2 = a $500 penalty. Catching up If you missed a payment, you can reduce the interest by paying your next instalment early or paying more than required. This earns instalment credit interest , which can offset interest charged on late payments for the same year. It isn't refunded to you and can't be used for other years, but it can cut or wipe out the charge. Ways to reduce or avoid instalments The simplest way to stop paying instalments is to have more tax withheld from income that allows it, so your net tax owing drops to $3,000 or less: Old Age Security (OAS): form ISP3520OAS, sent to Service Canada Canada Pension Plan (CPP): form ISP3520CPP, sent to Service Canada Employment Insurance or a workplace pension: form TD1, sent to your employer or pension administrator, asking for extra tax to be deducted Tax can't be withheld from self-employment, investment or rental income, or from capital gains. If that is your main income, instalments are usually the way to go. Example (made-up numbers): A retiree's net tax owing has been $3,500 a year. In January she asks her pension administrator to withhold an extra $250 a month. Her expected net tax owing falls to $500, so she no longer needs to pay instalments and can ignore her reminders. Our retirement income guide covers OAS, CPP and pension income in more detail. Proposed change: Budget 2026 (November 5, 2026) proposes raising the instalment threshold from $3,000 to $7,500 outside Quebec (and from $1,800 to $4,500 in Quebec), indexed to inflation, for tax years starting on or after January 1, 2028. People whose main income is from a business could make one payment by December 31 instead of four. These are proposals only and are not law yet. For 2026 and 2027, the $3,000 rule still applies. See our news article on the proposed May 15 deadline for related changes. Common mistakes and a quick checklist Common mistakes Ignoring reminders because you plan to pay "when I file." Interest builds up from each missed due date. Thinking a reminder is a bill. If your income fell, you may be able to pay less or nothing, using the current-year option. Underestimating with the current-year option. If your figures are too low, you can be charged interest on the shortfall. Forgetting CPP. If you're self-employed, the CPP contributions you owe on that income are part of the instalment calculation. Not claiming payments on line 47600, or not checking the INNS2 summary against your own records. Checklist Check your net tax owing for the last two years on your notices of assessment. Estimate this year's net tax owing. Is it over $3,000? Look for reminders in your CRA account in February and August. Choose the calculation option that suits you. Pay by March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15, and keep proof. If your income changes mid-year, revisit the amount. Claim all instalments on line 47600 when you file. Self-employed? Our guide to self-employed expenses can help lower the tax you owe in the first place. Landlords can see our rental income guide . Not sure if you need to pay instalments? We can look at your last two notices of assessment, estimate this year's tax and tell you which option keeps your payments lowest. Start your T1 form and we'll be in touch. title: WorkSafeBC for small businesses: registering, reporting and paying
description: Who must register with WorkSafeBC, coverage for owners, how premiums work, payroll reporting due dates, clearance letters and penalties, explained simply.
text: Guides · Payroll WorkSafeBC for small businesses: registering, reporting and paying If you hire even one worker in B.C., you need WorkSafeBC coverage. Here's who must register, what it costs, when to report and pay, and how to stay out of trouble with contractors and penalties. By Calcitax Advisors · Updated November 2, 2026 · Figures for 2026 In short If your business hires and pays workers in B.C., full-time, part-time, casual or contract, you must register with WorkSafeBC. Sole proprietors and partners aren't automatically covered; they can buy optional Personal Coverage. Premiums are a rate per $100 of payroll that depends on your industry; the 2026 average base rate is $1.55. Each worker's earnings count only up to $127,500 for 2026 ($130,800 for 2027). Small employers usually report and pay once a year in early March; larger ones report quarterly. Get clearance letters before and after using contractors, and report injuries within three days. On this page What WorkSafeBC is and why it matters Who must register Coverage for you as the owner How to register How premiums are calculated Reporting payroll and paying premiums Penalties and what happens if you don't register Hiring contractors: workers, independent operators and clearance letters When someone gets hurt, and your safety duties Checklist and common mistakes What WorkSafeBC is and why it matters WorkSafeBC is British Columbia's workers' compensation board. Employers pay premiums into a shared insurance system. If a worker is hurt or becomes ill because of their job, WorkSafeBC pays benefits such as health care and wage-loss payments. For a business owner, this means two separate jobs: Insurance: register, report your payroll and pay premiums on time. Health and safety: keep your workplace safe and report injuries and certain incidents. WorkSafeBC is separate from the CRA. Opening a CRA payroll account and paying CPP and EI is a different job from registering with WorkSafeBC and paying its premiums. Who must register The basic rule is simple: if your business hires and pays one or more workers in B.C., you must register for WorkSafeBC coverage. It doesn't matter whether the work is full-time, part-time, casual or on contract. All employers need coverage unless they are exempt. An "employer" can be a self-employed sole proprietor, a partnership, a corporation, a society or another legal entity. Once you are registered, all your workers are covered, including: part-time and casual staff, some contractors who are really working as your workers (see "Hiring contractors" below), and your children, if they work for your business and are paid by it. Some situations people often miss: Your spouse in a sole proprietorship. If your spouse is a paid worker in your proprietorship, WorkSafeBC says they are not covered automatically. You can apply for spousal coverage separately. Owners of a corporation. Shareholders, directors and officers who actively work in their company are treated as workers of that company. The corporation generally needs to be registered so they are covered. If a company that should be registered isn't, and a shareholder is injured, the claim can be rejected. Hiring help at home. Homeowners and renters who hire workers, for example a nanny or caregiver, may also need to register. WorkSafeBC's application covers this case. Not sure? Apply anyway. WorkSafeBC reviews each application and tells you in writing whether you need coverage. If it decides you're not eligible, you'll get a letter explaining why. Coverage for you as the owner Registering your business covers your workers. It may not cover you . Sole proprietors and partners are usually not covered automatically. You can buy optional Personal Coverage (formerly called Personal Optional Protection), whether or not you have workers. Owners of an incorporated company who work in the business can't buy Personal Coverage, because the company is the employer and the owner counts as its worker. Their protection comes through the company's registration. With Personal Coverage you choose a monthly coverage amount. Your monthly premium is that amount multiplied by the premium rate for your type of business. WorkSafeBC's own example: at a 3.87% rate, $3,100 of monthly coverage costs $119.97 a month. If you're injured at work, benefits can include health care, wage-loss payments (generally 90% of the coverage amount you chose, less deductions), rehabilitation and return-to-work help. Coverage starts the day WorkSafeBC receives your completed application, or on a later date you choose. It continues until you or WorkSafeBC cancel it, and it is cancelled if premiums aren't paid on time. WorkSafeBC doesn't mail payment reminders, so pre-authorized payments are a good idea. Why clients may ask: WorkSafeBC warns that if someone hires a contractor who has declined Personal Coverage and that contractor is hurt on the job, the hirer could face a lawsuit. Expect some clients to ask you for proof of coverage. How to register Most businesses apply online through WorkSafeBC's website. You create an online services profile, and the application saves as you go. WorkSafeBC says it takes about 20 minutes, and you get a confirmation number by email. You can also use the paper Employer's Registration Application (Form 1800), but that can be slower. Have this ready: If you are a... You'll typically need Corporation CRA business number, mailing and work site addresses, start date, what you sell with revenue estimates, shareholder details, and estimated payroll Sole proprietor or partnership Owners' legal names, contact details and birthdates, CRA business number, mailing and B.C. work addresses, start date, number of workers, estimated pay, and business vehicles and equipment Homeowner or renter hiring help Your legal name, contact details and birthdate, the start date of your first worker, the B.C. work location and estimated pay WorkSafeBC says it can take about 10 business days to review an application. It recommends applying at least 30 days before you start your business or hire your first worker. Your confirmation letter shows the date your coverage starts and your premium rate. How premiums are calculated Your premium is a rate per $100 of assessable payroll , which is basically the wages you pay to your workers. Your rate depends on your industry. WorkSafeBC sorts businesses into 512 "classification units" of similar businesses, grouped into 55 rate groups. Each group's rate reflects the cost of injuries in that kind of work, so rates differ by industry. The 2026 average base rate is $1.55 per $100 of payroll , unchanged from 2025. Your own rate can be higher or lower. Earnings are capped per worker. WorkSafeBC assesses each person's earnings only up to the maximum wage rate: $127,500 for 2026 and $130,800 for 2027 . Anything a worker earns above that isn't assessable. Assessable payroll includes wages and salaries paid to workers, including what you pay to working shareholders. It also includes payments to contractors who count as your workers and to unregistered subcontractors. Since January 1, 2026, the only tips that count are ones you can verify from your own records, such as tips paid through electronic payments or shown on a T4. You no longer need to track cash tips for WorkSafeBC. A simple illustration: if your industry rate were the 2026 average of $1.55 and your payroll for the year were $100,000, your premium would be about $1,550 ($100,000 ÷ 100 × $1.55). Check your own rate in your WorkSafeBC account. Reporting payroll and paying premiums How often you report depends on the size of your premiums: Annual reporters: employers expecting premiums under $2,000 a year generally report and pay once a year. Quarterly reporters: employers expecting $2,000 or more a year, or in certain industries where quarterly reporting is mandatory, report and pay every three months, then file a year-end reconciliation. Report Covers Due Annual payroll report and payment January–December Early March: one of March 3, 5, 7, 9 or 11. WorkSafeBC emails your date in January. Quarter 1 January–March April 20 Quarter 2 April–June July 20 Quarter 3 July–September October 20 Quarter 4 October–December January 20 Annual reconciliation (quarterly reporters) January–December February 28 You report and pay through WorkSafeBC's employer online services. If you don't have an online account, "Fast File & Pay" handles basic reporting for the current and previous year. You can pay by credit card (up to $10,000 per account every 30 days), direct debit, at your bank (allow five days) or by cheque. It helps to keep your T4 totals, WorkSafeBC payroll report and bookkeeping in step, so the numbers are easy to check. Penalties and what happens if you don't register Late reports or payments can attract a penalty. The minimum penalty is $50. Unpaid balances are charged a 1% overdue penalty each month. Under-reporting payroll or under-paying premiums can mean an 8% penalty. Not registering when you should is against the law. If an uncovered worker (including a shareholder) is injured or becomes ill from work, you could have to pay both the claim costs and the premiums you should have paid. WorkSafeBC reduces or cancels penalties only for extraordinary reasons, so it's far cheaper to register early and file on time. Hiring contractors: workers, independent operators and clearance letters Calling someone a "contractor" doesn't decide how WorkSafeBC sees them. A contractor is likely your worker if they don't run an independent business, for example if they supply only their labour, supply labour plus minor materials, or work regular hours for you on an ongoing basis. In that case you pay premiums for them. A contractor looks more like an independent operator if they have several clients, advertise to the public and bring their own major equipment. Even when you hire a properly registered contractor, you could be liable for premiums tied to their work for you if they fall behind on their WorkSafeBC payments. The protection is a clearance letter : It shows whether the contractor is registered and in good standing. WorkSafeBC recommends getting one before and after the contractor works for you. You can request letters online by the firm's WorkSafeBC account number or exact legal or trade name, for up to 150 firms at once. You can also sign up for email alerts when a contractor's status changes. Before buying another business's assets, contact WorkSafeBC first: if the seller owes premiums, WorkSafeBC may have a lien on those assets. Also remember that a contractor may be registered for their workers but not have Personal Coverage for themselves. WorkSafeBC can't tell you this for privacy reasons, so ask the contractor for proof. When someone gets hurt, and your safety duties Report a workplace injury or illness to WorkSafeBC within three days of the incident. Get the worker to medical care and pay for that transportation. Certain incidents must be reported immediately , even if nobody was hurt, and you must send WorkSafeBC a full investigation report within 30 days. Keep the workplace safe. Employers must follow the Workers Compensation Act and the Occupational Health and Safety Regulation. Tell WorkSafeBC about changes right away , such as closing the business, changing from a proprietorship to a corporation, or new contact details. Incorporating? A change in your legal entity, such as moving from a sole proprietorship to a corporation, is one of the changes WorkSafeBC wants to hear about right away. Checklist and common mistakes Before your first hire Apply to WorkSafeBC at least 30 days before your first worker starts. Decide whether you want Personal Coverage for yourself (sole proprietors and partners). Note your premium rate and whether you're an annual or quarterly reporter. Every year Report payroll and pay by your due date. Cap each worker at the maximum wage rate. Get clearance letters before and after using contractors, and keep copies. Tell WorkSafeBC about business changes. Common mistakes Assuming a CRA payroll account also registers you with WorkSafeBC. Forgetting working shareholders or family members in payroll. Treating workers as contractors to avoid premiums. Paying an unregistered subcontractor without a clearance letter. Reporting injuries late, or not at all. Want help with WorkSafeBC? We can register your business, keep your WorkSafeBC payroll in step with your T4s and bookkeeping, and file your annual or quarterly reports on time.
